# 6.15 VideoFrame Pipeline Philosophy

VideoFrames are the canonical representation of recorded pixels inside TryLipi.

Every downstream subsystem consumes VideoFrames directly or consumes metadata derived from them.

## Golden Rules

1. VideoFrames are immutable after timestamp assignment.
2. VideoFrames always have a single owner.
3. VideoFrames exist only briefly in memory.
4. Preview never modifies VideoFrames.
5. Timeline never stores VideoFrames.
6. AI never owns original VideoFrames.

---

## VideoFrame Pipeline Overview

```text
MediaStreamTrack
      │
TrackProcessor
      │
ReadableStream<VideoFrame>
      │
Capture Worker
      │
Frame Scheduler
 ┌────┼──────────┬─────────────┐
 │    │          │             │
 ▼    ▼          ▼             ▼
Recorder Preview Vision    Diagnostics
```

---

# 6.16 MediaStreamTrackProcessor Runtime

TrackProcessor converts browser capture into VideoFrames.

It is the only supported capture mechanism in Chromium-class browsers.

## Runtime Responsibilities

* Create processor.
* Read frames continuously.
* Detect stream end.
* Detect backpressure.
* Handle cancellation.

---

## Processor Initialization

```text
Video Track
    │
TrackProcessor Created
    │
Reader Created
    │
Read Loop Starts
```

Processor lifetime equals recording lifetime.

---

## Runtime Contract

```typescript
interface VideoTrackProcessorRuntime {

    trackId:string;

    processor:MediaStreamTrackProcessor;

    reader:ReadableStreamDefaultReader<VideoFrame>;

    startedAt:number;

}
```

---

# 6.17 Read Loop Architecture

The read loop continuously consumes frames.

## Read Loop Flow

```text
reader.read()
     │
VideoFrame
     │
Timestamp Validation
     │
Frame Packet Creation
     │
Scheduler Push
     │
Next Read
```

Loop never blocks on AI or rendering.

---

## Read Loop Rules

* Infinite while recording active.
* Cancel immediately on stop.
* Pause during session pause.
* Resume without creating new processor.

---

## Reader States

| State     | Meaning            |
| --------- | ------------------ |
| waiting   | Awaiting frame     |
| received  | Frame available    |
| paused    | Scheduler paused   |
| cancelled | Recording ending   |
| closed    | Processor disposed |

---

# 6.18 ReadableStream Scheduler

ReadableStream is asynchronous.

Capture scheduler controls consumption rate.

## Scheduler Responsibilities

* Pull next frame.
* Respect backpressure.
* Track latency.
* Detect stalled reads.

---

## Read Timing Budget

| Operation            | Budget       |
| -------------------- | ------------ |
| Read frame           | Under 2 ms   |
| Timestamp validation | Under 0.5 ms |
| Packet creation      | Under 0.5 ms |
| Queue insertion      | Under 1 ms   |

Target total: **4 ms per frame**.

---

## Stalled Reader Detection

Reader considered stalled if:

* no frame arrives beyond expected interval.
* track still live.
* heartbeat indicates capture active.

Recovery triggered automatically.

---

# 6.19 VideoFrame Metadata Engine

Every frame receives deterministic metadata.

## Metadata Generation Pipeline

```text
VideoFrame
     │
Extract Native Metadata
     │
Generate Runtime Metadata
     │
Freeze Metadata Object
```

Metadata survives after frame disposal.

---

## Canonical Frame Metadata

```typescript
interface FrameMetadata {

    frameId:string;

    sequence:number;

    timestampUs:number;

    durationUs:number;

    width:number;

    height:number;

    colorSpace:string;

    rotation:number;

}
```

---

## Sequence Numbers

Sequence numbers:

* start at 0.
* increase by one.
* never reused.
* survive crash recovery.

---

# 6.20 Frame Identity Engine

Every frame has globally unique identity.

## Frame ID Format

```text
frm_<session>_<sequence>
```

Example:

```text
frm_cap_172901_00000182
```

Never regenerated.

---

## Identity Rules

Frame IDs appear in:

* diagnostics
* AI metadata
* timeline references
* chunk indexes

But not exported video.

---

# 6.21 Timestamp Validation Engine

Browser timestamps require validation.

## Validation Checks

* monotonic increase
* duration positive
* timestamp not duplicated
* timestamp within expected FPS window

---

## Validation Pipeline

```text
Native Timestamp
      │
Monotonic Validator
      │
Duration Calculator
      │
Runtime Timestamp
```

Invalid timestamps generate diagnostics.

---

## Timestamp Correction Rules

Only permitted correction:

duplicate timestamp → advance by previous frame duration.

Never reorder frames.

---

# 6.22 Frame Ownership Lifecycle

Ownership prevents duplicate memory.

## Ownership Flow

```text
Capture Worker
      │
Transfer
      │
Vision Worker
      │
ImageBitmap
      │
Vision Complete
      │
Frame Released
```

---

## Ownership Contract

```typescript
interface FrameOwnership {

    frameId:string;

    ownerWorker:string;

    transferred:boolean;

}
```

Only one worker owns frame at a time.

---

## Ownership Rules

* Recorder reads before transfer.
* Vision receives transferable.
* Preview never owns original frame.
* Capture Worker closes after transfer.

---

# 6.23 ImageBitmap Conversion Pipeline

ImageBitmap is optimized for worker analysis.

## Conversion Flow

```text
VideoFrame
     │
createImageBitmap()
     │
Transfer ImageBitmap
     │
Vision Worker
```

No pixel copies after conversion.

---

## Bitmap Metadata

```typescript
interface BitmapMetadata {

    bitmapId:string;

    sourceFrameId:string;

    width:number;

    height:number;

}
```

---

## Conversion Rules

Convert only when frame selected for analysis.

Never convert every preview frame.

---

# 6.24 Frame Sampling Strategy

AI does not process every frame.

Sampling saves CPU and tokens.

## Sampling Reasons

* scene change
* cursor click
* scroll stop
* popup opened
* timer interval

---

## Sampling Modes

| Mode             | FPS                |
| ---------------- | ------------------ |
| Idle screen      | 5 FPS              |
| Recording        | 15–20 FPS          |
| Fast interaction | Event-driven burst |
| Export analysis  | Configurable       |

---

## Burst Sampling

```text
Click
 │
Frame-1
Frame-2
Frame-3
Frame-4
```

Captures context around important interactions.

---

# 6.25 High-FPS Recording Architecture

TryLipi supports displays above 60 Hz.

## Recording Modes

| Display | Recording             |
| ------- | --------------------- |
| 60 Hz   | 60 FPS                |
| 90 Hz   | 90 FPS (if supported) |
| 120 Hz  | 120 FPS (future flag) |

Preview may run lower.

---

## High-FPS Pipeline

```text
120 FPS Capture
        │
Recorder (120 FPS)
        │
Preview Scheduler
        │
60 FPS Preview
```

Recording and preview become independent.

---

## Adaptive Preview Decimation

Preview shows every second frame when recording exceeds preview budget.

Timeline timestamps remain unchanged.

---

# 6.26 Frame Decimation Engine

Preview frame skipping is deterministic.

## Decimation Example

```text
Captured

1 2 3 4 5 6

Preview

1   3   5
```

Recorder still stores all frames.

---

## Decimation Rules

* Never skip recorder frames.
* Never skip AI event frames.
* Skip only preview display frames.

---

# 6.27 Capture Backpressure

Capture can outrun consumers.

Backpressure protects memory.

## Backpressure Pipeline

```text
Frames Produced
      │
Queue Occupancy
      │
Threshold Reached
      │
Scheduler Intervention
```

---

## Threshold Levels

| Occupancy | Action             |
| --------- | ------------------ |
| Under 50% | Normal             |
| 50–75%    | Warning            |
| 75–90%    | Preview decimation |
| Above 90% | Pause AI sampling  |

---

## Capture Queue Rules

Recorder queue never discards frames.

Preview queue may discard oldest preview requests.

---

# 6.28 Frame Validation Engine

Frames are validated before scheduling.

## Validation Checklist

* dimensions present
* timestamp valid
* sequence valid
* duration computed
* ownership free

---

## Invalid Frame Policy

If frame invalid:

* log diagnostics
* discard frame
* continue recording
* increment dropped-frame metric

Recording session continues.

---

# 6.29 Frame Checkpoint Engine

Frames periodically generate checkpoints for recovery.

## Checkpoint Frequency

Every:

* 300 frames, or
* 5 seconds

whichever occurs first.

---

## Checkpoint Metadata

```typescript
interface FrameCheckpoint {

    checkpointId:string;

    lastFrameId:string;

    lastSequence:number;

    timestampUs:number;

}
```

---

## Recovery Rules

Restart resumes from latest checkpoint.

Sequence numbers continue.

No duplicate frames created.

---

# 6.30 Frame Statistics Engine

Capture Worker continuously records statistics.

## Metrics

* received frames
* dropped frames
* duplicate timestamps
* average latency
* queue occupancy

---

## Statistics Contract

```typescript
interface CaptureFrameStats {

    framesCaptured:number;

    framesDropped:number;

    duplicateTimestamps:number;

    averageLatencyMs:number;

}
```

Used only for diagnostics.

---

# 6.31 Read Loop Shutdown

Stopping recording must terminate read loop cleanly.

## Shutdown Pipeline

```text
Stop Requested
      │
Cancel Reader
      │
Drain Queue
      │
Flush Chunks
      │
Close Frames
      │
Dispose Processor
```

No dangling VideoFrames.

---

## Shutdown Guarantees

* reader cancelled
* processor released
* queue empty
* frame pool empty

---

# 6.32 Acceptance Tests

## Processor Tests

* TrackProcessor starts.
* Reader produces frames.
* Reader stops cleanly.

## Metadata Tests

* Sequence increments.
* Timestamp monotonic.
* Metadata frozen.

## Sampling Tests

* Burst sampling after click.
* Idle sampling reduced.
* Event-driven sampling works.

## High-FPS Tests

* 120 FPS recording.
* 60 FPS preview.
* Timeline preserved.

## Backpressure Tests

* AI paused first.
* Preview decimation active.
* Recorder queue lossless.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 6.2)

1. TrackProcessor is the canonical VideoFrame source.
2. Read loop is scheduler-controlled.
3. VideoFrame metadata is immutable.
4. Every frame has globally unique identity.
5. Timestamp validation occurs before scheduling.
6. ImageBitmap conversion is analysis-only.
7. High-FPS capture is independent from preview FPS.
8. Preview frame decimation never affects recording.
9. Recorder queue is lossless.
10. Frame checkpoints enable deterministic recovery.

---

# 6.33 Audio Engine Philosophy

Audio is recorded independently from video.

Synchronization happens through timestamps rather than shared clocks.

The Audio Engine guarantees deterministic playback regardless of browser jitter.

## Golden Audio Rules

1. Audio timestamps are immutable.
2. System audio and microphone remain separate tracks internally.
3. Mixing occurs after recording, not during capture.
4. Drift correction never modifies original audio packets.
5. Lip sync uses timestamp metadata, not wall-clock time.
6. Audio processing never blocks recording.

---

## Audio Responsibilities

* Capture system audio.
* Capture microphone.
* Produce AudioData packets.
* Timestamp packets.
* Detect drift.
* Mix tracks for preview.
* Preserve independent tracks for export.

---

# 6.34 End-to-End Audio Pipeline

Audio flows independently through dedicated workers.

```text id="p0xg5e"
System Audio Track
        │
TrackProcessor
        │
AudioData
        │
Audio Scheduler
        │
Audio Chunk Buffer
        │
Storage

Microphone Track
        │
TrackProcessor
        │
AudioData
        │
Audio Scheduler
```

Preview mixer consumes both streams.

---

## Audio Pipeline Separation

| Pipeline  | Purpose                      |
| --------- | ---------------------------- |
| Recording | Immutable audio chunks       |
| Preview   | Live monitoring              |
| Export    | Final synchronized mix       |
| AI        | Voice transcription (future) |

No pipeline mutates another.

---

# 6.35 AudioContext Graph

AudioContext powers preview playback and monitoring.

It is **not** the recording source.

## Graph Overview

```text id="yy4i0q"
System Audio Source
          │
          ▼
GainNode
          │
          ▼
Preview Mixer
          │
          ▼
Destination

Microphone Source
          │
          ▼
GainNode
          │
          ▼
Preview Mixer
```

Recording bypasses AudioContext.

---

## Graph Responsibilities

* Preview monitoring.
* Mute/unmute.
* Volume sliders.
* Live waveform generation.
* Peak meter.

---

## AudioContext Lifecycle

```text id="jbuw9h"
User Starts Recording
         │
AudioContext Created
         │
Audio Nodes Connected
         │
Preview Active
         │
Recording Ends
         │
Context Closed
```

Created only after user gesture.

---

# 6.36 AudioData Processing Pipeline

AudioData replaces raw PCM as canonical runtime audio representation.

## Pipeline

```text id="gjwkt4"
MediaStreamTrack
       │
TrackProcessor
       │
ReadableStream<AudioData>
       │
Audio Scheduler
       │
Chunk Encoder
```

---

## Audio Packet Contract

```typescript id="ddgdt0"
interface AudioPacket {

    packetId:string;

    timestampUs:number;

    durationUs:number;

    sampleRate:number;

    channels:number;

    trackId:string;

}
```

Packets are immutable.

---

## Packet Lifetime

1. Created.
2. Timestamped.
3. Scheduled.
4. Stored.
5. Released.

No packet reused.

---

# 6.37 System Audio Capture Engine

System audio originates from browser capture.

## Supported Sources

* Browser tab.
* Entire screen.
* Window (browser dependent).

---

## System Audio Validation

Immediately validate:

* audio track exists
* sample rate available
* channel count available
* readyState `"live"`

---

## System Audio Metadata

```typescript id="2rq6lc"
interface SystemAudioMetadata {

    trackId:string;

    sampleRate:number;

    channels:number;

    latencyMs:number;

}
```

---

## System Audio Failure Policy

If unavailable:

* Continue recording.
* Keep microphone active if enabled.
* Emit capability warning.

No recording cancellation.

---

# 6.38 Microphone Capture Engine

Microphone capture is optional.

## Pipeline

```text id="e2v6o9"
Microphone
     │
MediaStreamTrack
     │
TrackProcessor
     │
AudioData
```

Separate timestamp stream.

---

## Microphone Metadata

```typescript id="x8m0w5"
interface MicrophoneMetadata {

    deviceId:string;

    sampleRate:number;

    channels:number;

}
```

---

## Device Switching

Future feature:

* switch microphone without ending recording.
* timeline event inserted.
* new audio track begins.

---

# 6.39 Multi-Track Audio Architecture

Audio tracks remain independent.

## Internal Topology

```text id="bhxkyp"
Audio Engine
│
├── System Track
├── Microphone Track
└── Future Voice Track
```

Unlimited future track support.

---

## Track Registry

```typescript id="mni7ub"
interface AudioTrackRegistry {

    tracks:Map<string, AudioTrackMetadata>;

}
```

Used by export mixer.

---

# 6.40 Audio Mixing Engine

Preview requires mixing.

Recording does not.

## Preview Mixing Graph

```text id="tgb0p1"
System Audio
      │
GainNode
      │
      ▼
Preview Mixer
      ▲
GainNode
      │
Microphone
```

Live preview only.

---

## Export Mixing Graph

```text id="kp4nqs"
System Track
      │
Volume Automation
      │
Mixer
      │
Limiter
      │
Master Track
```

Microphone mixed later.

---

## Mixer Rules

* Preserve independent tracks.
* Apply gain automation.
* Apply mute automation.
* No destructive edits.

---

# 6.41 Gain Automation

Volume changes become timeline events.

## Gain Event

```typescript id="sjitj5"
interface GainAutomationEvent {

    trackId:string;

    timestampUs:number;

    gain:number;

}
```

Export reproduces automation.

---

## Gain Rules

Range:

0.0 → 2.0

Default:

1.0

Stored in timeline.

---

# 6.42 Audio Timestamp Engine

Audio timestamps are authoritative.

## Timestamp Sources

* AudioData.timestamp
* Sample count
* Packet duration

Never use playback clock.

---

## Timestamp Validation

Checks:

* monotonic increase
* duration positive
* packet overlap
* packet gap

---

## Timestamp Contract

```typescript id="zzs1u4"
interface AudioTimestampMetadata {

    packetId:string;

    timestampUs:number;

    durationUs:number;

}
```

---

# 6.43 Drift Detection Engine

Video and audio clocks drift over time.

TryLipi measures drift continuously.

## Drift Pipeline

```text id="lqnl9l"
Video Timestamp
      │
Drift Comparator
      │
Audio Timestamp
      │
Offset History
```

---

## Drift Window

Target maximum drift:

**±2 ms**

Warning threshold:

5 ms.

Critical threshold:

20 ms.

---

## Drift Metadata

```typescript id="4xlfys"
interface DriftMeasurement {

    timestampUs:number;

    offsetUs:number;

    confidence:number;

}
```

Stored separately from media.

---

# 6.44 Drift Correction Strategy

Correction happens during playback/export.

Never modify recorded packets.

## Correction Pipeline

```text id="cklajw"
Recorded Audio
      │
Drift Metadata
      │
Playback Offset
      │
Synchronized Output
```

---

## Correction Rules

Allowed:

* playback offset
* resynchronization marker

Not allowed:

* rewrite packets
* change timestamps
* resample recorded audio

---

# 6.45 Sample Rate Conversion

Internal canonical sample rate:

**48,000 Hz**

---

## Supported Inputs

| Input    | Internal   |
| -------- | ---------- |
| 44.1 kHz | Convert    |
| 48 kHz   | Native     |
| 96 kHz   | Downsample |

---

## Conversion Pipeline

```text id="x2fvyu"
Input Samples
      │
Resampler
      │
48 kHz Audio Packets
```

Conversion occurs only once.

---

## Resampler Rules

* High-quality linear interpolation.
* Preserve timestamps.
* Preserve duration.

---

# 6.46 AudioWorklet Runtime

AudioWorklet powers realtime preview processing.

## Responsibilities

* waveform
* peak meter
* monitoring
* noise visualization
* clipping detection

---

## Worklet Lifecycle

```text id="tkjwj1"
AudioContext
     │
AudioWorklet Module
     │
Processor
     │
Preview Metrics
```

Recording bypasses worklet.

---

## Worklet Contract

```typescript id="slyfvc"
interface AudioWorkletRuntime {

    processorName:string;

    initialized:boolean;

}
```

---

# 6.47 Audio Monitoring Engine

Preview includes monitoring tools.

## Metrics

* RMS level
* Peak level
* Clipping
* Silence detection
* Latency

---

## Peak Meter Pipeline

```text id="vqjxss"
Audio Samples
      │
Peak Analyzer
      │
Meter Values
```

UI only.

---

## Silence Detection

Useful for AI chapters later.

Rules:

Silence longer than configurable threshold becomes metadata event.

---

# 6.48 Lip Sync Engine

Lip sync is guaranteed through timestamps.

## Synchronization Pipeline

```text id="6hlsit"
Video Timestamp
      │
Sync Resolver
      │
Audio Timestamp
      │
Output Offset
```

---

## Lip Sync Rules

* Never use frame count.
* Never use playback position.
* Use timestamp alignment only.

---

## Sync Metadata

```typescript id="0hl0ig"
interface LipSyncMetadata {

    videoTimestampUs:number;

    audioTimestampUs:number;

    offsetUs:number;

}
```

---

# 6.49 Pause & Resume Synchronization

Pause affects clocks.

## Pause Pipeline

```text id="j0uuln"
Pause
  │
Pause Marker
  │
Resume
  │
Offset Marker
```

Timeline stores markers.

---

## Resume Rules

* Preserve timestamps.
* Resume packet sequence.
* Maintain sync metadata.

---

## Pause Event Contract

```typescript id="mnpifb"
interface AudioPauseMarker {

    pausedAt:number;

    resumedAt:number;

}
```

---

# 6.50 Audio Recovery

Microphone or system audio may disappear.

## Recovery Flow

```text id="h4ixuq"
Track Ended
     │
Observer Detects
     │
Attempt Restart
     │
New Track
     │
Timeline Marker
```

---

## Recovery Rules

* New track ID.
* Preserve session.
* Preserve timestamps.
* Insert recovery event.

---

# 6.51 Audio Statistics Engine

Audio Worker produces diagnostics.

## Metrics

* packets captured
* packets dropped
* average latency
* drift measurements
* clipping events

---

## Statistics Contract

```typescript id="8jfrhn"
interface AudioRuntimeStats {

    packetsCaptured:number;

    packetsDropped:number;

    averageLatencyMs:number;

    clippingEvents:number;

}
```

---

1. Audio packets are immutable.
2. Recording never mixes audio tracks destructively.
3. AudioContext is preview-only.
4. Internal sample rate is 48 kHz.
5. Drift detection is continuous.
6. Drift correction never rewrites recorded packets.
7. AudioWorklet powers monitoring only.
8. Lip sync uses timestamp metadata exclusively.
9. Pause/resume inserts synchronization markers.
10. Audio recovery creates new tracks without corrupting recording.

# 6.53 Recording Chunk Philosophy

The Capture Engine never stores one giant recording file.

Instead it stores a sequence of immutable recording chunks.

Every chunk is independently recoverable, checksum verified, timestamp indexed, and replayable.

## Golden Chunk Rules

1. Chunks are immutable after writing.
2. Chunks are append-only.
3. Chunk timestamps never overlap.
4. Chunk IDs are globally unique within a session.
5. Recording can recover from the latest completed chunk.

---

## Why Chunks Instead of One File

Problems with one continuous file:

* Browser crashes lose entire recording.
* Memory grows continuously.
* IndexedDB writes become expensive.
* Export restart becomes impossible.

Chunks solve all four problems.

---

# 6.54 Immutable Chunk Architecture

Recording is divided into sequential media chunks.

## Chunk Topology

```text
Capture Session
│
├── Chunk 0001
├── Chunk 0002
├── Chunk 0003
├── Chunk 0004
└── Chunk N
```

Chunks are ordered by timestamp, not write time.

---

## Chunk Contract

```typescript
interface RecordingChunk {

    chunkId:string;

    sessionId:string;

    sequence:number;

    startTimestampUs:number;

    endTimestampUs:number;

    durationUs:number;

    checksum:string;

}
```

---

## Chunk Identity

Format:

```text
chk_<session>_<sequence>
```

Example:

```text
chk_cap172901_000042
```

Never reused.

---

# 6.55 Chunk Creation Strategy

Chunks are created continuously during recording.

## Default Chunk Policy

| Condition                | Create Chunk      |
| ------------------------ | ----------------- |
| Every 5 seconds          | Yes               |
| Memory threshold reached | Yes               |
| Pause recording          | Flush chunk       |
| Surface switch           | Flush chunk       |
| Stop recording           | Flush final chunk |

---

## Chunk Lifecycle

```text
Collect Frames
      │
Chunk Open
      │
Append Frames
      │
Append Audio
      │
Finalize Metadata
      │
Checksum
      │
Persist
```

After persistence, chunk becomes immutable.

---

# 6.56 Chunk Encoder Pipeline

Chunk encoder converts packets into persistent storage format.

## Pipeline

```text
VideoFrame Packets
        │
Audio Packets
        │
Chunk Builder
        │
Encoded Chunk
        │
Storage Queue
```

Encoding never blocks capture.

---

## Chunk Builder Responsibilities

* Append video packets.
* Append audio packets.
* Track timestamps.
* Track packet counts.
* Generate checksum.

---

## Chunk Metadata

```typescript
interface ChunkMetadata {

    videoPacketCount:number;

    audioPacketCount:number;

    firstFrameId:string;

    lastFrameId:string;

}
```

---

# 6.57 Chunk Buffer Engine

ChunkBuilder owns temporary buffers.

## Buffers

```text
ChunkBuilder
│
├── Video Packet Buffer
├── Audio Packet Buffer
├── Metadata Buffer
└── Checksum Buffer
```

Buffers cleared immediately after persistence.

---

## Buffer Limits

| Buffer        | Limit            |
| ------------- | ---------------- |
| Video Packets | One active chunk |
| Audio Packets | One active chunk |
| Metadata      | One active chunk |

Memory never accumulates previous chunks.

---

# 6.58 Storage Queue Architecture

Writing storage happens asynchronously.

## Queue Pipeline

```text
Chunk Finalized
      │
Storage Queue
      │
IndexedDB Writer
      │
Verification
      │
Commit
```

Capture never waits for disk writes.

---

## Queue Priorities

1. Chunk writes.
2. Manifest updates.
3. Checkpoints.
4. Diagnostics.

Chunk persistence has highest priority.

---

# 6.59 IndexedDB Storage Engine

IndexedDB stores every chunk independently.

## Database Layout

```text
trylipi-recordings/

├── chunks/

├── manifests/

├── checkpoints/

├── thumbnails/

└── diagnostics/
```

Separate object stores improve recovery.

---

## Chunk Object Store

Primary key:

```text
chunkId
```

Indexes:

* sessionId
* sequence
* timestamp
* duration

---

## Chunk Storage Contract

```typescript
interface ChunkStorageRecord {

    chunkId:string;

    blob:Blob;

    metadata:ChunkMetadata;

}
```

---

# 6.60 Recording Manifest

Manifest represents complete recording.

## Manifest Responsibilities

* List chunks.
* Track timeline version.
* Track checkpoints.
* Track session metadata.

---

## Manifest Structure

```text
manifest.json

session.json

chunks[]

checkpoints[]

version
```

---

## Manifest Contract

```typescript
interface RecordingManifest {

    sessionId:string;

    chunkCount:number;

    durationUs:number;

    timelineVersion:number;

}
```

Manifest updates after every committed chunk.

---

# 6.61 Manifest Update Strategy

Manifest updates are append-only.

## Update Pipeline

```text
Chunk Commit
     │
Manifest Append
     │
Checkpoint Update
     │
Flush Metadata
```

Manifest never rewrites previous entries.

---

## Manifest Recovery Rules

If latest manifest corrupted:

* Read previous manifest.
* Replay chunk directory.
* Regenerate manifest.

---

# 6.62 Checkpoint Engine

Checkpoints protect long recordings.

## Checkpoint Frequency

Every:

* 5 seconds.
* Pause.
* Surface switch.
* Browser visibility loss.

---

## Checkpoint Contents

```typescript
interface RecordingCheckpoint {

    checkpointId:string;

    lastChunkId:string;

    timelineVersion:number;

    playbackTimestampUs:number;

}
```

---

## Checkpoint Topology

```text
Recording
│
├── Checkpoint 1
├── Checkpoint 2
├── Checkpoint 3
└── Latest
```

Only latest checkpoint needed for recovery.

---

# 6.63 Crash Recovery Pipeline

Recovery begins immediately on application restart.

## Recovery Flow

```text
Browser Restart
      │
Find Manifest
      │
Verify Checkpoints
      │
Verify Chunks
      │
Reconstruct Recording
      │
Restore Timeline
```

---

## Recovery Stages

| Stage               | Purpose           |
| ------------------- | ----------------- |
| Manifest Scan       | Locate session.   |
| Checksum Validation | Verify integrity. |
| Chunk Replay        | Recover timeline. |
| Session Restore     | Resume editing.   |

---

## Recovery Guarantees

* Preserve chunks.
* Preserve timestamps.
* Preserve sequence numbers.
* Preserve timeline.

---

# 6.64 Checksum Verification Engine

Every chunk is checksum validated.

## Validation Pipeline

```text
Stored Chunk
      │
Hash Blob
      │
Compare Stored Checksum
      │
Integrity Result
```

---

## Integrity States

| State     | Meaning          |
| --------- | ---------------- |
| Valid     | Safe             |
| Corrupted | Isolate          |
| Missing   | Recover previous |
| Partial   | Attempt repair   |

---

## Checksum Contract

```typescript
interface ChunkChecksum {

    algorithm:"SHA-256";

    hash:string;

}
```

---

# 6.65 Replay Engine

Replay reconstructs recording deterministically.

## Replay Pipeline

```text
Manifest
    │
Chunk Loader
    │
Timestamp Sort
    │
Replay Scheduler
    │
Timeline Frames
```

---

## Replay Rules

* Never reorder timestamps.
* Never interpolate missing chunks.
* Respect pause markers.
* Respect surface switches.

---

## Replay Metadata

```typescript
interface ReplayPacket {

    chunkId:string;

    startTimestampUs:number;

    endTimestampUs:number;

}
```

---

# 6.66 Long Recording Strategy

Support recordings lasting many hours.

## Long Recording Policies

* Constant memory.
* Chunk rotation.
* Checkpoint rotation.
* Thumbnail sampling independent.

---

## Resource Rotation

```text
Recording
 │
Chunk Rotation
 │
Checkpoint Rotation
 │
Thumbnail Rotation
```

Older runtime buffers released continuously.

---

## Target Recording Durations

| Duration | Supported    |
| -------- | ------------ |
| 30 min   | Yes          |
| 2 hours  | Yes          |
| 6 hours  | Yes          |
| 8+ hours | Designed for |

Only storage size limits recording.

---

# 6.67 Storage Integrity Verification

Verification runs in background.

## Verification Checks

* Missing chunk IDs.
* Duplicate sequence numbers.
* Timestamp overlap.
* Timestamp gaps.
* Corrupted blobs.

---

## Integrity Report

```typescript
interface RecordingIntegrityReport {

    missingChunks:number;

    corruptedChunks:number;

    duplicateSequences:number;

    timestampGaps:number;

}
```

---

## Repair Strategy

Allowed repairs:

* regenerate manifest.
* rebuild indexes.
* restore checkpoint.

Never rewrite chunk payloads.

---

# 6.68 Chunk Garbage Collection

Temporary runtime buffers removed after commit.

## Garbage Collection Pipeline

```text
Chunk Persisted
      │
Release VideoFrames
      │
Release Audio Buffers
      │
Release Metadata Buffers
```

Persistent chunks remain untouched.

---

## GC Rules

* No active chunk deleted.
* No committed chunk rewritten.
* Runtime buffers reclaimed immediately.

---

# 6.69 Storage Flush Strategy

Flush prevents data loss.

## Flush Triggers

* Every committed chunk.
* Pause recording.
* Browser hidden.
* Before unload.
* Stop recording.

---

## Flush Guarantees

* Chunk committed.
* Manifest committed.
* Checkpoint committed.

Only then acknowledge flush completion.

---

# 6.70 Session Finalization

Recording finalization produces immutable project.

## Finalization Pipeline

```text
Stop Recording
      │
Flush Chunk
      │
Write Manifest
      │
Write Final Checkpoint
      │
Close Session
```

Session becomes read-only.

---

## Final Session Metadata

```typescript
interface FinalRecordingSession {

    sessionId:string;

    completed:boolean;

    chunkCount:number;

    totalDurationUs:number;

}
```

---

# 6.71 Definition of Done

Capture Engine is complete only if:

### Recording

* Capture session implemented.
* Timestamp engine implemented.
* Chunk builder implemented.

### Storage

* IndexedDB stores immutable chunks.
* Manifest updates append-only.
* Checkpoints implemented.

### Recovery

* Crash recovery implemented.
* Replay implemented.
* Integrity verification implemented.

### Long Recording

* Constant memory behavior.
* Chunk rotation.
* Checkpoint rotation.

---

# 6.72 Canonical Acceptance Checklist

## Chunk Tests

* Chunks rotate every 5 seconds.
* Checksums generated.
* Metadata persisted.

## Manifest Tests

* Chunk list correct.
* Duration correct.
* Timeline version preserved.

## Recovery Tests

* Browser crash restores recording.
* Missing manifest regenerated.
* Corrupted chunk isolated.

## Replay Tests

* Replay timestamps deterministic.
* Pause markers preserved.
* Surface switches preserved.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 6.4)

1. Recording is stored as immutable chunks.
2. Chunk IDs are globally unique.
3. Manifest is append-only.
4. Checkpoints enable crash recovery.
5. Replay is timestamp-driven.
6. Checksums validate every chunk.
7. Long recordings use constant memory.
8. Storage queue never blocks capture.
9. Session finalization makes recording immutable.
10. Capture Engine guarantees deterministic recovery after crashes.

1. Zero-Copy Philosophy
2. Memory Architecture Overview
3. Memory Ownership Model

# 7.1 Zero-Copy Philosophy

Modern browsers are capable of handling enormous amounts of video data—but only if memory copies are minimized.

The biggest performance killer in browser video applications is **copying pixels**.

TryLipi is built around a **Zero-Copy Memory Architecture**, meaning pixels travel between workers using ownership transfer instead of cloning whenever possible.

## Golden Memory Rules

1. Pixels are transferred, not copied.
2. VideoFrames have exactly one owner.
3. ImageBitmaps are transferables.
4. Shared memory is used for metadata—not video pixels.
5. Buffers are reused instead of recreated.
6. Memory allocation during recording should approach zero after warm-up.

---

## Why Zero-Copy Matters

A single uncompressed 4K RGBA frame is approximately **33 MB**.

At **60 FPS**, copying every frame once would move nearly **2 GB/sec** through JavaScript memory.

That is unsustainable for long recordings.

Zero-copy keeps the browser responsive.

---

# 7.2 Memory Architecture Overview

Memory inside TryLipi is divided into isolated domains.

```text
Browser Memory
│
├── Capture Domain
│     ├── VideoFrames
│     ├── AudioData
│     └── Track Buffers
│
├── Shared Runtime Domain
│     ├── SharedArrayBuffers
│     ├── Ring Buffers
│     └── Atomic State
│
├── Rendering Domain
│     ├── GPU Textures
│     ├── ImageBitmaps
│     └── OffscreenCanvas
│
├── AI Domain
│     ├── Downscaled Bitmaps
│     ├── OCR Buffers
│     └── Gemini Payload Buffers
│
└── Storage Domain
      ├── Chunk Buffers
      ├── IndexedDB Writer Queue
      └── Checkpoints
```

Each domain owns different memory types.

---

## Memory Ownership Principle

No memory object belongs to two domains simultaneously.

Ownership is always explicit.

---

# 7.3 Memory Ownership Model

Ownership determines who is responsible for releasing memory.

## Ownership States

| State       | Description                   |
| ----------- | ----------------------------- |
| Created     | Object allocated.             |
| Owned       | Worker currently owns object. |
| Transferred | Ownership moved.              |
| Released    | Object disposed.              |

Objects never return to a previous owner.

---

## Ownership Lifecycle

```text
Capture Worker
      │
Owns VideoFrame
      │
Transfer
      │
Vision Worker
      │
ImageBitmap Created
      │
Release VideoFrame
      │
Transfer Bitmap
      │
Dispose Bitmap
```

Ownership always flows forward.

---

## Ownership Contract

```typescript
interface MemoryOwner {

    objectId:string;

    ownerWorker:string;

    createdAt:number;

    transferred:boolean;

    released:boolean;

}
```

Used only for diagnostics.

---

# 7.4 Memory Domains

Every runtime subsystem receives its own memory domain.

## Capture Domain

Owns:

* MediaStreams.
* VideoFrames.
* AudioData.
* Timestamp metadata.

Lifetime equals recording session.

---

## Rendering Domain

Owns:

* GPU textures.
* OffscreenCanvas.
* WebGL framebuffers.
* ImageBitmaps.

Lifetime equals preview session.

---

## AI Domain

Owns:

* Downscaled bitmaps.
* OCR tensors.
* Gemini payload buffers.

Lifetime measured in milliseconds.

---

## Storage Domain

Owns:

* Chunk buffers.
* Manifest buffers.
* IndexedDB transactions.

Persistent storage only.

---

# 7.5 SharedArrayBuffer Runtime

SharedArrayBuffer is the foundation of low-latency communication.

It is **never** used to store raw video pixels.

## Why SharedArrayBuffer Exists

SharedArrayBuffer enables:

* scheduler queues
* worker state
* timestamps
* cursor metadata
* performance counters

Without serialization.

---

## Shared Runtime Layout

```text
SharedArrayBuffer
│
├── Scheduler State
├── Queue Head/Tail
├── Atomic Flags
├── Performance Metrics
├── Cursor Metadata
└── Runtime Health
```

Pixels remain outside SAB.

---

## Shared Memory Rules

1. Metadata only.
2. No Blob storage.
3. No VideoFrames.
4. No ImageBitmaps.
5. Access through Atomics.

---

# 7.6 Shared Memory Coordinator

A dedicated coordinator initializes shared memory.

Responsibilities:

* Allocate SAB.
* Initialize typed arrays.
* Share references with workers.
* Version shared schema.

---

## Shared Runtime Contract

```typescript
interface SharedRuntimeMemory {

    schedulerBuffer:SharedArrayBuffer;

    metricsBuffer:SharedArrayBuffer;

    cursorBuffer:SharedArrayBuffer;

}
```

Workers receive references during startup.

---

## Shared Memory Versioning

Every shared layout has a schema version.

```typescript
interface SharedMemoryHeader {

    version:number;

    byteLength:number;

}
```

Prevents incompatible worker layouts.

---

# 7.7 Ring Buffer Philosophy

Ring Buffers provide lock-free communication between workers.

They replace message queues for high-frequency metadata.

## Why Ring Buffers

Advantages:

* Constant memory.
* No array reallocations.
* Lock-free reads.
* Lock-free writes.

Ideal for 60 FPS scheduling.

---

## Ring Buffer Layout

```text
SharedArrayBuffer
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ Head │ Tail │ Data Region   │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

Data wraps around.

---

## Ring Buffer Guarantees

* Fixed capacity.
* FIFO ordering.
* O(1) enqueue.
* O(1) dequeue.

---

# 7.8 Scheduler Ring Buffer

Scheduler uses ring buffers for lightweight metadata.

## Stored Metadata

* frame sequence
* timestamp
* worker destination
* queue priority

No pixel payloads.

---

## Metadata Packet

```typescript
interface SchedulerRingPacket {

    sequence:number;

    timestampUs:number;

    destination:number;

    priority:number;

}
```

Packet size intentionally small.

---

## Capacity Strategy

| Buffer         | Capacity     |
| -------------- | ------------ |
| Capture Queue  | 512 packets  |
| Vision Queue   | 256 packets  |
| Timeline Queue | 512 packets  |
| Metrics Queue  | 1024 packets |

Capacity never grows dynamically.

---

# 7.9 Atomic Operations

Ring buffers use Atomics for synchronization.

## Atomic Fields

* head
* tail
* state flags
* queue size
* worker heartbeat

---

## Atomic Guarantees

* Wait-free reads.
* Wait-free writes.
* Visibility across workers.

No mutexes.

---

## Runtime State Flags

```typescript
enum RuntimeAtomicFlag {

    RECORDING=1,

    PAUSED=2,

    STOPPING=3,

    RECOVERING=4

}
```

Shared across coordinator and workers.

---

# 7.10 Transferable Object Strategy

Transferables avoid cloning.

## Primary Transferables

| Object          | Transferable |
| --------------- | ------------ |
| VideoFrame      | Yes          |
| ImageBitmap     | Yes          |
| ArrayBuffer     | Yes          |
| OffscreenCanvas | Yes          |

Ownership moves between workers.

---

## Transfer Pipeline

```text
Capture Worker
      │
Transfer VideoFrame
      │
Vision Worker
      │
Create ImageBitmap
      │
Transfer Bitmap
```

No structured clone for pixels.

---

## Transfer Rules

1. Sender loses ownership immediately.
2. Receiver becomes sole owner.
3. Sender must not access transferred object.

---

# 7.11 VideoFrame Ownership Rules

VideoFrames have strict lifecycle rules.

## Lifecycle

```text
Created
 │
Timestamped
 │
Scheduled
 │
Transferred
 │
Consumed
 │
Closed
```

Every frame must reach **Closed**.

---

## Close Policy

`VideoFrame.close()` is mandatory.

Failure is treated as memory leak.

---

## Leak Conditions

A VideoFrame is leaked if:

* not closed,
* retained after transfer,
* stored in array beyond scheduler lifetime.

Diagnostics detect all three.

---

# 7.12 ImageBitmap Ownership Rules

ImageBitmaps exist for rendering and AI.

## Bitmap Lifecycle

```text
VideoFrame
    │
ImageBitmap
    │
Worker Rendering
    │
Release Bitmap
```

Bitmap lifetime should be under one render frame whenever possible.

---

## Bitmap Rules

* Never persist.
* Never store in IndexedDB.
* Never attach to timeline.
* Dispose immediately after use.

---

# 7.13 Memory Pool Philosophy

Repeated allocations trigger garbage collection.

TryLipi uses reusable memory pools.

## Pool Categories

| Pool                   | Objects          |
| ---------------------- | ---------------- |
| Video Packet Pool      | Metadata packets |
| Audio Packet Pool      | Audio metadata   |
| Bitmap Descriptor Pool | Bitmap metadata  |
| Timeline Packet Pool   | Timeline packets |

Pools contain metadata, not pixels.

---

## Pool Lifecycle

```text
Allocate Pool
      │
Acquire Object
      │
Use Object
      │
Reset Object
      │
Return To Pool
```

Objects are recycled.

---

# 7.14 Worker Memory Isolation

Each worker has independent heap memory.

## Worker Isolation Rules

* Capture Worker cannot access Vision heap.
* Vision Worker cannot access Timeline heap.
* Export Worker isolated entirely.

Communication uses transferables and shared metadata.

---

## Isolation Diagram

```text
Capture Heap

Vision Heap

Timeline Heap

Export Heap
```

No shared heap except SharedArrayBuffer metadata.

---

# 7.15 Memory Budget Targets

Memory budgets are defined before implementation.

## Target Budgets

| Component       | Target Budget |
| --------------- | ------------- |
| Capture Worker  | 120 MB        |
| Preview Worker  | 180 MB        |
| Vision Worker   | 150 MB        |
| Timeline Worker | 80 MB         |
| AI Worker       | 150 MB        |
| Storage Worker  | 100 MB        |

These are runtime targets, not hard limits.

---

## Total Runtime Budget

Target total browser memory:

**600–900 MB during a 4K60 recording with AI enabled.**

Older laptops automatically disable expensive preview features before exceeding this range.

---

# 7.16 Warm-Up Allocation Strategy

Memory allocations happen during initialization.

## Warm-Up Responsibilities

* Allocate pools.
* Allocate SharedArrayBuffers.
* Allocate scheduler queues.
* Allocate GPU texture descriptors.

Recording should perform minimal new allocations afterward.

---

## Warm-Up Timeline

```text
Application Starts
       │
Memory Pools
       │
Shared Buffers
       │
Worker Startup
       │
Recording Ready
```

---

# 7.17 Acceptance Tests

## Shared Memory Tests

* SharedArrayBuffer initialized.
* Workers receive references.
* Version validated.

## Ring Buffer Tests

* FIFO ordering.
* Constant capacity.
* Wrap-around behavior.

## Ownership Tests

* VideoFrame transferred once.
* ImageBitmap disposed.
* Leak detector reports zero leaks.

## Budget Tests

* Memory remains within targets.
* Warm-up allocations complete before recording.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 7.1)

1. Zero-copy is the default memory strategy.
2. SharedArrayBuffer stores metadata only.
3. VideoFrames have a single owner.
4. Transferables replace structured cloning whenever possible.
5. Ring buffers provide lock-free worker communication.
6. Memory pools recycle metadata objects.
7. Workers have isolated heaps.
8. Recording performs minimal allocations after warm-up.
9. Memory ownership always moves forward.
10. Leak detection is mandatory for every transferable object.

---

# 7.18 Memory Pool Philosophy

Garbage collection is one of the biggest causes of dropped frames in browser video applications.

Instead of allocating thousands of temporary objects every second, TryLipi pre-allocates reusable pools during startup.

## Golden Pool Rules

1. Pools are fixed-capacity.
2. Objects are reset before reuse.
3. Pools never grow automatically during recording.
4. Allocation failures trigger backpressure instead of uncontrolled heap growth.
5. Pools store metadata, descriptors, and reusable buffers—not persistent recording data.

---

## Why Pools Matter

At 60 FPS, even allocating a few objects per frame creates hundreds of thousands of objects during a long recording.

Pools reduce:

* GC pauses.
* Heap fragmentation.
* Memory churn.
* Allocation latency.

---

# 7.19 Global Pool Manager

A single runtime service owns every reusable pool.

## Responsibilities

* Initialize pools during startup.
* Hand out objects.
* Reset returned objects.
* Track utilization.
* Detect pool exhaustion.

---

## Global Pool Topology

```text id="hy9h7m"
Global Pool Manager
│
├── Video Packet Pool
├── Audio Packet Pool
├── Timeline Packet Pool
├── TypedArray Pool
├── AI Payload Pool
├── Bitmap Descriptor Pool
├── Texture Descriptor Pool
└── Export Task Pool
```

Each pool has independent capacity.

---

## Pool Manager Contract

```typescript id="xxvqfk"
interface GlobalPoolManager {

    acquire(pool:string):unknown;

    release(pool:string, object:unknown):void;

    stats():PoolStatistics;

}
```

Workers request objects through local pool adapters.

---

# 7.20 Pool Lifecycle

Every pooled object follows the same lifecycle.

## Lifecycle Diagram

```text id="zmnm0x"
Pool Created
     │
Acquire Object
     │
Initialize Fields
     │
Runtime Use
     │
Reset Fields
     │
Return To Pool
```

Objects are never destroyed during recording.

---

## Lifecycle Rules

* Acquire increments usage counter.
* Release clears mutable fields.
* Returned object becomes immediately reusable.
* Double release is treated as a runtime error.

---

# 7.21 Pool Capacity Planning

Capacities are calculated before recording begins.

## Example Capacities

| Pool            | Capacity |
| --------------- | -------- |
| Video Packet    | 2048     |
| Audio Packet    | 2048     |
| Timeline Packet | 4096     |
| AI Payload      | 512      |
| TypedArray      | 256      |
| Descriptor      | 2048     |

Capacities depend on Performance Tier.

---

## Tier-Based Capacity Scaling

| Performance Tier | Scaling |
| ---------------- | ------- |
| Tier 1           | 50%     |
| Tier 2           | 75%     |
| Tier 3           | 100%    |
| Tier 4           | 150%    |

Scaling happens only during startup.

---

# 7.22 Video Packet Pool

Video packet metadata is heavily reused.

## Pool Contents

Each object stores:

* frame ID
* timestamp
* duration
* sequence
* routing metadata

No pixel data.

---

## Video Packet Contract

```typescript id="5ptngv"
interface VideoPacket {

    frameId:string;

    timestampUs:number;

    durationUs:number;

    sequence:number;

    priority:number;

}
```

Returned immediately after scheduling completes.

---

## Reset Rules

Fields reset:

* IDs.
* Numbers.
* References.
* Flags.

Never allocate replacement objects during recording.

---

# 7.23 Audio Packet Pool

Audio metadata follows identical pooling strategy.

## Audio Packet Structure

```typescript id="tq9i6d"
interface AudioPacket {

    packetId:string;

    timestampUs:number;

    sampleCount:number;

    durationUs:number;

    trackId:string;

}
```

Packets reused after chunk persistence.

---

## Audio Pool Rules

* Separate pool from video.
* Supports multiple tracks.
* Supports future multichannel audio.

---

# 7.24 Timeline Packet Pool

Timeline events are extremely frequent.

## Timeline Event Categories

* cursor
* click
* scroll
* zoom
* blur
* caption
* camera

Every event uses pooled metadata.

---

## Timeline Packet Contract

```typescript id="h1uhkr"
interface TimelinePacket {

    eventId:string;

    timestampUs:number;

    trackId:string;

    payloadOffset:number;

}
```

Payload stored separately.

---

## Timeline Pool Strategy

Timeline packet lifetime:

milliseconds.

Returned immediately after serialization into Timeline Store.

---

# 7.25 TypedArray Pool Engine

TypedArrays are reused aggressively.

## Pooled TypedArrays

| Type         | Purpose                   |
| ------------ | ------------------------- |
| Uint8Array   | Binary metadata           |
| Uint16Array  | Small lookup tables       |
| Uint32Array  | Frame indices             |
| Float32Array | Camera matrices           |
| Float64Array | High precision timestamps |

---

## TypedArray Buckets

```text id="jhjzh1"
64B

256B

1KB

4KB

16KB

64KB

256KB
```

Requests rounded up to nearest bucket.

---

## Bucket Selection Rules

Never allocate arbitrary sizes repeatedly.

Use nearest reusable bucket.

---

# 7.26 TypedArray Reuse Pipeline

```text id="pvz2sh"
Request Buffer
      │
Nearest Bucket
      │
Acquire Array
      │
Runtime Use
      │
Fill(0)
      │
Return Bucket
```

Arrays retain capacity after reset.

---

## Large Buffer Policy

Buffers larger than pool maximum:

* allocated separately,
* destroyed immediately after use,
* never returned to pool.

Protects memory budget.

---

# 7.27 AI Payload Pool

Gemini and OCR generate temporary payload objects.

## Payload Components

* prompt metadata
* bitmap metadata
* OCR text buffers
* feature vectors

---

## Payload Lifecycle

```text id="g9wd9n"
Acquire Payload
      │
Attach Metadata
      │
Send To AI Worker
      │
Receive Result
      │
Reset Payload
```

Lifetime typically under one second.

---

## Payload Contract

```typescript id="a0ng3w"
interface AIPayload {

    payloadId:string;

    bitmapId:string;

    timestampUs:number;

    model:string;

}
```

---

# 7.28 Descriptor Pool Engine

Descriptors describe runtime resources.

## Descriptor Types

* bitmap descriptors
* texture descriptors
* cursor descriptors
* caption descriptors
* overlay descriptors

---

## Descriptor Contract

```typescript id="pzk9yk"
interface ResourceDescriptor {

    resourceId:string;

    width:number;

    height:number;

    format:string;

}
```

Descriptors avoid repeated object allocation.

---

## Descriptor Lifetime

Descriptors exist until associated resource released.

Then recycled.

---

# 7.29 Export Task Pool

Export engine schedules thousands of small tasks.

Tasks are pooled.

## Export Task Contract

```typescript id="0aopk4"
interface ExportTask {

    taskId:string;

    startTimestampUs:number;

    endTimestampUs:number;

    priority:number;

}
```

Released after encoding segment completes.

---

## Export Pool Rules

Export pools initialized only during export session.

Destroyed after export finishes.

---

# 7.30 Pool Exhaustion Strategy

Pools can become temporarily exhausted.

## Exhaustion Pipeline

```text id="ycdyxd"
Acquire
   │
Pool Empty
   │
Backpressure
   │
Retry Queue
```

Never allocate unlimited replacements.

---

## Exhaustion Policies

| Pool            | Policy              |
| --------------- | ------------------- |
| Video Packet    | Wait briefly        |
| Audio Packet    | Wait briefly        |
| Timeline Packet | Batch events        |
| AI Payload      | Pause AI scheduling |
| Descriptor      | Retry after release |

Recording remains highest priority.

---

# 7.31 Allocation Profiler

Developer diagnostics monitor allocations.

## Metrics

* allocations/sec
* releases/sec
* pool occupancy
* peak occupancy
* failed acquisitions

---

## Allocation Packet

```typescript id="1ydqon"
interface AllocationMetrics {

    pool:string;

    acquired:number;

    released:number;

    active:number;

}
```

Displayed in diagnostics dashboard.

---

## Allocation Timeline

Profiler records allocation bursts during:

* recording start
* export
* AI analysis
* timeline scrub

Useful for optimization.

---

# 7.32 Garbage Collection Avoidance

TryLipi intentionally minimizes GC pressure.

## Strategies

* object pools
* typed array pools
* descriptor reuse
* zero-copy transfers
* immutable recording chunks

---

## Avoid These Patterns

Never allocate:

* arrays every frame.
* objects inside render loop.
* closures inside frame scheduler.
* temporary vectors during camera calculations.

---

## Warm-Up Allocation

Startup allocates:

* pools
* ring buffers
* typed arrays
* descriptors

Runtime allocation should remain minimal.

---

# 7.33 Runtime Heap Fragmentation Prevention

Heap fragmentation increases over long recordings.

## Prevention Techniques

* fixed-size pools.
* bucketed TypedArrays.
* append-only manifests.
* immutable chunk buffers.

Large temporary buffers isolated.

---

## Fragmentation Watcher

Developer diagnostics detect:

* heap spikes.
* allocation bursts.
* pool misses.
* long GC pauses.

---

# 7.34 Pool Statistics Engine

Every pool exposes live statistics.

## Statistics

```typescript id="nkrmgv"
interface PoolStatistics {

    capacity:number;

    active:number;

    available:number;

    peak:number;

    misses:number;

}
```

Useful for tuning pool sizes.

---

## Occupancy Thresholds

| Occupancy | State    |
| --------- | -------- |
| Under 50% | Healthy  |
| 50–75%    | Busy     |
| 75–90%    | Warning  |
| Above 90% | Critical |

Critical occupancy triggers scheduler intervention.

---

# 7.35 Acceptance Tests

## Pool Tests

* Objects recycled.
* Capacity respected.
* Double release detected.

## TypedArray Tests

* Bucket reuse.
* Fill reset.
* Large buffer isolation.

## Allocation Tests

* Allocation profiler active.
* Warm-up allocations completed.
* Runtime allocations remain low.

## Exhaustion Tests

* AI pauses before recording affected.
* Timeline batching works.
* Recorder unaffected.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 7.2)

1. Global Pool Manager owns all reusable pools.
2. Pools are fixed-capacity during recording.
3. Video and audio metadata use independent pools.
4. TypedArrays are bucketed by size.
5. AI payloads are short-lived pooled objects.
6. Descriptors describe resources without owning them.
7. Pool exhaustion triggers backpressure, not heap growth.
8. Allocation profiler records every pool event.
9. Warm-up performs nearly all allocations before recording.
10. Garbage collection avoidance is a first-class runtime goal.

---

# 7.36 GPU Memory Philosophy

GPU memory is significantly faster than CPU memory, but GPU allocation is also expensive.

The renderer should allocate GPU resources during initialization and reuse them for the entire recording session.

## Golden GPU Rules

1. GPU textures are pooled.
2. Framebuffers are recycled.
3. Render targets are never recreated every frame.
4. Upload only changed textures.
5. Context loss must be recoverable.
6. GPU memory is bounded by Performance Tier.

---

## GPU Resource Categories

```text id="r2j9sm"
GPU Memory
│
├── Textures
├── Framebuffers
├── Render Targets
├── Shader Programs
├── Uniform Buffers
├── Vertex Buffers
└── Texture Atlases
```

Each category has its own lifecycle.

---

# 7.37 GPU Resource Manager

GPU Resource Manager owns every GPU allocation.

Responsibilities:

* Allocate textures.
* Allocate framebuffers.
* Allocate buffers.
* Recycle resources.
* Track GPU memory usage.
* Recover after context loss.

---

## Resource Manager Topology

```text id="hrv5lx"
GPU Resource Manager
│
├── Texture Pool
├── Framebuffer Pool
├── Render Target Pool
├── Shader Pool
├── Uniform Pool
├── Vertex Buffer Pool
└── Context Recovery Manager
```

No rendering engine allocates GPU resources directly.

---

## Resource Manager Contract

```typescript id="1wqqkb"
interface GPUResourceManager {

    acquireTexture():GPUTextureHandle;

    releaseTexture(id:string):void;

    acquireFramebuffer():FramebufferHandle;

    releaseFramebuffer(id:string):void;

}
```

---

# 7.38 Texture Pool Architecture

Textures are reused across frames.

## Texture Types

| Type              | Purpose                |
| ----------------- | ---------------------- |
| Frame Texture     | Current captured frame |
| Blur Texture      | Blur pipeline          |
| Camera Texture    | Camera crop            |
| Overlay Texture   | Highlights/Captions    |
| Composite Texture | Final preview          |

---

## Texture Lifecycle

```text id="h7wmaw"
Acquire Texture
      │
Upload Pixels
      │
Render Passes
      │
Release Texture
      │
Pool
```

Texture objects persist.

---

## Texture Handle

```typescript id="xyrpk5"
interface GPUTextureHandle {

    textureId:string;

    width:number;

    height:number;

    format:string;

    inUse:boolean;

}
```

---

# 7.39 Texture Buckets

Textures are grouped by dimensions.

## Bucket Sizes

| Bucket | Resolution |
| ------ | ---------- |
| XS     | 256×256    |
| SM     | 512×512    |
| MD     | 1024×1024  |
| LG     | 1920×1080  |
| XL     | 2560×1440  |
| XXL    | 3840×2160  |

Pools never mix bucket sizes.

---

## Bucket Selection Strategy

Round requested resolution to nearest supported bucket.

Reuse matching texture.

---

# 7.40 Texture Allocation Strategy

Textures allocated during warm-up.

## Warm-Up Allocation

Allocate:

* preview textures.
* blur textures.
* composite textures.
* overlay textures.

Number depends on Performance Tier.

---

## Tier Allocation Counts

| Tier   | Texture Count |
| ------ | ------------- |
| Tier 1 | 6             |
| Tier 2 | 10            |
| Tier 3 | 16            |
| Tier 4 | 24            |

---

## Allocation Rules

Never allocate inside render loop unless absolutely required.

---

# 7.41 Framebuffer Pool Engine

Framebuffers store intermediate render results.

## Framebuffer Types

* Blur framebuffer.
* Camera framebuffer.
* Composite framebuffer.
* Thumbnail framebuffer.

---

## Pool Topology

```text id="q8j4l4"
Framebuffer Pool
│
├── Blur FB
├── Camera FB
├── Composite FB
└── Export FB
```

---

## Framebuffer Contract

```typescript id="l9oxzm"
interface FramebufferHandle {

    framebufferId:string;

    width:number;

    height:number;

}
```

---

## Lifecycle

Acquire → Render → Release.

---

# 7.42 Render Target Recycling

Render targets receive output of render passes.

## Render Graph

```text id="sl13dd"
Frame Texture
      │
Blur Target
      │
Camera Target
      │
Caption Target
      │
Composite Target
```

Targets reused every frame.

---

## Recycling Rules

Targets cleared after pass.

No reallocation.

---

## Target Rotation

Double buffering supported for preview.

---

# 7.43 Double Buffering Strategy

Double buffering prevents tearing.

## Buffer Rotation

```text id="sfbx7s"
Frame A → Display

Frame B → Render

Swap
```

---

## Triple Buffering (Future)

Used only for HDR / WebGPU renderer.

Feature flagged.

---

# 7.44 OffscreenCanvas Memory Engine

OffscreenCanvas owns worker rendering surfaces.

## Surface Types

* Preview surface.
* Blur surface.
* Thumbnail surface.
* Export staging surface.

---

## Surface Lifecycle

```text id="2oqe7b"
Canvas Created
     │
Transferred To Worker
     │
Rendering
     │
Disposed
```

One owner only.

---

## Canvas Contract

```typescript id="h2cznt"
interface OffscreenCanvasHandle {

    canvasId:string;

    width:number;

    height:number;

}
```

---

# 7.45 Canvas Resize Strategy

Resizing canvas reallocates GPU memory.

Avoid frequent resize.

## Resize Rules

Resize only when:

* capture resolution changes.
* export resolution changes.
* preview scale changes.

Never resize during steady recording.

---

## Resize Pipeline

```text id="s34cna"
Pause Rendering
      │
Allocate New Surface
      │
Swap Surface
      │
Release Old Surface
```

---

# 7.46 Texture Upload Strategy

Uploading textures is expensive.

Uploads happen only when pixels change.

## Upload Pipeline

```text id="j9fhaf"
VideoFrame
      │
GPU Upload
      │
Frame Texture
```

Subsequent render passes reuse texture.

---

## Upload Rules

* One upload per captured frame.
* No upload for unchanged overlays.
* No upload for cached captions.

---

## Partial Uploads

Future optimization:

upload damaged regions only.

---

# 7.47 Shader Resource Pools

Shader programs compiled once.

## Shader Categories

| Shader    | Purpose           |
| --------- | ----------------- |
| Blur      | Gaussian blur     |
| Camera    | Crop & transform  |
| Highlight | Spotlight         |
| Caption   | Text rendering    |
| Composite | Final composition |

---

## Shader Lifecycle

```text id="q85pqj"
Compile
   │
Cache
   │
Bind
   │
Render
```

Compilation never occurs during recording.

---

## Shader Contract

```typescript id="yt4nxr"
interface ShaderProgramHandle {

    shaderId:string;

    compiled:boolean;

}
```

---

# 7.48 Uniform Buffer Management

Uniforms change every frame.

Buffers do not.

## Uniform Categories

* camera matrix
* zoom amount
* blur radius
* cursor position
* animation progress

---

## Uniform Update Pipeline

```text id="q9qifq"
Frame Metadata
      │
Uniform Buffer
      │
Shader Bind
```

Reuse buffer objects.

---

## Uniform Contract

```typescript id="ygjh4m"
interface UniformBuffer {

    bufferId:string;

    byteLength:number;

}
```

---

# 7.49 Vertex Buffer Pool

Geometry reused between frames.

## Geometry Types

* fullscreen quad
* rounded rectangle
* spotlight mesh
* text quad
* cursor quad

---

## Pool Strategy

Buffers uploaded once.

Transform through uniforms.

---

## Vertex Buffer Contract

```typescript id="k0z8hl"
interface VertexBufferHandle {

    bufferId:string;

    vertexCount:number;

}
```

---

# 7.50 Texture Atlas Engine

Icons and UI overlays share atlases.

## Atlas Contents

* cursor icons
* emojis
* social icons
* toolbar graphics
* stickers

---

## Atlas Pipeline

```text id="1wlq1b"
Atlas PNG
    │
GPU Texture
    │
UV Coordinates
```

One upload serves many draws.

---

## Atlas Metadata

```typescript id="wmyu95"
interface TextureAtlasEntry {

    atlasId:string;

    x:number;

    y:number;

    width:number;

    height:number;

}
```

---

# 7.51 Render Cache Engine

Some render passes produce identical outputs.

Cache them.

## Cache Candidates

* static captions
* logo watermark
* creator branding
* static overlays

---

## Cache Pipeline

```text id="9mujk2"
Render Once
     │
Texture Cache
     │
Reuse Every Frame
```

---

## Cache Invalidation

Invalidate only when content changes.

---

# 7.52 GPU Memory Budget Engine

GPU memory depends on tier.

## Target Budgets

| Tier   | GPU Budget |
| ------ | ---------- |
| Tier 1 | 128 MB     |
| Tier 2 | 256 MB     |
| Tier 3 | 512 MB     |
| Tier 4 | 1 GB       |

---

## Budget Enforcement

Before allocating new texture:

check remaining GPU budget.

Trigger texture eviction if needed.

---

# 7.53 GPU Eviction Policy

Temporary textures may be evicted.

Priority:

1. Thumbnail textures.
2. AI staging textures.
3. Blur intermediates.
4. Preview textures.
5. Composite textures.

Recorder textures never evicted during active frame.

---

## Eviction Rules

Only unused textures eligible.

---

# 7.54 GPU Context Loss Recovery

Browsers may lose GPU context.

## Recovery Flow

```text id="aof5yq"
Context Lost
     │
Stop Rendering
     │
Dispose Handles
     │
Recreate Resources
     │
Resume Rendering
```

Recording continues.

---

## Recovery Responsibilities

* recreate shaders.
* recreate textures.
* recreate framebuffers.
* restore atlas.

---

## Context Recovery Contract

```typescript id="wyjtdw"
interface GPURecoveryState {

    recovered:boolean;

    texturesRestored:number;

    framebuffersRestored:number;

}
```

---

# 7.55 GPU Diagnostics

Developer Mode exposes GPU metrics.

## Metrics

* active textures
* active framebuffers
* upload latency
* render latency
* context losses
* memory usage

---

## GPU Statistics Contract

```typescript id="3j8lkw"
interface GPUStatistics {

    activeTextures:number;

    activeFramebuffers:number;

    uploadLatencyMs:number;

    gpuMemoryMB:number;

}
```

---

# 7.56 Acceptance Tests

## Texture Tests

* Texture reuse.
* Bucket selection.
* Upload once per frame.

## Framebuffer Tests

* Pool reuse.
* Double buffering.
* Render target recycling.

## Shader Tests

* Compile once.
* Uniform updates.
* Cache reuse.

## Recovery Tests

* Context loss recovery.
* Atlas restoration.
* Preview resumes.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 7.3)

1. GPU Resource Manager owns all GPU allocations.
2. Textures are pooled by resolution bucket.
3. Framebuffers are recycled after each pass.
4. OffscreenCanvas surfaces have single ownership.
5. Upload textures only when pixels change.
6. Shader compilation happens only during initialization.
7. Uniform buffers are reused.
8. Texture atlases minimize uploads.
9. GPU budgets depend on Performance Tier.
10. Context loss is fully recoverable without corrupting recording.

# 7.57 Memory Pressure Philosophy

Memory usage during recording is inevitable.

The goal is **not** to use as little memory as possible.

The goal is:

* predictable memory,
* bounded memory,
* recoverable memory,
* observable memory.

The runtime must react **before** the browser reaches critical pressure.

## Golden Memory Pressure Rules

1. Detect pressure continuously.
2. React before OOM.
3. Free temporary memory first.
4. Never sacrifice recorded media.
5. Recording is the highest priority workload.

---

## Memory Pressure Levels

| Level  | Meaning            |
| ------ | ------------------ |
| Green  | Healthy usage.     |
| Yellow | Elevated usage.    |
| Orange | Recovery begins.   |
| Red    | Critical pressure. |
| Black  | OOM imminent.      |

Every level triggers different runtime behavior.

---

# 7.58 Runtime Memory Pressure Engine

A dedicated worker monitors runtime memory.

## Responsibilities

* Heap monitoring.
* GPU memory monitoring.
* Shared memory monitoring.
* Pool occupancy.
* Queue pressure.
* GC event monitoring.

---

## Pressure Monitoring Pipeline

```text id="lvr5qs"
Runtime Metrics
      │
Memory Pressure Engine
      │
Pressure Score
      │
Recovery Policy
```

Runs continuously during recording.

---

## Pressure Snapshot Contract

```typescript id="bydpvd"
interface MemoryPressureSnapshot {

    heapMB:number;

    gpuMB:number;

    sharedMemoryMB:number;

    poolOccupancy:number;

    pressureLevel:"green"|"yellow"|"orange"|"red";

}
```

Immutable snapshot every few seconds.

---

# 7.59 Heap Monitoring System

Heap monitoring detects JavaScript memory growth.

## Metrics Collected

* used heap
* total heap
* heap limit
* allocation rate
* GC frequency

---

## Heap Timeline

```text id="l1f2zm"
Time
 │
Heap Usage
 │
Peak
 │
GC
 │
Recovery
```

Used for diagnostics.

---

## Heap Thresholds

| Heap Usage | State    |
| ---------- | -------- |
| Under 50%  | Healthy  |
| 50–70%     | Warning  |
| 70–85%     | Recovery |
| Above 85%  | Critical |

Thresholds scale with Performance Tier.

---

# 7.60 Memory Growth Detector

The runtime tracks memory trends instead of single values.

## Growth Metrics

* MB/minute
* Peak delta
* Sustained increase
* Allocation spikes

---

## Growth Categories

| Pattern            | Meaning            |
| ------------------ | ------------------ |
| Stable             | Expected           |
| Linear Growth      | Possible leak      |
| Burst Growth       | Temporary workload |
| Exponential Growth | Critical leak      |

Recovery depends on pattern.

---

## Growth Metadata

```typescript id="tazbh5"
interface MemoryGrowthMetrics {

    growthRateMBPerMinute:number;

    sustainedGrowth:boolean;

    spikeDetected:boolean;

}
```

---

# 7.61 Leak Detection Philosophy

Leaks are resources whose lifetime exceeds expected ownership.

Leaks include:

* VideoFrames.
* ImageBitmaps.
* GPU textures.
* TypedArrays.
* Timeline packets.
* Event listeners.
* Shared buffers.

---

## Leak Categories

| Category      | Example                 |
| ------------- | ----------------------- |
| CPU Leak      | Unreleased arrays       |
| GPU Leak      | Texture never released  |
| Transfer Leak | VideoFrame not closed   |
| Listener Leak | Event listener retained |
| Pool Leak     | Object never returned   |

Every category has dedicated detection logic.

---

# 7.62 VideoFrame Leak Detector

VideoFrames are the highest-priority leak target.

## Detection Rules

Leak if:

* ownership expired,
* frame older than threshold,
* frame transferred twice,
* frame never closed.

---

## Leak Pipeline

```text id="twgxmf"
Frame Registry
      │
Lifetime Check
      │
Ownership Check
      │
Leak Report
```

---

## Leak Report

```typescript id="bllr6d"
interface VideoFrameLeakReport {

    frameId:string;

    ownerWorker:string;

    lifetimeMs:number;

}
```

---

# 7.63 ImageBitmap Leak Detector

Bitmaps are temporary analysis/rendering objects.

## Detection Rules

Bitmap lifetime target:

less than one preview frame.

Flag if bitmap survives longer than configured threshold.

---

## Bitmap Registry

Tracks:

* bitmap ID
* owner worker
* creation timestamp
* release timestamp

---

## Bitmap Recovery

Leaked bitmap automatically released if ownership expired.

---

# 7.64 GPU Leak Detection

GPU leaks are difficult to detect manually.

Resource Manager tracks all allocations.

## GPU Leak Checks

* active textures
* orphan framebuffers
* unused render targets
* shader references
* atlas references

---

## Texture Lifetime Validation

```text id="p14vhq"
Texture Allocated
      │
Bound
      │
Rendered
      │
Released?
```

Missing release generates warning.

---

## GPU Leak Contract

```typescript id="gnttdn"
interface GPULeakReport {

    textureId:string;

    framebufferId?:string;

    lifetimeFrames:number;

}
```

---

# 7.65 Pool Leak Detection

Pools should return to baseline occupancy.

## Leak Indicators

* active objects increasing.
* releases missing.
* pool misses increasing.
* occupancy never decreases.

---

## Pool Validation

```text id="8ic0t7"
Acquire
  │
Release
  │
Pool Occupancy Stable
```

Missing release increments leak counter.

---

## Pool Leak Metrics

```typescript id="e5z06l"
interface PoolLeakMetrics {

    unreleasedObjects:number;

    peakOccupancy:number;

    misses:number;

}
```

---

# 7.66 SharedArrayBuffer Health Monitoring

Shared memory should remain stable.

## Monitor

* queue head/tail.
* atomic contention.
* stale pointers.
* heartbeat timestamps.
* version mismatch.

---

## Shared Runtime Checks

```text id="yctbq2"
Scheduler Buffer
Metrics Buffer
Cursor Buffer
Heartbeat Buffer
```

Every buffer validated independently.

---

## Health Contract

```typescript id="l0cypm"
interface SharedMemoryHealth {

    schedulerHealthy:boolean;

    metricsHealthy:boolean;

    heartbeatHealthy:boolean;

}
```

---

# 7.67 Automatic Memory Recovery Engine

Recovery begins before OOM.

## Recovery Priority

1. Release temporary AI payloads.
2. Release thumbnail cache.
3. Release preview cache.
4. Release blur intermediates.
5. Pause AI sampling.
6. Lower preview FPS.

Recording memory never discarded.

---

## Recovery Pipeline

```text id="lkjpmk"
Pressure Orange
      │
Recovery Manager
      │
Release Temporary Resources
      │
Recalculate Pressure
```

---

## Recovery Levels

| Level | Action                    |
| ----- | ------------------------- |
| L1    | Clear caches              |
| L2    | Pause AI                  |
| L3    | Lower preview FPS         |
| L4    | Reduce preview resolution |
| L5    | Stop preview rendering    |

Recording continues throughout.

---

# 7.68 Cache Eviction Strategy

Caches are safest memory to reclaim.

## Eviction Order

1. Thumbnail cache.
2. OCR cache.
3. AI bitmap cache.
4. Static overlay cache.
5. Caption cache.

---

## Eviction Rules

Only regenerated resources eligible.

Timeline data never evicted.

---

## Cache Metadata

```typescript id="pgm4s8"
interface CacheEntry {

    cacheId:string;

    lastUsed:number;

    sizeMB:number;

}
```

LRU eviction policy.

---

# 7.69 Out-of-Memory Prevention Engine

OOM prevention predicts failure before it happens.

## Prediction Inputs

* heap trend
* allocation rate
* GPU usage
* pool misses
* GC frequency

---

## Prevention Pipeline

```text id="8grwxu"
Metrics
 │
Risk Score
 │
Recovery Action
 │
OOM Avoided
```

---

## OOM Risk Levels

| Risk     | Action            |
| -------- | ----------------- |
| Low      | None              |
| Medium   | Cache cleanup     |
| High     | AI throttling     |
| Critical | Preview downgrade |

Recording stops only if browser itself becomes unstable.

---

# 7.70 Garbage Collection Observer

GC pauses affect frame timing.

## Observer Metrics

* GC duration
* GC frequency
* reclaimed memory
* frame impact

---

## GC Events

```typescript id="vfys9p"
interface GCEvent {

    timestamp:number;

    durationMs:number;

    reclaimedMB:number;

}
```

Diagnostics only.

---

## GC Policies

Repeated long GC pauses trigger allocation profiler warnings.

---

Developer Mode exposes complete memory dashboard.

## Dashboard Panels

* Heap usage.

# 7.72 Memory Stress Testing

Memory engine must pass stress tests.

## Stress Scenarios

* 4K60 recording for 6 hours.
* AI enabled continuously.
* Timeline scrubbing while recording.
* Thumbnail generation every minute.
* Browser tab hidden/restored repeatedly.

---

## Expected Behavior

* bounded heap.
* bounded GPU memory.
* no leaked VideoFrames.
* no leaked textures.
* recovery never interrupts recording.

---

## Stress Metrics

Record:

* peak heap.
* peak GPU.
* total GC time.
* recovery count.

---

# 7.73 Runtime Memory Audit

Audit runs periodically.

## Audit Checks

* orphan resources.
* pool occupancy.
* timestamp buffer health.
* shared memory integrity.
* descriptor counts.

---

## Audit Frequency

Every 60 seconds during active recording.

Every 5 minutes while idle.

---

## Audit Report

```typescript id="5xydzi"
interface MemoryAuditReport {

    timestamp:number;

    passed:boolean;

    warnings:string[];

}
```

---

# 7.74 Definition of Done

Memory Management subsystem is complete only if:

### Zero-Copy

* Ownership enforced.
* Transferables used.
* SharedArrayBuffer metadata only.

### Pools

* Fixed-capacity pools.
* TypedArray buckets.
* Descriptor reuse.

### GPU

* Texture pools.
* Framebuffer pools.
* Context recovery.

### Recovery

* Pressure engine.
* Leak detection.
* Automatic recovery.
* OOM prevention.

---

# 7.75 Canonical Acceptance Checklist

## Leak Tests

* VideoFrame leaks detected.
* Bitmap leaks detected.
* Texture leaks detected.

## Pressure Tests

* Heap thresholds trigger recovery.
* Cache eviction works.
* AI throttling works.

## Recovery Tests

* GPU memory reclaimed.
* Shared memory healthy.
* Recording unaffected during recovery.

## Stress Tests

* 6-hour recording remains bounded.
* No increasing leak counters.
* Memory dashboard reports zero unrecovered leaks.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 7.4)

1. Memory pressure is monitored continuously.
2. Recovery starts before OOM.
3. Recording media is never discarded during recovery.
4. VideoFrame leaks are fatal diagnostics.
5. GPU resources must be explicitly released.
6. SharedArrayBuffer health is continuously verified.
7. Cache eviction follows deterministic priority.
8. Allocation trends matter more than single snapshots.
9. Memory dashboard is developer-only.
10. Chapter 07 defines the canonical runtime memory model.

---
