# 9.77 Cinematic Camera Rendering Philosophy

Smart Camera rendering is separate from Smart Camera planning.

Planning produces **camera keyframes**.

Rendering converts keyframes into pixels.

## Golden Rendering Rules

1. Renderer never modifies timeline.
2. Renderer consumes immutable camera track.
3. Preview and export use identical keyframes.
4. Rendering is deterministic.
5. Effects are composited after camera crop.

---

## Camera Rendering Pipeline

```text id="zz9mkt"
Timeline Clock
      │
Camera Keyframes
      │
Interpolation Engine
      │
Viewport Crop
      │
Effects Pipeline
      │
Preview / Export
```

---

# 9.78 Camera Render Graph

Rendering occurs in ordered passes.

## Render Graph

```text id="2s2o2u"
Master Video
     │
Camera Crop
     │
Spotlight Pass
     │
Blur Pass
     │
Cursor Pass
     │
Caption Pass
     │
Overlay Pass
     │
Composite Output
```

Camera always renders before overlays.

---

## Render Pass Contract

```typescript id="n9nsh4"
interface CameraRenderPass {

    passId:string;

    order:number;

    enabled:boolean;

}
```

---

# 9.79 Preview Renderer vs Export Renderer

Preview prioritizes responsiveness.

Export prioritizes accuracy.

## Preview Characteristics

* Proxy video.
* Cached interpolation.
* Adaptive frame skipping.
* Lower texture resolution.

---

## Export Characteristics

* Master recording.
* Full precision interpolation.
* Exact timestamps.
* No dropped frames.

---

## Shared Guarantee

Both consume identical camera timeline events.

---

# 9.80 Camera Crop Engine

The crop engine transforms recording into viewport.

## Crop Inputs

* viewport rectangle
* zoom
* aspect ratio
* safe margins

---

## Crop Pipeline

```text id="oxj88p"
Recording Frame
      │
Viewport Solver
      │
Crop Rectangle
      │
Render Target
```

---

## Crop Contract

```typescript id="pzpr2s"
interface CameraCrop {

    x:number;

    y:number;

    width:number;

    height:number;

}
```

---

# 9.81 Spotlight Rendering Engine

Spotlight dims the rest of the screen.

## Spotlight Components

* focus circle
* dim overlay
* feather edge
* animation

---

## Spotlight Pipeline

```text id="dfgpnw"
Subject Bounds
      │
Spotlight Shape
      │
Mask Renderer
      │
Composite
```

---

## Spotlight Contract

```typescript id="8ahtmx"
interface SpotlightEffect {

    centerX:number;

    centerY:number;

    radius:number;

    feather:number;

}
```

---

## Spotlight Rules

Cursor spotlight follows smoothed cursor path.

---

# 9.82 Punch Zoom Engine

Punch zoom emphasizes interactions.

## Trigger Sources

* click
* keyboard shortcut
* AI suggestion
* manual marker

## Animation Timeline

```text id="tn0pvf"
1.0×

↓

1.35×

↓

1.42×

↓

1.35×

↓

Release
```

Small overshoot creates cinematic feel.

---

## Punch Zoom Contract

```typescript id="v7ihs5"
    durationUs:number;

}
```

# 9.83 Reveal Animation Engine

Reveal introduces new UI regions.

## Reveal Types

| Reveal       | Usage     |

| Pan Reveal   | Sidebar   |

Transition between subjects smoothly.

# 9.86 AI Director Mode

AI Director creates camera movements automatically.

* choose subjects
* generate zooms
* insert holds
* reveal panels
* ignore unimportant movement

---

```text id="ys2l1e"
Timeline
   │
Gemini Vision
   │
Director Suggestions
   │
Camera Track
```

Suggestions become editable keyframes.

---

## Director Output

```typescript id="mhf1z8"
interface AIDirectorSuggestion {

    timestampUs:number;

    subjectId:string;

    reason:string;

    zoom:number;

}
```

---

# 9.87 Director Confidence Engine

Every AI suggestion includes confidence.

## Confidence Levels

| Confidence | Behavior          |
| ---------- | ----------------- |
| High       | Auto insert       |
| Medium     | Suggested marker  |
| Low        | Hidden suggestion |

## Confidence Contract

```typescript id="qdqdlx"

    accepted:boolean;

}
```

# 9.88 Manual Override Priority

Users retain complete control.

## Override Rules

| Action          | Result                  |
| --------------- | ----------------------- |
| Edit keyframe   | AI disabled for segment |
| Delete keyframe | AI suggestion removed   |
| Lock camera     | AI cannot modify        |
| Reset segment   | AI regenerated          |

---

## Segment Lock Contract

# 10.1 Rendering Philosophy

The Rendering Engine is responsible for converting immutable timeline state into pixels displayed during preview and export.

The renderer **never modifies source media**. Every visible element—camera crop, blur, captions, cursor effects, annotations, overlays, branding—is generated dynamically through a deterministic render graph.

Rendering behaves identically during preview and export.

## Golden Rendering Rules

1. Source recording is immutable.
2. Rendering consumes timeline state only.
3. Effects execute through ordered GPU render passes.
4. Render order is deterministic.
5. Preview and export share the same render graph.
6. Render passes communicate only through textures.
7. Effects are stateless unless explicitly cached.

---

## Rendering Responsibilities

The Rendering Engine owns:

* Camera crop rendering.
* Blur rendering.
* Cursor rendering.
* Highlight rendering.
* Shapes & annotations.
* Caption rendering.
* Background composition.
* Mask rendering.
* Final frame compositing.

---

# 10.2 Renderer Architecture Overview

The renderer is built as a GPU pipeline running inside the Rendering Worker.

## High-Level Pipeline

```text
Video Decoder
      │
Frame Texture
      │
Camera Pass
      │
Effects Graph
      │
Overlay Graph
      │
Composite Pass
      │
Preview Canvas / Video Encoder
```

The pipeline is identical whether rendering a single preview frame or exporting millions of frames.

---

## Renderer Modules

```text
Rendering Engine
│
├── Render Graph Manager
├── Layer Manager
├── Pass Scheduler
├── Texture Pool
├── Shader Library
├── Mask Engine
├── Composite Engine
└── Diagnostics Engine
```

Each module has one responsibility.

---

# 10.3 Render Graph Architecture

The render graph is a **Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG)** describing how textures flow through the renderer.

## Render Graph Principles

* Immutable inputs.
* Ordered dependencies.
* No cycles.
* Explicit texture ownership.
* Deterministic execution.

---

## Canonical Render Graph

```text
Recording Texture
       │
Camera Crop
       │
Blur Pass
       │
Highlight Pass
       │
Cursor Pass
       │
Caption Pass
       │
Overlay Pass
       │
Branding Pass
       │
Composite Pass
       │
Output Texture
```

Every pass consumes textures and produces a new texture.

---

## Render Node Contract

```typescript
interface RenderNode {
    nodeId: string;
    pass: string;
    inputTextures: string[];
    outputTexture: string;
    enabled: boolean;
}
```

---

## Graph Validation Rules

Before playback/export:

* Every node has inputs.
* Every node has outputs.
* No cyclic dependency.
* Pass ordering validated.

---

# 10.4 Render Graph Scheduler

The scheduler executes render nodes in dependency order.

## Scheduler Responsibilities

* Topological ordering.
* Texture reuse.
* Pass skipping.
* Dirty-region optimization.

---

## Scheduler Pipeline

```text
Timeline State
      │
Render Graph
      │
Dependency Sort
      │
GPU Pass Queue
      │
Frame Output
```

---

## Scheduler Contract

```typescript
interface RenderPassScheduler {
    orderedPasses: string[];
    dirtyPasses: string[];
}
```

Only dirty passes rerender during preview.

---

# 10.5 Layer Composition Model

Everything visible is a layer.

Layers are independent timeline objects.

## Canonical Layer Order

| Z Index | Layer                |
| ------- | -------------------- |
| 0       | Background           |
| 10      | Screen Recording     |
| 20      | Camera Crop          |
| 30      | Blur Masks           |
| 40      | Highlights           |
| 50      | Cursor               |
| 60      | Shapes & Annotations |
| 70      | Captions             |
| 80      | Branding             |
| 90      | Debug Layer          |

---

## Layer Hierarchy

```text
Composite Frame
│
├── Branding
├── Captions
├── Shapes
├── Cursor
├── Highlights
├── Blur
├── Camera Crop
└── Recording
```

---

## Render Layer Contract

```typescript
interface RenderLayer {
    layerId: string;
    order: number;
    opacity: number;
    visible: boolean;
    locked: boolean;
}
```

---

## Layer Rules

* Layers are timeline-driven.
* Layers support opacity animation.
* Layers can be disabled without deleting events.

---

# 10.6 Effect Timeline Tracks

Effects are stored separately from media.

## Supported Effect Tracks

| Track            | Purpose                     |
| ---------------- | --------------------------- |
| Blur Track       | Blur regions                |
| Highlight Track  | Spotlight effects           |
| Cursor FX Track  | Cursor halo, clicks         |
| Caption Track    | Subtitle rendering          |
| Shape Track      | Rectangles, circles, arrows |
| Overlay Track    | Images, logos               |
| Color Track      | LUTs, grading               |
| Transition Track | Scene transitions           |

---

## Effect Event Contract

```typescript
interface EffectEvent {
    eventId: string;
    effectType: string;
    startUs: number;
    endUs: number;
    payload: unknown;
}
```

---

## Timeline Rules

Effects activate only within their time interval.

---

# 10.7 Render Pass Pipeline

Rendering happens in isolated passes.

## Pass Order

```text
Decode Frame
     │
Camera Pass
     │
Blur Pass
     │
Highlight Pass
     │
Cursor Pass
     │
Caption Pass
     │
Overlay Pass
     │
Composite Pass
```

---

## Pass Responsibilities

| Pass      | Responsibility   |
| --------- | ---------------- |
| Camera    | Crop & zoom      |
| Blur      | Gaussian blur    |
| Highlight | Spotlight/glow   |
| Cursor    | Cursor rendering |
| Caption   | Text rendering   |
| Overlay   | Shapes/images    |
| Composite | Final RGBA frame |

---

## Render Pass Contract

```typescript
interface RenderPass {
    passId: string;
    framebufferId: string;
    outputTexture: string;
    dependencies: string[];
}
```

---

## Pass Isolation

Each pass writes into a separate framebuffer.

---

# 10.8 Render Surface Architecture

The renderer owns multiple OffscreenCanvas render targets.

## Render Surfaces

| Surface           | Usage            |
| ----------------- | ---------------- |
| Camera Surface    | Camera crop      |
| Blur Surface      | Blur shader      |
| Highlight Surface | Spotlight/glow   |
| Cursor Surface    | Cursor rendering |
| Caption Surface   | Text rendering   |
| Composite Surface | Final output     |

---

## Surface Lifecycle

```text
Create Surface
      │
Bind Texture
      │
Render Pass
      │
Release To Pool
```

---

## Surface Contract

```typescript
interface RenderSurface {
    surfaceId: string;
    width: number;
    height: number;
    textureId: string;
}
```

---

## Surface Rules

* Surfaces come from GPU texture pools.
* Surfaces never allocate during playback.
* Recycled after frame completion.

---

# 10.9 Texture Ownership Model

Every render pass owns textures temporarily.

## Ownership Flow

```text
Frame Texture
      │
Camera Pass
      │
Camera Texture
      │
Blur Pass
      │
Blur Texture
      │
Composite Pass
```

---

## Texture Contract

```typescript
interface RenderTexture {
    textureId: string;
    width: number;
    height: number;
    ownerPass: string;
}
```

---

## Ownership Rules

* Single writer.
* Multiple readers allowed.
* Returned to pool after composite.

---

# 10.10 Blend Mode Engine

Effects blend together using GPU shaders.

## Supported Blend Modes

| Blend Mode | Usage            |
| ---------- | ---------------- |
| Normal     | Default          |
| Multiply   | Shadows          |
| Screen     | Glow             |
| Overlay    | Highlights       |
| Add        | Cursor glow      |
| Darken     | Spotlight mask   |
| Lighten    | Reveal animation |

---

## Blend Contract

```typescript
interface BlendMode {
    mode:
        | "normal"
        | "multiply"
        | "screen"
        | "overlay"
        | "add"
        | "darken"
        | "lighten";
    opacity: number;
}
```

---

## Blend Rules

Blend occurs during composite pass only.

---

# 10.11 Alpha Compositing Engine

The renderer uses **premultiplied alpha** internally.

## Alpha Pipeline

```text
RGBA Texture
     │
Premultiply Alpha
     │
Blend Shader
     │
Composite Output
```

---

## Alpha Rules

* Prevent edge halos.
* Preserve caption edges.
* Preserve spotlight feathering.

---

## Alpha Texture Contract

```typescript
interface AlphaTexture {
    textureId: string;
    premultiplied: boolean;
}
```

---

# 10.12 Mask System

Masks determine where effects apply.

## Mask Types

| Mask              | Use               |
| ----------------- | ----------------- |
| Rectangle         | Blur              |
| Rounded Rectangle | Highlight         |
| Circle            | Spotlight         |
| Ellipse           | Face blur         |
| Polygon           | Object blur       |
| Freeform          | Future brush tool |

---

## Mask Generation Pipeline

```text
Timeline Effect
      │
Geometry Generator
      │
Mask Texture
```

---

## Mask Contract

```typescript
interface EffectMask {
    maskId: string;
    shape: string;
    featherRadius: number;
}
```

---

## Mask Rules

Masks render into alpha textures before effects execute.

---

# 10.13 Feather Engine

Feather softens mask boundaries.

## Feather Pipeline

```text
Binary Mask
     │
Distance Field
     │
Smoothstep Shader
     │
Soft Alpha Mask
```

---

## Feather Parameters

```typescript
interface FeatherParameters {
    radius: number;
    curve: "linear" | "smoothstep" | "gaussian";
}
```

---

## Feather Rules

Feather is independent of blur radius.

---

# 10.14 Color Pipeline Integration

Rendering operates in Linear RGB internally.

## Color Flow

```text
Video Decoder
     │
BT.709 Texture
     │
Linear RGB
     │
Shaders
     │
Composite
     │
BT.709 Output
```

---

## Color Responsibilities

* Gamma correction.
* Linear blending.
* Consistent caption colors.
* Consistent blur colors.

---

## Color Profile Contract

```typescript
interface RenderColorProfile {
    inputColorSpace: string;
    workingColorSpace: string;
    outputColorSpace: string;
}
```

---

## Supported Profiles

| Stage   | Profile        |
| ------- | -------------- |
| Input   | BT.709 SDR     |
| Working | Linear RGB     |
| Output  | BT.709 SDR     |
| Future  | Display-P3 HDR |

---

# 10.15 Render Resource Lifecycle

GPU resources are pooled.

## Resource Lifecycle

```text
Allocate Pool
      │
Acquire Texture
      │
Bind Pass
      │
Render
      │
Release Texture
```

---

## Resource Rules

* Never allocate textures during playback.
* Framebuffers reused.
* Shader programs compiled once.

---

## Resource Contract

```typescript
interface RenderResourcePool {
    textures: string[];
    framebuffers: string[];
    shaders: string[];
}
```

---

# 10.16 Renderer Diagnostics

Developer Mode exposes renderer metrics.

## Metrics

* Frame render time.
* Active render passes.
* GPU texture count.
* VRAM usage estimate.
* Dirty pass count.
* Composite latency.

---

## Diagnostics Contract

```typescript
interface RenderDiagnostics {
    renderTimeMs: number;
    activePasses: number;
    texturePoolUsage: number;
}
```

---

### Render Graph

* Graph validates successfully.
* No cyclic dependency.
* Pass ordering deterministic.

### Layer Tests

* Layer ordering correct.
* Opacity composited correctly.
* Visibility toggles without rerendering unrelated layers.

### Texture Tests

* Texture pooling works.
* No texture leaks after long playback.
* Framebuffers reused.

### Color Tests

* Linear blending matches export.
* Gamma correction applied once.
* Captions retain color fidelity.

### Performance Tests

* Dirty pass optimization works.
* Static layers skipped during preview.
* Preview render graph matches export graph.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 10.1)

1. Rendering is a deterministic GPU effect graph.
2. The render graph is a DAG with explicit dependencies.
3. Every visible feature is rendered as a layer.
4. GPU render passes communicate only through textures.
5. Effects activate only during timeline intervals.
6. Blend modes execute during composite pass.
7. Masks are rendered as alpha textures.
8. Internal rendering uses Linear RGB.
9. GPU resources are pooled and reused.
10. Preview and export share the exact same render graph.

# 10.16 Blur Engine Philosophy

The Blur Engine is a first-class rendering subsystem inside TryLipi. Blur is not treated as a CSS filter or a post-processing trick; instead, it is rendered as a GPU effect driven by timeline events and tracking metadata.

The engine supports:

* Privacy blur.
* Cursor spotlight blur.
* Face blur.
* Background blur.
* Region blur.
* Dynamic tracked blur.
* AI-generated blur suggestions.
* Animated blur transitions.

Every blur region exists independently on the timeline and can be edited, tracked, animated, duplicated, grouped, and exported.

---

## Golden Blur Rules

1. Source recording remains immutable.
2. Blur is applied only through masks.
3. Blur regions are timeline-driven objects.
4. Blur can attach to tracked subjects.
5. Blur intensity is keyframe animatable.
6. Multiple blur regions render simultaneously.
7. Preview and export produce identical blur output.

---

# 10.17 Blur Engine Architecture

The blur renderer is implemented as a dedicated GPU render graph.

```text
Video Frame
     │
Camera Crop
     │
Mask Generation
     │
Horizontal Gaussian Pass
     │
Vertical Gaussian Pass
     │
Feather Pass
     │
Composite Pass
```

Each stage writes into reusable render targets.

---

## Blur Engine Modules

```text
Blur Engine
│
├── Blur Track Store
├── Blur Region Manager
├── Mask Generator
├── Gaussian Shader
├── Subject Tracker Adapter
├── Blur Animator
├── Blur Texture Cache
└── Composite Integrator
```

Each module is isolated and communicates through immutable descriptors.

---

# 10.18 Blur Timeline Track

Blur regions are timeline events.

```typescript
interface BlurTrack {
    trackId: string;
    regionIds: string[];
    visible: boolean;
    locked: boolean;
}
```

Each region activates only during its timeline interval.

Supported timeline operations:

* Create.
* Delete.
* Resize.
* Animate.
* Track Subject.
* Duplicate.
* Group.

---

# 10.19 Blur Region Model

```typescript
interface BlurRegion {
    regionId: string;
    shape: "rectangle" | "roundedRect" | "circle" | "ellipse" | "polygon";
    startUs: number;
    endUs: number;
    intensity: number;
    featherRadius: number;
    trackingMode: "static" | "tracked";
}
```

A region references geometry only. Pixels are never stored.

---

## Region Coordinate System

Blur coordinates use normalized recording coordinates.

```typescript
interface BlurBounds {
    x: number;
    y: number;
    width: number;
    height: number;
}
```

Normalization guarantees resolution-independent behavior.

---

# 10.20 Blur Mask Generation Engine

Masks determine where blur exists.

### Supported Masks

| Shape             | Primary Use      |
| ----------------- | ---------------- |
| Rectangle         | Passwords        |
| Rounded Rectangle | Search bars      |
| Circle            | Cursor spotlight |
| Ellipse           | Faces            |
| Polygon           | Objects          |
| Freeform (future) | Brush blur       |

---

## Mask Generation Pipeline

```text
Blur Region
    │
Geometry Builder
    │
Alpha Mask Texture
```

Masks render into grayscale textures.

---

## Mask Texture Contract

```typescript
interface BlurMaskTexture {
    maskId: string;
    textureId: string;
    resolution: number;
}
```

Masks can be cached independently from blur textures.

---

# 10.21 Feather Engine

Blur edges should be soft.

The feather shader converts binary masks into distance-field masks.

```text
Binary Mask
     │
Distance Field
     │
Feather Shader
     │
Soft Mask
```

---

## Feather Parameters

```typescript
interface BlurFeather {
    radius: number;
    curve: "linear" | "smoothstep" | "gaussian";
}
```

Feather is independent from blur radius.

---

# 10.22 Gaussian Blur Pipeline

TryLipi uses separable Gaussian blur.

### Horizontal Pass

Samples neighboring pixels horizontally.

### Vertical Pass

Uses horizontal output.

This reduces complexity dramatically compared to a full 2D kernel.

---

## Blur Shader Parameters

```typescript
interface GaussianBlurShader {
    radius: number;
    sigma: number;
    direction: "horizontal" | "vertical";
}
```

---

# 10.23 Blur Radius Engine

Blur presets expose normalized intensity.

| Preset  | Radius |
| ------- | ------ |
| Light   | 8 px   |
| Medium  | 16 px  |
| Heavy   | 28 px  |
| Privacy | 48 px  |

Renderer converts normalized radius into device pixels.

---

## Radius Interpolation

Radius can animate through keyframes.

---

# 10.24 Multi-Pass GPU Optimization

Large blur kernels are expensive.

Optimization pipeline:

```text
4K Frame
   │
Downsample ×2
   │
Blur
   │
Upsample
   │
Composite
```

Downsampling is skipped for very small blur regions.

---

## Adaptive Resolution

| Radius | Internal Scale     |
| ------ | ------------------ |
| 8 px   | Full resolution    |
| 16 px  | Half resolution    |
| 28 px  | Quarter resolution |
| 48 px  | Quarter resolution |

---

# 10.25 Dynamic Subject Blur

Blur can follow moving subjects.

Supported subjects:

* Cursor.
* Face.
* Dialog.
* UI element.
* Custom tracked object.

---

## Tracking Contract

```typescript
interface TrackedBlurRegion {
    regionId: string;
    subjectId: string;
    padding: number;
}
```

Bounding boxes update every render frame.

---

# 10.26 Face Blur Engine

Automatic face blur uses Vision Engine outputs.

Pipeline:

```text
Video Frame
    │
Face Detector
    │
Landmarks
    │
Ellipse Generator
    │
Blur Mask
```

---

## Face Padding

Default padding expands beyond detected landmarks to avoid clipping hair and chin.

---

## Multiple Faces

Each face receives an independent blur region.

---

# 10.27 Background Blur Engine

Background blur keeps attention on the subject.

Pipeline:

```text
Subject Mask
    │
Invert Mask
    │
Blur Background
    │
Composite Subject
```

Useful for webcam overlays and talking-head tutorials.

---

# 10.28 Region Blur Engine

Manual blur is the primary privacy tool.

Typical use cases:

* API keys.
* Email addresses.
* Phone numbers.
* Notifications.
* Personal chats.

Regions support resize and move without regenerating source media.

---

## Manual Blur Contract

```typescript
interface ManualBlurRegion {
    regionId: string;
    bounds: BlurBounds;
    intensity: number;
}
```

---

# 10.29 Multi-Region Blur Composition

Multiple blur masks merge into one render pass.

Pipeline:

```text
Mask A
Mask B
Mask C
   │
Mask Merge Shader
   │
Combined Blur Mask
```

Overlapping masks share blurred pixels.

---

## Composition Rules

* Union overlapping regions.
* Preserve feather transitions.
* Maintain deterministic ordering.

---

# 10.30 Blur Cache Engine

Static blur should never rerender every frame.

### Cache Candidates

* Static privacy masks.
* Persistent webcam background blur.
* Long-duration blur overlays.

---

## Cache Lifecycle

```text
Mask Created
    │
Blur Generated
    │
Cache Texture
    │
Reuse
```

Invalidate only when geometry changes.

---

# 10.31 Blur Animation Engine

Blur properties are timeline keyframes.

Animatable properties:

* Radius.
* Feather.
* Opacity.
* Position.
* Scale.

---

## Blur Keyframe Contract

```typescript
interface BlurKeyframe {
    timestampUs: number;
    radius: number;
    opacity: number;
}
```

Interpolation uses Chapter 09 easing curves.

---

# 10.32 Reveal Blur Animation

Blur can animate away to reveal content.

Example tutorial flow:

```text
Blur Password

↓

Narration

↓

Blur Radius ↓

↓

Content Visible
```

---

## Reveal Modes

* Fade radius.
* Fade opacity.
* Scale reveal.
* Directional reveal (future).

---

# 10.33 Blur Performance Engine

Blur is GPU-expensive.

Optimization strategies:

* Downsample.
* Texture pooling.
* Static cache.
* Visibility culling.
* Region batching.

---

## Runtime Metrics

```typescript
interface BlurPerformanceMetrics {
    maskGenerationMs: number;
    blurShaderMs: number;
    compositeMs: number;
}
```

---

## Target Budgets

| Stage           | Budget     |
| --------------- | ---------- |
| Mask generation | Under 1 ms |
| Blur shader     | Under 3 ms |
| Composite       | Under 2 ms |

Target total blur cost: **Under 6 ms/frame**.

---

# 10.34 Blur Memory Strategy

Blur uses pooled GPU textures.

Texture pool includes:

* Source texture.
* Horizontal blur texture.
* Vertical blur texture.
* Mask texture.
* Composite texture.

Intermediate textures are recycled through the GPU Resource Manager (Chapter 07).

---

## Memory Rules

* Never allocate textures during playback.
* Reuse framebuffer attachments.
* Destroy cached blur only after timeline invalidation.

---

# 10.35 Acceptance Tests

### Blur Rendering

* Rectangle blur renders correctly.
* Circle blur renders correctly.
* Polygon blur renders correctly.

### Tracking

* Face blur follows face.
* Cursor blur follows cursor.
* Dialog blur follows tracked dialog.

### Animation

* Radius interpolation.
* Feather interpolation.
* Reveal blur transition.

### Performance

* Static masks cached.
* Dynamic masks updated.
* Multi-pass blur stays within GPU budget.
* Preview matches export pixel-for-pixel.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 10.2)

1. Blur is always mask-driven.
2. Gaussian blur uses separable horizontal and vertical passes.
3. Blur regions are immutable timeline objects.
4. Feathering is implemented in shaders.
5. Dynamic blur follows tracked subjects.
6. Background blur uses inverted subject masks.
7. Static blur textures are cached.
8. Blur properties are keyframe animatable.
9. Downsampling is used for large-radius blur.
10. Preview and export share identical blur rendering behavior.

# 10.36 Highlight & Annotation Philosophy

Highlights and annotations are storytelling tools.

They should guide attention without obscuring UI or creating visual noise.

Unlike traditional editors, every highlight is timeline-aware and GPU-rendered.

## Golden Highlight Rules

1. Highlights never modify source pixels.
2. Every highlight is timeline-driven.
3. Shapes are vector objects.
4. Cursor effects are rendered independently.
5. Animations are keyframe-based.
6. Preview equals export.
7. Annotations remain resolution independent.

---

## Highlight Responsibilities

* Spotlight.
* Glow.
* Cursor halo.
* Click ripple.
* Cursor trails.
* Boxes.
* Circles.
* Arrows.
* Freeform SVG annotations.
* Callouts.

---

# 10.59 Caption Rendering Philosophy

Captions are not static subtitles.

In TryLipi, captions are animated visual elements synchronized with speech, timeline events, cursor interactions, and AI emphasis.

Every caption is rendered through the GPU compositor and behaves like any other timeline effect.

## Golden Caption Rules

1. Captions are immutable timeline objects.
2. Word timing is independent from sentence timing.
3. Captions are resolution independent.
4. Every animation is keyframe driven.
5. Preview and export produce identical typography.
6. Multilingual rendering is a first-class feature.
7. Caption layout is deterministic.

---

## Caption Responsibilities

* Sentence captions.
* Word-level captions.
* Karaoke captions.
* Emoji rendering.
* Highlighted keywords.
* Background capsules.
* Animated text.
* Multilingual typography.

---

| --------------- | ---------------- |
| Create Caption  | Add subtitle     |

| Delete Caption  | Remove           |
| Split Caption   | Divide sentence  |
| Merge Caption   | Combine captions |
| Animate Caption | Apply animation  |

Captions activate only during their temporal interval.

# 10.82 GPU Compositor Philosophy

The GPU Compositor is the **final authority** responsible for producing every rendered frame inside TryLipi.

All timeline effects eventually become GPU commands executed in deterministic order.

The compositor receives immutable render instructions and produces exactly one output frame.

## Golden Compositor Rules

1. One input frame → one deterministic output frame.
2. Effects execute in canonical order.
3. Textures are immutable within a render pass.
4. Intermediate textures are pooled.
5. Preview and export share identical compositor logic.
6. Rendering is deterministic across devices.
7. The compositor owns no business logic.

---

## Responsibilities

* Execute render graph.
* Manage framebuffers.
* Schedule GPU passes.
* Blend layers.
* Reuse textures.
* Synchronize preview/export.
* Produce final RGBA texture.

---

# 10.83 GPU Compositor Architecture

The compositor lives inside the Rendering Worker.

## High-Level Architecture

```text
Timeline Snapshot
        │
Render Graph Scheduler
        │
GPU Compositor
│
├── Framebuffer Manager
├── Texture Pool
├── Shader Manager
├── Pass Executor
├── Composite Engine
└── Diagnostics
        │
Output Texture
```

The compositor never reads UI state directly.

---

## Compositor Contract

```typescript
interface GPUCompositor {

    render(frameTimestampUs:number):Promise<GPUTexture>;

}
```

---

# 10.84 Framebuffer Orchestration Engine

Every render pass renders into its own framebuffer.

```text
↓

↓

↓

↓

Caption Pass

↓

↓

Composite Framebuffer
```

## Framebuffer Contract

```typescript
    framebufferId:string;

    textureId:string;

    width:number;

    height:number;

}
```

---

## Framebuffer Rules

* Never allocate during playback.
* Acquire from pool.
* Release immediately after final consumer.

# 11.1 Export Pipeline Philosophy

The Export Engine is the subsystem responsible for transforming a completed TryLipi project into a distributable video file.

Unlike live preview, export is **offline deterministic rendering**.

The export engine **never records the screen again**. It reconstructs the project entirely from timeline state and renders every frame using the Rendering Engine defined in Chapter 10.

## Golden Export Principles

1. Export begins from an immutable project snapshot.
2. Rendering is independent from playback.
3. Export timing never depends on display refresh rate.
4. Export is deterministic across supported browsers and operating systems.
5. Export continues even when the UI is minimized or hidden (subject to browser capabilities).
6. Export supports recovery after recoverable failures.
7. Preview and export use identical rendering code.

---

## Responsibilities of Export Engine

The Export Engine owns:

* Timeline freezing.
* Asset validation.
* Frame scheduling.
* Timeline replay.
* Video rendering.
* Audio rendering.
* Video encoding.
* Audio encoding.
* Container muxing.
* Progress reporting.
* Export recovery.

---

# 11.2 Export Engine Architecture

Export runs inside dedicated workers separate from React UI.

```text
React UI
   │
Export Controller
   │
Export Worker
   │
Timeline Replay
   │
Rendering Worker
   │
GPU Compositor
   │
WebCodecs Encoder
   │
Muxer Worker
   │
Final MP4
```

---

## Major Components

| Component              | Responsibility           |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Export Controller      | Starts/stops exports     |
| Snapshot Loader        | Freezes project          |
| Timeline Replay Engine | Reconstructs frame state |
| Frame Scheduler        | Generates timestamps     |
| Render Dispatcher      | Sends frames to renderer |
| Video Encoder          | WebCodecs encoding       |
| Audio Renderer         | PCM generation           |
| Audio Encoder          | AAC/Opus encoding        |
| Muxer                  | Builds MP4/WebM          |
| Progress Manager       | ETA/progress             |
| Recovery Manager       | Resume/cancel/retry      |

---

# 11.3 Export Job Lifecycle

Every export is represented by an immutable export job.

## Lifecycle

```text
Created
   │
Queued
   │
Preparing
   │
Rendering Frames
   │
Encoding Video
   │
Encoding Audio
   │
Muxing
   │
Finalizing
   │
Completed
```

Alternative terminal states:

* Cancelled
* Failed

---

## Export Job Contract

```typescript
interface ExportJob {

    exportId:string;

    snapshotId:string;

    configurationId:string;

    state:"queued" | "preparing" | "rendering" | "encoding" | "muxing" | "completed" | "failed" | "cancelled";

    progress:number;

    createdAt:number;

}
```

---

## Lifecycle Rules

* Job references snapshot only.
* Job never mutates timeline.
* Jobs survive UI reload if persistence is enabled.

---

```typescript
}
```

* Unsupported fonts.

* Invalid export settings.
* Missing audio.

# 11.9 Render Clock

```typescript
}
```

---

## Timestamp Formula

<math block value="timestampUs = frameIndex \\times frameDurationUs"/>

Where:

<math block value="frameDurationUs = \\frac{1,000,000}{fps}"/>

---

## Supported FPS

* 24
* 25
* 30
* 50
* 60

Future:

* 120

| ------------------------- | ---------------------- |

```typescript
    reason:string;

}
```

* Completed frames remain valid.

# Canonical Rules (Part 11.1)

1. Export begins from an immutable snapshot.
2. Timeline replay reconstructs frame state deterministically.
3. Render Clock is independent from playback.
4. Frame Scheduler generates fixed timestamps.
5. Export configuration is immutable during rendering.
6. Progress reflects completed work, not elapsed time.
7. Queue Manager isolates export jobs.
8. Cancellation safely drains encoder resources.
9. Recovery uses snapshot checkpoints.
10. Preview and export share identical timeline replay.

# 11.17 WebCodecs Philosophy

TryLipi uses the **WebCodecs API** as the primary video encoding interface.

Unlike MediaRecorder, WebCodecs provides:

* deterministic frame encoding,
* frame-level timestamps,
* bitrate control,
* hardware acceleration,
* low-latency encoding.

The Rendering Engine produces raw GPU frames. WebCodecs converts those frames into compressed video packets.

## Golden WebCodecs Rules

1. Every rendered frame is explicitly encoded.
2. Encoder never requests frames from the renderer.
3. Presentation timestamps come from Render Clock.
4. Hardware acceleration is preferred when available.
5. Software encoding is supported as fallback.
6. Encoded chunks are immutable.
7. Video encoding is deterministic.

---

## Responsibilities

The Video Encoder subsystem owns:

* VideoEncoder lifecycle.
* Hardware capability detection.
* Frame submission.
* Keyframe scheduling.
* Bitrate control.
* Timestamp generation.
* Backpressure management.
* Encoder diagnostics.

---

# 11.18 VideoEncoder Architecture

The encoder lives inside the Export Worker.

## Encoding Pipeline

```text
GPU Renderer
      │
VideoFrame
      │
Frame Queue
      │
VideoEncoder
      │
EncodedVideoChunk
      │
Muxer Queue
```

The encoder receives `VideoFrame` objects directly from WebCodecs-compatible GPU textures whenever possible.

---

## Encoder Modules

```text
Video Encoder Engine
│
├── Capability Detector
├── Encoder Config Builder
├── Frame Queue
├── Timestamp Manager
├── Bitrate Controller
├── Keyframe Scheduler
├── Chunk Dispatcher
└── Diagnostics Engine
```

---

# 11.19 Hardware Acceleration Detection

Hardware encoding dramatically reduces export time.

TryLipi detects browser capabilities before export begins.

## Detection Pipeline

```text
Browser
   │
VideoEncoder.isConfigSupported()
   │
Supported Configurations
   │
Hardware Preference
```

---

## Detection Contract

```typescript
interface HardwareEncoderSupport {
    codec: string;
    hardwareAccelerated: boolean;
    supported: boolean;
}
```

---

## Detection Priority

| Priority | Encoder               |
| -------- | --------------------- |
| 1        | Hardware H.264        |
| 2        | Hardware VP9 (future) |
| 3        | Software H.264        |
| 4        | Software VP9          |

---

## Rules

* Hardware is preferred.
* Software fallback is automatic.
* Unsupported codecs never start export.

---

# 11.20 Codec Capability Matrix

Supported codec capabilities are cached for the session.

## Capability Fields

| Field      | Example     |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| Codec      | avc1.640028 |
| Resolution | 3840×2160   |
| FPS        | 60          |
| Bitrate    | 35 Mbps     |
| Hardware   | true        |

---

## Capability Contract

```typescript
interface CodecCapability {
    codec: string;
    maxWidth: number;
    maxHeight: number;
    maxFps: number;
}
```

---

## Cache Rules

Capabilities are cached until browser restart.

---

# 11.21 Encoder Configuration Engine

The configuration builder converts export presets into WebCodecs settings.

## Configuration Inputs

* Width.
* Height.
* FPS.
* Bitrate.
* Codec.
* Hardware preference.

---

## Encoder Config Contract

```typescript
interface VideoEncoderConfiguration {
    codec: string;
    width: number;
    height: number;
    bitrate: number;
    framerate: number;
    hardwareAcceleration:
        | "prefer-hardware"
        | "prefer-software";
}
```

---

## Configuration Rules

Encoder configuration is immutable after initialization.

---

# 11.22 H.264 Encoding Pipeline

TryLipi MVP exports H.264 MP4.

## Pipeline

```text
Rendered Frame
      │
VideoFrame
      │
VideoEncoder.encode()
      │
Encoded Chunk
      │
Muxer
```

---

## Supported Profiles

| Profile  | Usage         |
| -------- | ------------- |
| Baseline | Compatibility |
| Main     | Standard HD   |
| High     | 4K Export     |

---

## Profile Selection

Automatically selected from export preset.

---

# 11.23 VideoFrame Construction Engine

Every rendered texture becomes a WebCodecs `VideoFrame`.

## Frame Construction Pipeline

```text
GPU Texture
      │
RGBA Surface
      │
VideoFrame
      │
Encoder Queue
```

---

## VideoFrame Contract

```typescript
interface ExportVideoFrame {
    timestampUs: number;
    durationUs: number;
}
```

---

## Rules

* Frames closed immediately after encoding.
* No VideoFrame leaks.
* GPU-backed frames preferred.

---

# 11.24 Timestamp & Presentation Time Engine

Every encoded frame receives deterministic timestamps.

## Timestamp Flow

```text
Frame Index
     │
Render Clock
     │
PTS
     │
VideoFrame.timestamp
```

---

## Timestamp Formula

<math block value="PTS = frameIndex \\times frameDurationUs"/>

---

## Timestamp Contract

```typescript
interface PresentationTimestamp {
    ptsUs: number;
    durationUs: number;
}
```

---

## Rules

PTS always increases monotonically.

---

# 11.25 Decode Timestamp (DTS) Strategy

H.264 requires decode timestamps internally.

## DTS Rules

* Equal to PTS for MVP.
* Future B-frame support separates DTS/PTS.

---

## DTS Contract

```typescript
interface DecodeTimestamp {
    dtsUs: number;
}
```

---

# 11.26 Keyframe Scheduler

Keyframes improve seeking and editing.

## Default Strategy

* First frame.
* Every 2 seconds.
* Scene transition.
* Manual forced keyframe.

---

## Scheduler Pipeline

```text
Frame Timestamp
      │
Keyframe Policy
      │
encode({ keyFrame:true })
```

---

## Keyframe Contract

```typescript
interface KeyframeSchedule {
    intervalFrames: number;
}
```

---

## Rules

Scene transitions always receive keyframes.

---

# 11.27 Scene-Aware Keyframes

The scheduler inserts additional keyframes.

## Triggers

* Camera jump.
* Large blur reveal.
* Hard cut.
* Aspect ratio change (future).

---

## Benefits

* Faster seeking.
* Cleaner edits.
* Better compression after transitions.

---

# 11.28 Bitrate Controller

Bitrate is adaptive based on export preset.

## Default Targets

| Export  | Bitrate |
| ------- | ------- |
| 1080p30 | 8 Mbps  |
| 1080p60 | 12 Mbps |
| 1440p60 | 20 Mbps |
| 4K30    | 25 Mbps |
| 4K60    | 35 Mbps |

---

## Bitrate Contract

```typescript
interface BitrateController {
    targetBitrate: number;
    maxBitrate: number;
}
```

---

## Rules

Bitrate remains constant for MVP.

---

# 11.29 Quality Controller

Quality presets map to bitrate ranges.

## Presets

| Preset       | Behavior               |
| ------------ | ---------------------- |
| Draft        | Lower bitrate          |
| Balanced     | Default                |
| High Quality | Higher bitrate         |
| Creator Pro  | Maximum preset bitrate |

---

## Quality Contract

```typescript
interface QualityPreset {
    presetId: string;
    bitrateMultiplier: number;
}
```

---

# 11.30 Frame Queue Engine

The renderer may produce frames faster than encoder consumption.

The Frame Queue buffers frames safely.

## Queue Pipeline

```text
Renderer

↓

Frame Queue

↓

VideoEncoder

↓

Encoded Queue
```

---

## Queue Contract

```typescript
interface FrameQueue {
    queuedFrames: number;
    maxFrames: number;
}
```

---

## Queue Rules

* FIFO ordering.
* Bounded memory.
* Timestamp order preserved.

---

# 11.31 Backpressure Management Engine

The encoder may become temporarily slower than rendering.

## Strategy

* Pause renderer.
* Drain encoder queue.
* Resume rendering.
* Preserve timestamps.

---

## Backpressure Contract

```typescript
interface EncoderBackpressure {
    queueDepth: number;
    paused: boolean;
}
```

---

## Rules

Renderer never drops frames because of encoder pressure.

---

# 11.32 Encoded Chunk Dispatcher

Encoded chunks move to muxer asynchronously.

## Dispatcher Pipeline

```text
EncodedVideoChunk

↓

Chunk Queue

↓

Muxer Worker
```

---

## Chunk Contract

```typescript
interface EncodedChunkMetadata {
    timestampUs: number;
    isKeyframe: boolean;
}
```

---

## Rules

Chunks remain ordered by timestamp.

---

# 11.33 Encoder Flush Engine

The encoder must flush remaining frames.

## Flush Pipeline

```text
Last Frame

↓

VideoEncoder.flush()

↓

Remaining Chunks

↓

Muxer
```

---

## Flush Rules

Export never finalizes before successful flush.

---

# 11.34 Encoder Reset & Recovery

Recoverable encoder failures should restart encoding safely.

## Recovery Pipeline

```text
Encoder Error

↓

Flush Queue

↓

Reinitialize Encoder

↓

Resume Frame Queue
```

---

## Recovery Contract

```typescript
interface EncoderRecovery {
    recovered: boolean;
    resumeFrame: number;
}
```

---

## Recoverable Errors

| Error              | Recovery          |
| ------------------ | ----------------- |
| Encoder reset      | Restart encoder   |
| Hardware failure   | Software fallback |
| Memory pressure    | Drain queue       |
| Context recreation | Rebuild encoder   |

---

# 11.35 Encoder Diagnostics

Developer Mode exposes encoder metrics.

## Metrics

* Queue depth.
* Encoded FPS.
* Hardware/software mode.
* Bitrate.
* Average encode latency.
* Keyframe count.

---

## Diagnostics Contract

```typescript
interface EncoderDiagnostics {
    encodeLatencyMs: number;
    queueDepth: number;
    hardwareAcceleration: boolean;
}
```

---

# 11.36 Performance Budgets

## Target Encode Latency

| Export  | Budget            |
| ------- | ----------------- |
| 1080p30 | Under 5 ms/frame  |
| 1080p60 | Under 7 ms/frame  |
| 4K30    | Under 10 ms/frame |
| 4K60    | Under 14 ms/frame |

---

## Memory Budgets

| Resource        | Budget        |
| --------------- | ------------- |
| Frame Queue     | 32 frames max |
| Encoded Queue   | 64 chunks     |
| Encoder Buffers | 64 MB         |

---

# 11.37 Acceptance Tests

### Capability Tests

* Hardware detection succeeds.
* Software fallback succeeds.

### Encoding Tests

* Every frame encoded.
* Timestamps monotonic.
* Keyframes scheduled correctly.

### Queue Tests

* Backpressure pauses renderer.
* Queue drains correctly.

### Recovery Tests

* Encoder reset recovers.
* Hardware fallback works.
* Flush completes successfully.

---

# Canonical Rules (Part 11.2)

1. WebCodecs is the primary encoding API.
2. Hardware encoding is preferred when supported.
3. Encoder configuration is immutable after initialization.
4. Every rendered frame becomes one `VideoFrame`.
5. Presentation timestamps come from Render Clock.
6. Keyframes are deterministic and scene-aware.
7. Frame Queue preserves ordering under backpressure.
8. Encoded chunks are immutable.
9. Encoder flush completes before muxing.
10. Hardware failures fall back to software encoding without changing timeline output.

# 11.38 Audio Rendering Philosophy

Audio is rendered offline exactly like video.

TryLipi never exports audio captured from playback. Every sample is reconstructed from immutable timeline events.

The Audio Engine produces deterministic PCM buffers synchronized with the Render Clock.

## Golden Audio Rules

1. Audio timeline is immutable during export.
2. Audio rendering is sample accurate.
3. Audio uses the same timeline clock as video.
4. Audio effects never modify source assets.
5. Mixing is deterministic.
6. Exported audio is independent from browser playback latency.
7. Preview and export share identical audio graph logic.

---

## Responsibilities

The Audio Engine owns:

* Voiceover rendering.
* Background music rendering.
* Sound effects.
* Audio fades.
* Volume automation.
* Auto ducking.
* PCM generation.
* Waveform generation.
* Audio synchronization.
* AAC preparation.

---

# 11.39 Audio Engine Architecture

Audio rendering executes inside the Export Worker.

## High-Level Pipeline

```text
Audio Timeline
      │
Timeline Replay
      │
Audio Graph
      │
PCM Mixer
      │
Audio Renderer
      │
PCM Output
      │
AAC Encoder
```

Unlike preview playback, export renders audio offline without real-time constraints.

---

## Audio Engine Modules

```text
Audio Engine
│
├── Timeline Resolver
├── Clip Scheduler
├── Audio Graph Builder
├── PCM Mixer
├── Voiceover Processor
├── Music Processor
├── Envelope Processor
├── Ducking Processor
├── Waveform Generator
└── Diagnostics
```

---

# 11.40 Audio Timeline Track

Audio clips live on dedicated timeline tracks.

## Track Types

| Track          | Purpose                |
| -------------- | ---------------------- |
| Voice Track    | Narration              |
| Music Track    | Background music       |
| SFX Track      | Clicks, whooshes       |
| Imported Audio | External files         |
| System Audio   | Screen recording audio |

---

## Audio Track Contract

```typescript
interface AudioTrack {
    trackId:string;
    clipIds:string[];
    muted:boolean;
    solo:boolean;
    volume:number;
}
```

---

## Timeline Rules

Tracks are independent and mix together during rendering.

---

# 11.41 Audio Clip Data Model

Every audio asset becomes an immutable clip.

## Audio Clip Contract

```typescript
interface AudioClip {
    clipId:string;
    assetId:string;
    startUs:number;
    endUs:number;
    trimStartUs:number;
    trimEndUs:number;
    gainDb:number;
}
```

---

## Clip Metadata

* Language.
* Source type.
* Sample rate.
* Channels.
* Loudness metadata.
* AI generated flag.

---

# 11.42 Audio Graph System

Audio rendering uses a directed graph similar to the Render Graph.

## Audio Graph

```text
Voiceover
      │
Gain
      │
EQ
      │
Compressor
      │
Mixer
```

Multiple tracks merge into a Master Bus.

---

## Graph Principles

* Immutable inputs.
* Ordered processors.
* Sample-accurate scheduling.
* Deterministic output.

---

## Audio Graph Contract

```typescript
interface AudioGraphNode {
    nodeId:string;
    inputNodes:string[];
    outputNode:string;
}
```

---

# 11.43 Audio Clip Scheduler

The scheduler activates clips by timestamp.

## Scheduler Pipeline

```text
Render Timestamp
      │
Clip Resolver
      │
Active PCM Streams
```

---

## Responsibilities

* Activate clips.
* Apply trims.
* Apply fades.
* Route clips into graph.

---

## Scheduler Contract

```typescript
    timestampUs:number;

}
```

---

# 11.44 PCM Rendering Engine

All audio processing occurs in floating-point PCM.

## Internal Format

| Property      | Value     |
| ------------- | --------- |
| Sample Format | Float32   |
| Channels      | Stereo    |
| Sample Rate   | 48,000 Hz |

---

## PCM Pipeline

```text
Audio Asset
     │
Decode PCM
     │
Process Effects
     │
Mixer
     │
Master PCM
```

---

## PCM Contract

```typescript
interface PCMBuffer {
    sampleRate:number;
    channels:number;
    samples:Float32Array[];
}
```

---

## Rules

PCM buffers remain normalized between -1 and 1.

---

# 11.45 Sample Clock Engine

Audio uses sample timestamps instead of frame timestamps.

## Formula

Sample index derives from Render Clock timestamp.

<math block value="sampleIndex = timestampUs \\times \\frac{sampleRate}{1,000,000}"/>

---

## Sample Clock Contract

```typescript
interface SampleClock {
    sampleRate:number;
    currentSample:number;
}
```

---

## Rules

No cumulative floating-point drift.

---

# 11.46 Audio Mixing Engine

The mixer combines multiple PCM streams.

## Mixing Pipeline

```text
Voice PCM
Music PCM
SFX PCM
System PCM
     │
Gain Stage
     │
Master Mix
```

---

## Mixing Rules

* Sample aligned.
* Gain applied before summing.
* Soft clipping prevention.
* Master limiter after mix.

---

## Mixer Contract

```typescript
interface AudioMixer {
    masterGain:number;
    outputChannels:number;
}
```

---

# 11.57 Drift Detection Engine

Long exports require sync verification.

## Drift Formula

<math block value="driftUs = videoTimestampUs - audioTimestampUs"/>

---

## Thresholds

| Drift         | Action                   |
| ------------- | ------------------------ |
| Under 500 µs  | Ignore                   |
| 500–2000 µs   | Correct sample alignment |
| Above 2000 µs | Diagnostics event        |

## Audio Tests

# Canonical Rules (Part 11.3)

1. Audio rendering is offline and deterministic.
2. PCM Float32 is the internal working format.
3. Audio timeline is sample accurate.
4. Voiceover has priority during ducking.
5. Volume automation is logarithmic.

# 11.62 Container Philosophy

Encoded audio and video packets are not directly playable files.

The **Muxer Engine** combines encoded streams into a valid media container while preserving timestamps, synchronization, metadata, and seekability.

The muxer never re-encodes media. It only packages encoded chunks.

## Golden Container Rules

1. Muxing never modifies encoded packets.
2. Audio and video timestamps remain unchanged.
3. Output container is deterministic.
4. Metadata is injected after track creation.
5. MP4 supports fast-start playback.
6. Progressive writing minimizes memory usage.
7. Output file passes integrity validation.

---

## Responsibilities

The Container Engine owns:

* MP4 box generation.
* WebM segment generation.
* Audio/video interleaving.
* Metadata injection.
* Poster frame creation.
* Progressive writing.
* Integrity validation.

---

# 11.63 MP4 Container Architecture

MP4 is the default export container for TryLipi.

## MP4 Structure

```text id="jlwm01"
ftyp
 ├── moov
 │     ├── mvhd
 │     ├── trak(video)
 │     ├── trak(audio)
 │     └── udta
 ├── mdat
 └── free
```

The `moov` atom contains metadata.

The `mdat` atom contains encoded media packets.

---

## MP4 Module Responsibilities

```text id="jlwm02"
MP4 Builder
│
├── Box Generator
├── Track Builder
├── Chunk Indexer
├── Sample Table Builder
├── Metadata Writer
└── FastStart Optimizer
```

---

Every MP4 file is built from ISO BMFF boxes.

| ---- | ------------------ |
| ftyp | File compatibility |

| mvhd | Movie header       |
| trak | Audio/video tracks |
| mdia | Media info         |
| stbl | Sample table       |
| mdat | Encoded media      |

```typescript id="jlwm03"
}
```

1. Muxing never re-encodes media.
2. MP4 is the default export container.
3. Audio/video packets are interleaved by timestamp.

5. Progressive writing avoids full-file buffering.
6. Metadata is injected after track creation.
7. Poster frame generation skips empty frames.
8. Output integrity is validated before completion.
9. Export manifests describe every generated artifact.
10. Output files are deterministic for identical snapshots.

# 11.85 Resumable Export Philosophy

Large exports should survive interruptions whenever possible.

Instead of treating export as one long process, TryLipi treats it as a sequence of deterministic checkpoints.

If rendering fails, the export engine resumes from the latest completed checkpoint instead of starting over.

## Golden Resume Rules

1. Project snapshot is immutable.
2. Checkpoints never modify rendered output.
3. Resume never changes timestamps.
4. Previously encoded packets remain valid.
5. Recovery is deterministic.
6. Failed exports preserve diagnostics.
7. Resume is transparent to users.

---

## Supported Recovery Events

| Failure                   | Resume Supported              |
| ------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Worker crash              | Yes                           |
| GPU context loss          | Yes                           |
| Temporary memory pressure | Yes                           |
| Browser tab reload        | Planned                       |
| Browser closed            | Planned (persistent snapshot) |

---

# 11.86 Export Checkpoint Engine

The export engine periodically writes checkpoints.

## Checkpoint Frequency

| Export Length | Interval          |
| ------------- | ----------------- |
| Under 5 min   | Every 300 frames  |
| 5–20 min      | Every 600 frames  |
| Over 20 min   | Every 1200 frames |

---

## Checkpoint Pipeline

```text id="expchk01"
Rendered Frames
      │
Encoder Flush
      │
Checkpoint Manifest
      │
IndexedDB Storage
```

---

## Checkpoint Contract

```typescript id="expchk02"
interface ExportCheckpoint {
    exportId:string;
    frameIndex:number;
    videoChunkCount:number;
    audioChunkCount:number;
    createdAt:number;
}
```

---

## Checkpoint Rules

* Checkpoints created only after encoder flush.
* Audio/video queues must both be synchronized.
* Checkpoints are immutable.

---

Checkpoint metadata is stored separately from media buffers.

## Storage Layers

| Layer            | Storage                |
| ---------------- | ---------------------- |
| Snapshot         | IndexedDB              |

| Diagnostics      | IndexedDB              |
| Temporary chunks | Memory / OPFS (future) |

---

## Storage Contract

```typescript id="expchk03"
}
```

## Rules

```text id="expchk04"
Restore Snapshot

Restore Timeline Clock
```

# 12.1 Audio Engine Philosophy

The **Audio Engine** is the subsystem responsible for capturing, processing, synchronizing, monitoring, recording, and exporting every audio signal inside TryLipi.

Unlike traditional browser screen recorders that merge microphone and system audio into one compressed stream, TryLipi treats audio as **structured timeline data**.

Every source is recorded independently, timestamped independently, processed independently, and mixed only during preview or export.

This architecture enables future AI features such as:

* AI captions.
* Voice cleanup.
* Speaker diarization.
* Dubbing.
* Voice cloning.
* Lip sync alignment.
* Auto silence removal.
* Multilingual translation.

The foundational engine never depends on AI.

---

## Audio Engine Design Goals

<table columnSizing=auto><table-row><table-cell width="220">**Goal**</table-cell><table-cell>**Reason**</table-cell></table-row><table-row><table-cell>Sample Accurate</table-cell><table-cell>Perfect caption and lip-sync timing.</table-cell></table-row><table-row><table-cell>Low Latency Preview</table-cell><table-cell>Comfortable microphone monitoring while recording.</table-cell></table-row><table-row><table-cell>Multi Track</table-cell><table-cell>Independent microphone, system audio, music and SFX.</table-cell></table-row><table-row><table-cell>Non Destructive</table-cell><table-cell>Original recordings always preserved.</table-cell></table-row><table-row><table-cell>Deterministic</table-cell><table-cell>Preview equals exported audio exactly.</table-cell></table-row><table-row><table-cell>Recoverable</table-cell><table-cell>Recording survives interruptions whenever possible.</table-cell></table-row><table-row><table-cell>Extensible</table-cell><table-cell>Future AI voice features plug into the pipeline.</table-cell></table-row></table>

---

## Golden Audio Principles

1. Every audio source owns an independent timeline track.
2. PCM Float32 is the canonical internal representation.
3. Original recordings are immutable.
4. Every sample receives a deterministic timestamp.
5. Audio processing never mutates source assets.
6. Preview and export share identical DSP logic.
7. Export timing never depends on browser playback latency.

## Latency Tests

## Diagnostics Tests

* RMS meter accurate.
* Silence events generated.
* Dropped sample warnings emitted.

# Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 12.1)

1. Float32 PCM at **48 kHz stereo** is the canonical internal audio format.
2. Every audio source owns an independent timeline track.
3. Capture timestamps originate from the Capture Clock.
4. AudioWorklet performs deterministic real-time DSP only.
5. Ring buffers isolate capture from recording.
6. Preview latency never affects export timing.
7. Silence detection is annotation-only and non-destructive.
8. Waveforms are generated incrementally and cached.
9. Diagnostics expose latency, clipping, and buffer health.
10. Preview and export share identical foundational audio processing logic.

# 12.21 Voice Enhancement Philosophy

The Voice Enhancement Engine improves microphone recordings **without modifying the original recording**. Every enhancement is applied as a reversible DSP layer during preview and export.

The raw PCM captured in Part 12.1 always remains immutable.

## Golden Principles

* Enhancement is non-destructive.
* Original PCM is always preserved.
* Preview and export use identical DSP.
* Processing is deterministic.
* Every DSP stage has a fixed execution order.

---

# 12.22 DSP Processing Graph

Every microphone recording passes through the same enhancement pipeline.

```text
Raw Microphone PCM
        │
High-Pass Filter
        │
Noise Suppression
        │
Echo Cancellation
        │
Voice Isolation
        │
Automatic Gain Control
        │
Dynamic Compressor
        │
Voice Equalizer
        │
Limiter
        │
Enhanced PCM Output
```

### DSP Graph Model

```ts
interface VoiceDSPGraph {
  graphId: string;
  nodeOrder: string[];
}
```

### Processing Order

| Stage             | Purpose                             |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| High-Pass Filter  | Remove low-frequency rumble.        |
| Noise Suppression | Remove stationary background noise. |
| Echo Cancellation | Remove playback leakage.            |
| Voice Isolation   | Separate speech from noise.         |
| AGC               | Normalize voice loudness.           |
| Compressor        | Smooth dynamic range.               |
| Equalizer         | Improve clarity.                    |
| Limiter           | Prevent clipping.                   |

---

# 12.23 Voice Isolation Engine

Voice isolation separates the creator's speech from environmental sounds.

## Supported Background Sounds

| Noise           | Expected Behavior |
| --------------- | ----------------- |
| Ceiling Fan     | Suppressed        |
| Air Conditioner | Suppressed        |
| Keyboard Typing | Reduced           |
| Mouse Clicks    | Reduced           |
| Traffic         | Reduced           |
| Café Ambience   | Reduced           |
| Music Leakage   | Reduced           |

### Isolation Pipeline

```text
PCM Audio
    │
Short-Time Fourier Transform
    │
Voice Mask Estimator
    │
Speech Mask
    │
Inverse STFT
    │
Voice PCM
```

### Configuration

```ts
interface VoiceIsolationConfig {
  enabled: boolean;
  aggressiveness: number;
}
```

### Modes

| Mode     | Description          |
| -------- | -------------------- |
| Off      | Original microphone. |
| Mild     | Light cleanup.       |
| Balanced | Default preset.      |
| Strong   | Heavy suppression.   |
| Studio   | Maximum isolation.   |

### Rules

* Voice isolation is optional.
* Original recording is never replaced.
* Runs before AGC.

---

# 12.24 Noise Suppression Engine

Noise suppression removes stationary environmental noise while preserving speech.

## Supported Noise Types

| Noise Source   | Support |
| -------------- | ------- |
| Fan Noise      | ✅       |
| AC Hum         | ✅       |
| White Noise    | ✅       |
| Electrical Hum | ✅       |
| Keyboard Noise | Partial |
| Wind Noise     | Partial |

### Pipeline

```text
PCM
 │
FFT
 │
Noise Profile Estimation
 │
Spectral Mask
 │
Filtered PCM
```

### Configuration

```ts
interface NoiseSuppressionConfig {
  enabled: boolean;
  strength: number;
}
```

### Strength Scale

| Value | Meaning  |
| ----- | -------- |
| 0     | Disabled |
| 25    | Mild     |
| 50    | Balanced |
| 75    | Strong   |
| 100   | Maximum  |

### Rules

Speech frequencies receive higher priority than background frequencies.

---

# 12.25 RNNoise Integration

RNNoise is the primary real-time WASM noise suppression engine.

## Why RNNoise?

* Lightweight neural model.
* Browser-friendly.
* Low latency.
* Works entirely offline.

### Runtime Pipeline

```text
PCM Frames
     │
RNNoise WASM
     │
Enhanced PCM Frames
```

### Configuration

| Property    | Value           |
| ----------- | --------------- |
| Sample Rate | 48 kHz          |
| Frame Size  | 20 ms           |
| Runtime     | WebAssembly     |
| Channels    | Mono Internally |

### Runtime Model

```ts
interface RNNoiseRuntime {
  initialized: boolean;
  frameSize: number;
  sampleRate: number;
}
```

### Rules

* Runs inside WASM Worker.
* Never blocks UI thread.
* Uses SIMD when supported.

---

# 12.26 Echo Cancellation Engine

Echo cancellation removes speaker playback leaking into microphone capture.

## Echo Sources

| Source                | Removed |
| --------------------- | ------- |
| Laptop Speakers       | ✅       |
| External Speakers     | ✅       |
| Preview Playback      | ✅       |
| Browser Audio Leakage | ✅       |

### Pipeline

```text
Speaker Output Reference
        │
Adaptive Echo Filter
        │
Microphone PCM
        │
Echo-Free PCM
```

### Configuration

```ts
interface EchoCancellationConfig {
  enabled: boolean;
  adaptive: boolean;
}
```

### Modes

| Mode            | Description            |
| --------------- | ---------------------- |
| Browser Native  | Default MVP.           |
| Adaptive DSP    | Future implementation. |
| AI Echo Removal | Future neural model.   |

### Rules

Echo cancellation always runs before AGC.

---

# 12.27 Automatic Gain Control (AGC)

AGC maintains consistent narration loudness without clipping.

### AGC Pipeline

```text
Voice PCM
    │
Loudness Detector
    │
Gain Calculator
    │
Gain Smoother
    │
Normalized Voice PCM
```

### Configuration

```ts
interface AutomaticGainControlConfig {
  targetDb: number;
  attackMs: number;
  releaseMs: number;
}
```

### Default Settings

| Parameter       | Value  |
| --------------- | ------ |
| Target Loudness | -18 dB |
| Attack          | 40 ms  |
| Release         | 250 ms |

### Rules

* Never clips samples.
* Smooth gain transitions.
* Preserves natural speech dynamics.

---

# 12.28 Voice Activity Detection (VAD)

VAD identifies speech regions inside the recording.

### Responsibilities

* Detect speech.
* Detect silence.
* Trigger transcription.
* Trigger ducking.
* Optimize AI processing.

### Pipeline

```text
PCM Audio
     │
Frame Energy
     │
Spectral Features
     │
Speech Probability
     │
Speech Segments
```

### Model

```ts
interface VoiceActivitySegment {
  startUs: number;
  endUs: number;
  confidence: number;
}
```

### Confidence Levels

| Probability | Meaning         |
| ----------- | --------------- |
| 0.0–0.2     | Silence         |
| 0.2–0.5     | Possible Speech |
| 0.5–0.8     | Speech Detected |
| 0.8–1.0     | Strong Speech   |

### Rules

VAD generates annotations only.

---

# 12.29 Spectral Noise Reduction

Traditional DSP fallback when neural suppression is disabled.

### Pipeline

```text
PCM Frames
     │
FFT
     │
Noise Spectrum Estimate
     │
Spectral Mask
     │
Magnitude Reduction
     │
Inverse FFT
     │
Enhanced PCM
```

### Configuration

```ts
interface SpectralNoiseReductionConfig {
  fftSize: number;
  overlap: number;
  reductionDb: number;
}
```

### FFT Defaults

| Property | Value |
| -------- | ----- |
| FFT Size | 1024  |
| Window   | Hann  |
| Overlap  | 50%   |
| Hop Size | 512   |

### Rules

Adaptive masking updates only during silence windows.

---

# 12.30 Dynamic Range Compression

Compression smooths loudness differences across narration.

### Compression Pipeline

```text
Voice PCM
    │
Envelope Detector
    │
Threshold
    │
Gain Reduction
    │
Compressed Voice PCM
```

### Configuration

```ts
interface VoiceCompressorConfig {
  thresholdDb: number;
  ratio: number;
  attackMs: number;
  releaseMs: number;
}
```

### Default Creator Preset

| Parameter | Value  |
| --------- | ------ |
| Threshold | -20 dB |
| Ratio     | 3:1    |
| Attack    | 10 ms  |
| Release   | 120 ms |

### Rules

Compression executes after AGC.

---

# 12.31 Voice Equalizer

Equalization improves speech intelligibility.

### Five-Band EQ

| Band     | Default Gain |
| -------- | ------------ |
| Bass     | 0 dB         |
| Low Mid  | +1 dB        |
| Mid      | +2 dB        |
| Presence | +3 dB        |
| Air      | +1 dB        |

### Pipeline

```text
PCM Audio
     │
Five-Band Equalizer
     │
Enhanced Voice
```

### Model

```ts
interface VoiceEQ {
  bands: number[];
}
```

### Rules

EQ presets are reusable timeline styles.

---

# 12.32 Voice Enhancement Presets

Creators choose presets instead of manually tuning DSP.

## Built-In Presets

| Preset    | Use Case                   |
| --------- | -------------------------- |
| Natural   | Minimal processing.        |
| Creator   | Default YouTube narration. |
| Podcast   | Warm conversational voice. |
| Studio    | Professional narration.    |
| Gaming    | Bright energetic voice.    |
| Classroom | High speech clarity.       |

### Preset Model

```ts
interface VoicePreset {
  presetId: string;
  eq: VoiceEQ;
  compressor: VoiceCompressorConfig;
  agc: AutomaticGainControlConfig;
}
```

### Rules

---

# 12.33 WASM DSP Runtime

Heavy DSP processing runs inside a dedicated WebAssembly runtime.

### Runtime Architecture

```text
AudioWorklet
     │
Shared Ring Buffer
     │
WASM DSP Runtime
     │
Enhanced PCM
```

### Responsibilities

* RNNoise execution.
* FFT transforms.
* Filters.
* Compression.
* Equalization.

### Runtime Model

```ts
interface WASMDSPRuntime {
  initialized: boolean;
  simdSupported: boolean;
}
```

### SIMD Optimizations

| Operation       | SIMD Enabled |
| --------------- | ------------ |
| FFT             | Yes          |
| RMS Calculation | Yes          |
| Gain Processing | Yes          |
| Equalizer       | Yes          |
| Spectral Mask   | Yes          |

### Rules

Fallback scalar implementation always exists.

---

# 12.34 CPU Performance Strategy

Voice enhancement must work on mid-range Windows laptops.

### CPU Budget

| Component  | Budget       |
| ---------- | ------------ |
| RNNoise    | Under 4 ms   |
| FFT        | Under 1 ms   |
| Compressor | Under 0.5 ms |
| Equalizer  | Under 0.5 ms |
| Total DSP  | Under 6 ms   |

### Memory Budget

| Resource           | Budget |
| ------------------ | ------ |
| RNNoise Model      | 2–4 MB |
| FFT Buffers        | 1 MB   |
| Ring Buffers       | 4 MB   |
| DSP Working Memory | 8 MB   |

### Performance Rules

* Allocate buffers once.
* Reuse FFT memory.
* SIMD preferred.
* Never allocate memory per frame.

---

# 12.35 Voice Enhancement Diagnostics

Developer Mode exposes DSP internals.

### Metrics

* DSP latency.
* Noise reduction amount.
* AGC gain.
* Compression gain reduction.
* Speech probability.
* RNNoise runtime status.
* Echo cancellation status.
* SIMD enabled.

### Diagnostics Model

```ts
interface VoiceEnhancementDiagnostics {
  dspLatencyMs: number;
  agcGainDb: number;
  noiseReductionDb: number;
  speechProbability: number;
}
```

### Warning Events

| Warning            | Trigger                            |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------- |
| DSP Over Budget    | Processing exceeds latency target. |
| Clipping Prevented | Limiter engaged.                   |
| Echo Detected      | Echo cancellation activated.       |
| Excessive Noise    | Suppression threshold exceeded.    |

---

# 12.36 Acceptance Tests

## Voice Enhancement Tests

* Fan noise reduced.
* AC hum reduced.
* Speech preserved.
* Keyboard noise minimized.
* Echo removed from preview playback.

## DSP Tests

* High-pass removes rumble.
* AGC normalizes loudness.
* Compressor smooths dynamics.
* Limiter prevents clipping.
* EQ presets modify frequency response correctly.

## Runtime Tests

* RNNoise loads successfully.
* SIMD path selected when supported.
* Scalar fallback produces identical output.

## Export Tests

* Preview matches exported enhancement.
* Raw PCM remains unchanged.
* DSP parameters serialize into project snapshot.

---

# Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 12.2)

1. Voice enhancement is completely non-destructive.
2. Original PCM recordings are immutable.
3. High-pass filtering executes before noise suppression.
4. Echo cancellation executes before AGC.
5. Compression executes before equalization.
6. Limiter is always the final DSP stage.
7. RNNoise executes inside a WASM runtime, never on the UI thread.
8. Voice Activity Detection produces timeline annotations only.
9. Enhancement presets modify DSP parameters, never source audio.
10. Preview and export always share the identical DSP graph.

# 12.41 AI Transcription Philosophy

The AI Transcription Engine converts spoken audio into a structured, editable timeline representation instead of plain text.

Every transcript produced by TryLipi contains:

* Speakers
* Sentences
* Individual words
* Word timestamps
* Confidence scores
* Language metadata
* Timeline alignment

This transcript powers captions, dubbing, searchable timelines, AI editing, script generation, and multilingual translation.

## Golden Principles

1. Original audio is immutable.
2. Every word receives start/end timestamps.
3. Speaker information is independent from transcript text.
4. Transcript edits never modify audio.
5. AI transcription is reproducible from the same audio.
6. Multiple STT providers normalize into one schema.
7. Timeline timestamps use microsecond precision.

---

# 12.42 AI Transcription Architecture

## High-Level Pipeline

```text
Audio Timeline Track
        │
        ▼
Speech Activity Detection
        │
        ▼
Audio Segment Builder
        │
        ▼
Language Detection
        │
        ▼
Speech-to-Text Engine
      ┌───────────────┐
      │               │
      ▼               ▼
 Gemini Flash     Whisper
      │               │
      └──────┬────────┘
             ▼
Canonical Transcript Builder
             │
      ┌──────┼─────────────┐
      ▼      ▼             ▼
 Caption   Search      Script Engine
 Timeline   Index
```

---

## Core Modules

| Module             | Responsibility            |
| ------------------ | ------------------------- |
| Segment Builder    | Break audio into chunks   |
| Language Detector  | Detect spoken language(s) |
| Gemini Engine      | Primary speech-to-text    |
| Whisper Engine     | Fallback STT              |
| Transcript Builder | Merge chunks              |
| Diarization Engine | Identify speakers         |
| Caption Generator  | Build subtitle timeline   |

---

# 12.43 Canonical Transcript Schema

Every transcription provider outputs the same structure.

## Transcript Hierarchy

```text
Transcript
├── Segments
│   ├── Speaker
│   ├── Sentences
│   │   └── Words
│   └── Confidence
└── Metadata
```

---

## Transcript Interface

```ts
interface Transcript {
  transcriptId: string;
  language: string;
  segments: TranscriptSegment[];
  createdAt: number;
}
```

### Segment Interface

```ts
interface TranscriptSegment {
  segmentId: string;
  speakerId: string;
  startUs: number;
  endUs: number;
  text: string;
  confidence: number;
  words: TranscriptWord[];
}
```

### Word Interface

```ts
interface TranscriptWord {
  word: string;
  startUs: number;
  endUs: number;
  confidence: number;
}
```

---

## Rules

* Words belong to one sentence.
* Sentences belong to one speaker segment.
* Speaker segments never overlap.

---

# 12.44 Audio Segmentation Pipeline

Long recordings are segmented before transcription.

## Why Segment Audio?

* Reduce AI context size.
* Enable retries.
* Enable parallel transcription.
* Improve multilingual accuracy.
* Reduce latency.

### Segmentation Pipeline

```text
Audio Track
     │
Speech Activity Detection
     │
Sentence Boundary Detection
     │
Audio Segments
     │
Parallel STT Requests
```

### Segment Strategy

| Recording Length | Chunk Size |
| ---------------- | ---------- |
| Under 5 min      | 15–20 sec  |
| 5–30 min         | 20–30 sec  |
| Over 30 min      | 30 sec     |

### Segment Model

```ts
interface TranscriptionChunk {
  chunkId: string;
  startUs: number;
  endUs: number;
}
```

### Rules

* Segments overlap by 250–500 ms.
* Merge removes duplicated words.

---

# 12.45 Gemini Transcription Engine

Gemini Flash is the primary STT provider.

## Responsibilities

* Speech recognition.
* Punctuation.
* Sentence detection.
* Mixed-language transcription.
* Context-aware formatting.

### Pipeline

```text
Audio Chunk
     │
Gemini Flash API
     │
Structured JSON
     │
Transcript Builder
```

### Gemini Response Model

```ts
interface GeminiTranscriptResponse {
  language: string;
  segments: TranscriptSegment[];
}
```

### Why Gemini?

| Capability   | Benefit                  |
| ------------ | ------------------------ |
| Multilingual | Indian language support  |
| Context      | Better punctuation       |
| Long Context | Better sentence grouping |
| Mixed Speech | Hinglish support         |

### Retry Strategy

| Failure            | Action                   |
| ------------------ | ------------------------ |
| Timeout            | Retry chunk              |
| Invalid JSON       | Repair parser            |
| Partial Transcript | Retry missing chunk only |

---

# 12.46 Whisper Fallback Engine

Whisper provides a secondary transcription engine.

## When Whisper Runs

* Gemini unavailable.
* Offline mode.
* Cost optimization.
* Local inference (future).

### Pipeline

```text
Audio Chunk
     │
Whisper
     │
Canonical Transcript
```

### Whisper Interface

```ts
interface WhisperTranscriptResponse {
  language: string;
  words: TranscriptWord[];
}
```

### Rules

Whisper output is normalized before entering the timeline.

---

# 12.47 Word-Level Timestamp Engine

Every recognized word receives timestamps.

```text
     │

Word Start Time
     │
Word End Time
```

| Word End          | ±20 ms |

```ts
  endUs: number;
}
```

### Rules

---

The transcript builder groups words into readable sentences.

* Language model context.

```text
     │

     │
Punctuation Predictor
     │
Sentence Builder
```

```ts
}
```

# Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 12.3)

1. Every recognized word receives a timestamp.
2. Gemini Flash is the primary transcription engine.
3. Whisper output is normalized into the canonical transcript schema.
4. Speaker metadata is independent from transcript words.
5. Hinglish and multilingual speech are preserved exactly as spoken.
6. Transcript edits never modify source audio.
7. Low-confidence words remain reviewable.
8. Caption tracks are generated from transcript segments.
9. Transcript revisions are immutable.
