# 08.41 Zoom Target Prediction Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **TryLipi should know where the camera needs to move before the creator clicks.**

This is one of the biggest differences between an ordinary screen recorder and a cinematic recording platform.

Instead of reacting to clicks...

TryLipi predicts user intent from cursor movement, visual context and workflow understanding.

The camera begins moving **before** the interaction happens.

---

## Traditional Zoom Timeline

```text
Cursor Click

↓

Zoom Starts

↓

Camera Moves
```

The viewer notices a delay.

---

## TryLipi Predictive Zoom Timeline

```text
Cursor Starts Moving

↓

Intent Prediction

↓

Camera Begins Moving

↓

Cursor Click

↓

Already Focused
```

The movement feels intentional and cinematic.

---

## What the Runtime Predicts

Before every click, TryLipi predicts:

* Target button.
* Target input field.
* Target menu.
* Target window.
* Target image.
* Target code block.
* Target dropdown.
* Target card.
* Target notification.

The prediction updates every frame.

---

## Prediction Responsibilities

| Runtime           | Responsibility               |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Intent Engine     | Predict creator intention.   |
| Trajectory Engine | Predict cursor destination.  |
| Candidate Engine  | Generate zoom candidates.    |
| Zoom Score Engine | Rank candidates.             |
| Camera Runtime    | Start camera movement early. |
| Prediction Cache  | Store predicted targets.     |

---

## Design Principles

1. Prediction happens continuously.
2. Camera movement is reversible.
3. Predictions have confidence scores.
4. DOM and Pixel Tracking both contribute.
5. Semantic context influences prediction.
6. Wrong predictions recover smoothly.
7. No sudden zoom jumps.

---

## Prediction Lifecycle

```text
Cursor Movement

↓

Intent Prediction

↓

Target Candidates

↓

Confidence Ranking

↓

Camera Anticipation

↓

Zoom Lock
```

---

## Cursor Behavior States

| State      | Meaning                    |

| Navigating | Moving toward target.      |

```text
↓

↓

↓

↓

↓
```

| ------------ | ----------------- |
| 0–40 ms      | Ignore.           |
| 50–120 ms    | Candidate.        |
| 120–250 ms   | Strong candidate. |
| Above 250 ms | Lock prediction.  |

Detects:

* Fast flick.
* Precision slowdown.

* Current chapter.

* AI tutorial focus.

Camera reverses smoothly.

Supports:

# 08.49 Acceptance Principles

## Intent Tests

* Hover prediction works.
* Click prediction works.
* Drag prediction ignored.
* Idle cursor ignored.

### Trajectory Tests

* Straight path prediction.
* Curved path prediction.
* Deceleration prediction.
* Micro-correction prediction.

### Candidate Tests

* DOM candidates generated.
* Pixel candidates generated.
* OCR candidates generated.
* Semantic candidates generated.

### Camera Tests

* Anticipation begins before click.
* Prediction cancellation smooth.
* Camera locks correctly.

---

# 08.50 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 08.4.1)

1. Zoom Prediction Runtime predicts camera targets before user interaction occurs.
2. Cursor Intent Engine continuously estimates interaction intent using velocity, acceleration, hover behavior and movement state.
3. Cursor Trajectory Runtime predicts future cursor destinations from historical motion paths.
4. Candidate Engine combines DOM, Pixel Tracking, OCR and Semantic Scene Understanding into one unified target list.
5. Zoom Score Engine ranks candidates using geometric, behavioral and semantic signals.
6. Camera Anticipation Runtime begins cinematic camera movement before click confirmation while remaining reversible.
7. Prediction confidence updates every rendered frame.
8. Camera anticipation is independent from Smart Zoom rendering and only supplies predicted targets.
9. Prediction runtime never creates visible camera jumps when targets change.
10. Chapter 08.4.1 establishes TryLipi's predictive camera intelligence—the system that makes zooms feel human instead of reactive.

# 08.51 Camera Trajectory Planning Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **A cinematic camera should never teleport — it should plan smooth motion through future interaction space.**

This chapter defines how TryLipi generates **cinematic camera paths**.

Instead of jumping between zoom targets...

The camera plans motion using future interaction predictions.

This is inspired by:

* Screen Studio.
* Cursorful.
* Apple Keynote camera animations.
* Professional motion graphics.

---

## Reactive Camera

```text
Target A

↓

Instant Camera Jump

↓

Target B
```

Feels robotic.

---

## Predictive Camera

```text
Target A

↓

Camera Path Planned

↓

Target B

↓

Target C
```

Feels intentional.

---

## Camera Planner Responsibilities

| Runtime             | Responsibility                |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Path Planner        | Generate camera path.         |
| Anchor Planner      | Select intermediate anchors.  |
| Framing Planner     | Compute viewport composition. |
| Zoom Window Planner | Determine zoom timing.        |
| Motion Planner      | Smooth transitions.           |

---

## Design Principles

1. Motion begins before interaction.
2. Paths minimize jerk.
3. Camera never overshoots targets.
4. Multi-target transitions are continuous.
5. Dynamic reframing allowed.
6. Camera respects safe zones.
7. Timeline is deterministic.

---

## Planning Lifecycle

```text
Target Predictions

↓

Path Planning

↓

Anchor Generation

↓

Framing Planning

↓

Camera Timeline
```

---

| Button Click   | Short window.      |
| Form Fill      | Medium window.     |
| Code Reading   | Long window.       |
| Modal Dialog   | Adaptive window.   |

## Release Runtime

```ts
interface ZoomWindow {
```

# 08.60 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 08.4.2)

1. Camera Trajectory Planner converts predicted targets into continuous cinematic camera paths.
2. Multi-Target Prediction plans sequences of interactions rather than isolated clicks.
3. Workflow-Aware Camera Intelligence uses semantic workflow context to improve prediction confidence.
4. Dynamic Framing continuously recomputes safe camera composition as tracked objects change geometry.
5. Predictive Zoom Windows define entry, peak, hold and release phases for every zoom interaction.
6. Prediction Memory stores recent interaction context to stabilize camera planning.
7. Camera trajectories remain deterministic and reversible until prediction confirmation.
8. Framing decisions always respect export safe zones and aspect ratios.
9. Camera planning produces immutable timeline metadata consumed by Smart Zoom and Export Rendering.
10. Chapter 08.4.2 establishes TryLipi's cinematic camera planning runtime—the system responsible for smooth predictive camera movement across complex creator workflows.

# 08.61 Zoom Decision Engine Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Predictions suggest camera targets. The Zoom Decision Engine decides whether the camera should actually move.**

Prediction and decision are intentionally separated.

**Prediction answers:** *Where is the user probably going?*

**Decision answers:** *Is it worth zooming?*

This separation prevents distracting camera behavior.

---

## Why Prediction Alone Isn't Enough

### Prediction

```text
Cursor Moving

↓

Settings Button (94%)
```

### Decision

```text
Prediction

↓

Check Confidence

↓

Check Context

↓

Zoom or Ignore
```

---

## Decision Responsibilities

| Runtime            | Responsibility               |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------- |
| Decision Engine    | Final zoom approval.         |
| Confidence Runtime | Validate prediction quality. |
| Camera Gate        | Allow or deny zoom.          |
| Timeline Runtime   | Create zoom event.           |
| Recovery Runtime   | Cancel or modify zoom.       |

---

## Decision Pipeline

```text
Prediction

↓

Confidence Validation

↓

Semantic Validation

↓

Timeline Validation

↓

Zoom Approved
```

---

## Decision Principles

1. Every zoom is intentional.
2. Ignore accidental cursor movement.
3. Ignore decorative UI.
4. Respect creator workflow.
5. Prevent excessive zoom frequency.
6. Camera movement must remain readable.
7. Decisions are replayable.

---

# 08.62 Zoom Decision Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Combine behavioral, semantic and visual signals into one final camera decision.**

---

## Runtime Architecture

```text
Prediction Runtime
Pixel Runtime
Semantic Runtime
Timeline Runtime
        │
Zoom Decision Runtime
        │
├── Decision Validator
├── Confidence Gate
├── Frequency Gate
├── Context Gate
└── Timeline Event Builder
```

---

## Decision Pipeline

```text
Candidate Target

↓

Context Validation

↓

Decision Score

↓

Zoom Timeline Event
```

---

## Decision Signals

| Signal                | Purpose                 |
| --------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Prediction Confidence | Reliability.            |
| Hover Duration        | Interaction likelihood. |
| Semantic Importance   | Workflow relevance.     |
| Object Size           | Readability.            |
| Object Visibility     | Camera quality.         |
| Previous Zoom         | Prevent spam.           |
| Timeline Density      | Viewer comfort.         |

---

## Zoom Decision Thresholds

| Decision Score | Action                    |
| -------------- | ------------------------- |
| 95–100         | Immediate cinematic zoom. |
| 80–94          | Standard predictive zoom. |
| 65–79          | Soft zoom.                |
| 50–64          | Hold prediction.          |
| Below 50       | Ignore.                   |

---

## Zoom Frequency Runtime

Avoid zooming too often.

Example:

```text
Button A

↓

Button B (100 ms later)

↓

No second zoom
```

Instead, extend the first zoom window.

---

## Timeline Event Builder

Every approved zoom becomes:

```text
Zoom Event

↓

Timeline

↓

Renderer

↓

Export
```

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ZoomDecision {
  decisionId: string;
  decisionScore: number;
  approved: boolean;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Decision Runtime is the only runtime allowed to create zoom timeline events.

---

# 08.63 Confidence Recovery Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Wrong predictions should recover gracefully without viewers noticing.**

---

## Recovery Architecture

```text
Camera Prediction

↓

Prediction Changed

↓

Recovery Runtime

↓

Camera Replanned
```

---

## Recovery Scenarios

| Scenario                     | Recovery          |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------- |
| Cursor Changes Direction     | Cancel zoom.      |
| Hover Leaves Target          | Reduce zoom.      |
| New Higher Confidence Target | Switch target.    |
| Scroll Interrupts Prediction | Recompute path.   |
| Window Changes               | Reset prediction. |

---

## Camera Recovery Timeline

```text
Prediction A

↓

Camera Starts

↓

Cursor Turns Away

↓

Camera Slows

↓

Prediction B
```

---

## Recovery Modes

| Mode     | Purpose                        |
| -------- | ------------------------------ |
| Cancel   | Undo anticipation.             |
| Redirect | Switch target.                 |
| Merge    | Continue toward nearby target. |
| Extend   | Hold current zoom.             |

---

## Merge Runtime

If two buttons are close together:

```text
Save Button

↓

Settings Button

↓

Merge Camera Path
```

Avoids jitter.

---

## Confidence Decay Runtime

Prediction confidence decays when behavior changes.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ZoomRecoveryState {
  recoveryMode: RecoveryMode;
  previousPredictionId?: string;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Recovery runtime preserves smooth camera continuity.

---

* Prediction confidence.

```text
Zoom Entry

Frame 260–320

Zoom Exit
```

| Blur Pass       | Background blur.    |
| Focus Mask      | Preserve subject.   |

Exports remain identical regardless of hardware.

---

```ts
interface ZoomRenderEvent {
```

## Engineering Rules

# 08.65 Performance Optimization Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Predictive zoom must operate in realtime without dropping recording FPS.**

---

## Optimization Architecture

```text
Prediction Runtime

↓

ROI Detection

↓

GPU Scheduling

↓

Frame Budget Runtime
```

---

## Performance Budget

| Resolution | Budget      |
| ---------- | ----------- |
| 1080p60    | 16 ms/frame |
| 1440p60    | 16 ms/frame |
| 4K30       | 33 ms/frame |
| 4K60       | 16 ms/frame |

---

## Optimization Strategies

### Region of Interest (ROI)

Only evaluate nearby objects.

### Prediction Sampling

Skip expensive inference on unchanged frames.

### Motion Cache

Reuse recent trajectory calculations.

### Candidate Cache

Reuse semantic candidates.

---

## Frame Scheduler

```text
Frame

↓

Pixel Tracking

↓

Prediction

↓

Decision

↓

Camera Planner
```

All within frame budget.

---

## GPU Scheduling

Prediction compute runs alongside optical flow compute.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ZoomPerformanceState {
  frameBudgetMs: number;
  reusedPredictionCount: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Performance optimizations must not change zoom decisions.

---

---

```text
Decision

```

# 06.41 Mouse Physics Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **A cursor should move like a physical object with weight, momentum and smoothness—not like raw operating system coordinates.**

This chapter defines the **Mouse Physics Engine**, one of TryLipi's biggest visual differentiators from Loom and Tella.

The raw operating system cursor is often:

* Jittery.
* Pixel-perfect.
* Abrupt.
* Robotic.
* Different across devices.

TryLipi renders a **cinematic virtual cursor** that preserves the creator's intent while improving visual quality.

---

## Why Mouse Physics Exists

### Raw Cursor Movement

```text
Mouse Position

(100,120)

↓

(105,121)

↓

(110,123)

↓

(115,123)
```

Small jitters become visible in recordings.

---

### TryLipi Cursor Movement

```text
Mouse Samples

↓

Velocity Filter

↓

Spring Motion

↓

Smooth Cursor Path
```

Motion becomes fluid.

---

## Responsibilities

| Runtime          | Responsibility             |
| ---------------- | -------------------------- |
| Sampling Engine  | Capture raw cursor input.  |
| Velocity Engine  | Compute movement velocity. |
| Physics Engine   | Apply spring & damping.    |
| Momentum Runtime | Preserve natural inertia.  |
| State Runtime    | Cursor movement states.    |
| Timeline Runtime | Record motion history.     |

---

## Mouse Physics Principles

1. Preserve creator intent.
2. Remove hardware jitter.
3. Never introduce lag noticeable to creators.
4. Support 60/120/144Hz mice.
5. Physics deterministic during export.
6. Motion independent of DPI.
7. GPU-rendered virtual cursor.

---

## Mouse Physics Lifecycle

```text
Raw Mouse Event

↓

Sampling

↓

Velocity Calculation

↓

Spring Simulation

↓

Momentum Update

↓

Rendered Cursor
```

---

## Mission Statement

> **Every cursor movement flows through a deterministic physics simulation before rendering.**

---

## High-Level Architecture

```text
OS Cursor Events
        │
Mouse Sampling Runtime
        │
Physics Runtime
        │
├── Velocity Calculator
├── Spring Simulator
├── Momentum Simulator
├── Motion Filter
├── Cursor Renderer
└── Timeline Recorder
```

---

## Runtime Pipeline

```text
Mouse Event

↓

Normalize Position

↓

Velocity

↓

Acceleration

↓

Spring Physics

↓

Render Position
```

---

## Runtime Layers

```text
Mouse Physics Runtime
│
├── Sampling Runtime
├── Velocity Runtime
├── Acceleration Runtime
├── Spring Runtime
├── Momentum Runtime
├── Constraint Runtime
└── Render Runtime
```

---

## Runtime Metadata

```ts
interface MousePhysicsRuntime {
  physicsVersion: number;
  sampleRateHz: number;
  renderRateHz: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Physics runtime executes before cursor rendering and before Smart Zoom.

# 06.43 Cursor Sampling Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Capture high-frequency cursor input independent of recording frame rate.**

The mouse may update at **125 Hz**, **500 Hz**, **1000 Hz**, or even **8000 Hz**.

The video may record at **60 FPS**.

Sampling decouples input from rendering.

---

## Sampling Pipeline

```text
Hardware Cursor

↓

Sampling Buffer

↓

Normalized Samples

↓

Physics Runtime
```

---

## Sampling Sources

| Source              | Example      |
| ------------------- | ------------ |
| Windows Pointer API | Desktop app. |
| Pointer Events API  | Browser app. |
| Touch Pointer       | Tablet.      |
| Pen Input           | Stylus.      |

---

## Sampling Buffer

Stores timestamped cursor events.

```text
t=100 ms → (210,180)

t=101 ms → (214,182)

t=102 ms → (219,184)
```

---

## Sampling Rate Runtime

| Device                 | Sample Rate  |
| ---------------------- | ------------ |
| Standard Mouse         | 125 Hz       |
| Gaming Mouse           | 500–1000 Hz  |
| High-End Gaming        | 2000–8000 Hz |
| Browser Pointer Events | Event-driven |

---

## Timestamp Normalization

All samples convert into a unified timeline clock.

---

## Buffer Compression

If multiple samples occur inside one render frame:

```text
8 Cursor Samples

↓

Interpolation Buffer

↓

Single Render Frame
```

No information is lost.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface CursorSample {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  timestamp: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Sampling runtime preserves every hardware cursor event before filtering.

---

# 06.44 Velocity Smoothing Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Convert noisy cursor samples into stable cinematic motion.**

Velocity is the foundation of every cursor animation.

---

## Velocity Pipeline

```text
Cursor Samples

↓

Delta Position

↓

Velocity Vector

↓

Velocity Filter

↓

Smooth Velocity
```

---

## Velocity Components

| Component           | Purpose        |
| ------------------- | -------------- |
| Horizontal Velocity | X movement.    |
| Vertical Velocity   | Y movement.    |
| Magnitude           | Cursor speed.  |
| Direction           | Heading angle. |

---

## Velocity Graph

```text
Time →

Raw Velocity

/\/\/\/\

↓

Filtered Velocity

───────
```

Jitter disappears.

---

## Adaptive Velocity Filter

Different filters apply based on speed.

| Cursor Speed | Filter                   |
| ------------ | ------------------------ |
| Very Slow    | Minimal filtering.       |
| Slow         | Light smoothing.         |
| Medium       | Standard smoothing.      |
| Fast         | Strong smoothing.        |
| Flick        | Preserve responsiveness. |

---

## Velocity Thresholds

```text
0 px/ms

↓

Idle

↓

Micro Movement

↓

Movement

↓

Fast Movement

↓

Flick
```

---

## Low-Speed Precision Mode

Tiny movements receive higher precision for UI selection.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface CursorVelocityState {
  velocityX: number;
  velocityY: number;
  filteredVelocity: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Velocity filtering reduces jitter without increasing perceived latency.

---

# 06.45 Spring Motion Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Cursor movement behaves like a spring connected to the user's actual pointer.**

This creates the signature **Screen Studio feel**.

---

## Spring Architecture

```text
Real Cursor

↓

Virtual Cursor

↓

Spring Constraint

↓
```

# 06.49 Acceptance Principles

## Sampling Tests

* Preserve 1000 Hz mouse samples.
* Preserve timestamps.
* Compress correctly into render frames.

### Velocity Tests

* Remove jitter.
* Preserve precision.
* Preserve flick responsiveness.

### Spring Tests

* Smooth catch-up motion.
* No oscillation.
* Stable stop.

### Momentum Tests

* Natural decay.
* No overshoot.
* Stable after drag.

# 06.50 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 06.4.1)

1. Mouse Physics Runtime converts raw cursor events into cinematic virtual cursor motion.
2. Cursor Sampling Runtime captures hardware input independently of recording frame rate.
3. Velocity Smoothing Runtime removes jitter while preserving creator precision.
4. Spring Motion Runtime simulates weighted cursor movement using deterministic spring and damping physics.
5. Cursor Momentum Runtime preserves realistic inertia for fast cursor movement.
6. Motion State Machine defines deterministic cursor behavior across idle, movement, flick and settling states.
7. Physics simulation remains independent of operating system cursor rendering.
8. Timeline metadata records every cursor motion state transition.
9. Export rendering reproduces identical cursor motion regardless of playback hardware.
10. Chapter 06.4.1 establishes the physical foundation for cinematic cursor rendering, click effects, motion blur and Smart Zoom synchronization.

# 06.51 Cursor Interaction Physics Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Clicks, hovers, drags and cursor interactions should feel alive with subtle physical feedback while remaining faithful to the creator's actual actions.**

A professional screen recording should communicate interaction through motion.

Instead of simply rendering:

* Mouse Down
* Mouse Up

TryLipi renders:

* Compression.
* Bounce.
* Hover attraction.
* Drag resistance.
* Elastic release.
* Momentum continuation.

These effects are subtle enough to improve readability without becoming distracting.

---

## Why Interaction Physics Exists

### Standard Cursor Recording

```text id="gn4f34"
Cursor

↓

Click

↓

Nothing Changes
```

The viewer may miss interactions.

### TryLipi Interaction Physics

```text id="tnyl3n"
Cursor

↓

Compression

↓

Ripple

↓

Bounce

↓

Release
```

Every interaction becomes visually understandable.

---

## Responsibilities

| Runtime          | Responsibility                     |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Click Physics    | Animate press/release.             |
| Bounce Engine    | Natural rebound after click.       |
| Magnetic Runtime | Cursor attraction toward targets.  |
| Hover Physics    | Hover emphasis animation.          |
| Drag Physics     | Cursor resistance during dragging. |
| Elastic Runtime  | Stretch/compress interactions.     |
| Timeline Runtime | Record interaction physics events. |

---

## Design Principles

1. Preserve creator accuracy.
2. Never fake clicks.
3. Physics are subtle.
4. Animation duration adapts to interaction speed.
5. GPU-renderable.
6. Replay deterministic.
7. Fully configurable by theme.

---

## Interaction Lifecycle

```text id="vsdrls"
Hover

↓

Mouse Down

↓

Compression

↓

Release

↓

Bounce

↓

Momentum Continues
```

---

# 06.60 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 06.4.2)

1. Click Physics Engine renders compression, hold and release independently of cursor tracking.
2. Cursor Bounce Runtime simulates damped spring rebound after click release.
3. Magnetic Cursor Runtime visually attracts the rendered cursor toward interactive objects without changing actual pointer coordinates.
4. Hover Physics Runtime communicates interaction readiness using scale, glow and magnetic alignment.
5. Drag Physics Runtime introduces resistance and elasticity during drag interactions while preserving precision.
6. Elastic Cursor Runtime stretches cursor rendering based on movement velocity and drag direction.
7. Interaction Physics Timeline records every hover, click, drag and elastic event for deterministic replay.
8. Physics effects blend continuously rather than restarting between interaction states.
9. Cursor interaction animations are GPU-renderable and deterministic during export.
10. Chapter 06.4.2 establishes the interaction physics layer that makes TryLipi's cursor feel cinematic and physically responsive.

# 06.61 Premium Cursor Rendering Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **The rendered cursor is an animated visual layer independent of the operating system pointer, designed for cinematic recordings.**

The operating system cursor is **never** exported directly.

Instead, TryLipi recreates the cursor using GPU rendering with animation metadata collected during recording.

This allows:

* Pixel-perfect cursor scaling.
* Smooth trails.
* Motion blur.
* Glow effects.
* Shadows.
* Ripple animations.
* Theme customization.
* Retina-quality exports.

---

## Rendering Pipeline Philosophy

```text
Operating System Cursor
        │
Capture Position + Metadata
        │
Cursor Physics Runtime
        │
Cursor Renderer
        │
GPU Effects Pipeline
        │
Rendered Cursor Layer
```

The cursor becomes its own rendering layer, just like subtitles or annotations.

---

## Why This Matters

Without a custom renderer:

* Cursor looks different on Windows/macOS.
* DPI scaling becomes inconsistent.
* Cursor trails become blurry.
* Exports depend on OS rendering.

With TryLipi:

* Identical cursor across every platform.
* Resolution-independent rendering.
* Theme-aware cursor.
* Animation-aware exports.

---

## Cursor Rendering Responsibilities

| Runtime         | Responsibility               |
| --------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Cursor Renderer | Draw virtual cursor.         |
| Trail Renderer  | Render historical positions. |
| Blur Renderer   | Motion blur layer.           |
| Glow Renderer   | Highlight active cursor.     |
| Ripple Renderer | Click feedback.              |
| Shadow Renderer | Depth simulation.            |

---

## Design Principles

1. GPU-first rendering.
2. Resolution independent.
3. Theme customizable.
4. Physics synchronized.
5. Timeline deterministic.
6. HDR compatible.
7. Export identical across devices.

---

| Blur Length    | Speed dependent.       |
| Blur Opacity   | Fade with speed.       |
| Blur Softness  | Edge quality.          |

---

## Velocity-Based Blur

| Speed  | Blur Length       |
| ------ | ----------------- |
| Idle   | None              |
| Slow   | Minimal           |
| Medium | Short             |
| Fast   | Long              |
| Flick  | Maximum safe blur |

---

## Directional Blur

Blur always follows velocity vector.

---

## Blur Profiles

| Profile   | Use Case           |
| --------- | ------------------ |
| Minimal   | Tutorials.         |
| Balanced  | Productivity.      |
| Cinematic | Marketing videos.  |
| Gaming    | High-speed cursor. |

---

## Blur Constraints

* Never blur clicks.
* Never blur idle cursor.
* Reduce blur during hover.

---

```ts
interface CursorMotionBlurState {
```

## Engineering Rules

Motion blur is computed after cursor physics but before glow rendering.

```text
├── Blur

├── Ripple
```

## Render Order

1. Trail.
2. Motion blur.
3. Shadow.
4. Cursor.
5. Glow.
6. Ripple.
7. Overlay effects.

| -------------- | ------------------- |

| Trail Pass     | Trail geometry.     |
| Blur Pass      | Motion blur shader. |
| Composite Pass | Final cursor layer. |

# 06.70 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 06.4.3)

1. Cursor rendering is fully virtualized and independent of the operating system pointer.
2. Cursor Trails are generated from interpolated motion history rather than raw frame positions.
3. Motion Blur uses velocity-aware directional blur and is synchronized with cursor physics.
4. Click Ripples are timeline-based visual events anchored to the rendered cursor hotspot.
5. Glow and Shadow Runtime provide depth and focus while preserving cursor geometry.
6. GPU Cursor Rendering composites cursor effects using layered WebGPU render passes.
7. Export Rendering reproduces identical cursor animation regardless of recording hardware or operating system.
8. Cursor themes are customizable without changing interaction metadata.
9. Accessibility runtime overrides visual effects when reduced-motion or high-contrast modes are enabled.
10. Chapter 06.4 completes TryLipi's Mouse Physics & Motion Engine—the cinematic cursor rendering foundation powering every interaction throughout the recording pipeline.

# 06.71 Cursor Morphing Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **The cursor should intelligently transform into the correct interaction tool based on visual context, not just operating system events.**

The operating system cursor changes shape only when the application requests it.

TryLipi goes further.

The Cursor Morphing Engine understands:

* HTML elements.
* Canvas applications.
* Desktop applications.
* Images.
* PDFs.
* Code editors.
* Whiteboards.
* Figma.
* Canva.
* VS Code.
* Terminal.
* AI-detected interaction zones.

This creates a universal cursor identity system.

---

## Why Cursor Morphing Exists

### Standard Recording

```text id="vwu8ls"
Arrow Cursor

↓

Text Field

↓

OS Changes Cursor
```

Works only when applications expose cursor state.

---

### TryLipi Cursor Morphing

```text id="7otxxy"
Pixel + DOM + Semantic Runtime

↓

Interaction Classification

↓

Cursor Morph Prediction

↓

Animated Cursor Transition
```

Cursor morphs consistently everywhere.

---

## Responsibilities

| Runtime             | Responsibility              |
| ------------------- | --------------------------- |
| State Engine        | Determine cursor state.     |
| Recognition Runtime | Identify interaction type.  |
| Morph Pipeline      | Select cursor shape.        |
| Transition Runtime  | Animate shape transition.   |
| Timeline Runtime    | Store cursor state history. |
| Theme Runtime       | Render cursor identity.     |

---

## Cursor Morphing Principles

1. Cursor identity is semantic.
2. DOM is optional.
3. Pixel tracking acts as fallback.
4. Morphing is animated.
5. Cursor state is deterministic.
6. Export reproduces identical morphing.
7. Themes never change cursor semantics.

---

## Cursor Morph Lifecycle

```text id="v1gmbh"
Cursor Movement

↓

Interaction Detection

↓

Cursor State Selected

↓

Shape Transition

↓

Rendered Cursor
```

---

# 06.75 Cursor Morph Pipeline

# 06.80 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 06.5.1)

1. Cursor Morphing Engine separates semantic cursor identity from rendered cursor appearance.
2. Pointer Recognition Runtime combines DOM, Pixel Tracking, OCR and Semantic Scene Understanding before selecting cursor states.
3. Cursor Identity System provides platform-independent interaction identities.
4. Cursor Morph Pipeline animates transitions between cursor identities using deterministic timelines.
5. Shape Transition Runtime interpolates cursor geometry while preserving cursor hotspot accuracy.
6. Cursor State Timeline records every cursor identity transition for replay and export rendering.
7. Recognition confidence prevents unnecessary cursor flickering during ambiguous interactions.
8. Accessibility cursor variants preserve semantic identity while adapting appearance.
9. Cursor morphing remains deterministic across browser, desktop and export runtimes.
10. Chapter 06.5.1 establishes TryLipi's intelligent cursor identity system—the foundation for animated cursor morphing, branded cursors and cross-platform interaction rendering.

# 06.81 Animated Cursor Morph Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Cursor shape transitions should feel like one living object changing form instead of replacing one image with another.**

A morph is not a fade.

It is a geometry-aware animation that preserves:

* Cursor hotspot.
* Motion physics.
* Interaction continuity.
* Creator intent.

Every transition feels intentional and cinematic.

---

## Why Animated Morphing Exists

### Instant Cursor Replacement

```text
Arrow Cursor

↓

Hand Cursor
```

Feels abrupt.

### Animated Cursor Morph

```text
Arrow

↓

Geometry Interpolation

↓

Hand
```

Feels natural.

---

## Morph Responsibilities

| Runtime               | Responsibility            |
| --------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Geometry Morph Engine | Animate cursor shape.     |
| Timing Runtime        | Transition duration.      |
| Motion Sync Runtime   | Preserve cursor velocity. |
| Theme Runtime         | Match creator theme.      |
| Export Runtime        | Deterministic replay.     |

---

## Morph Principles

1. Preserve cursor hotspot.
2. Maintain velocity continuity.
3. Animate geometry.
4. Theme independent.
5. GPU accelerated.
6. Interruptible transitions.
7. Timeline replayable.

---

## Morph Lifecycle

```text
State Change

↓

Morph Planning

↓

Geometry Animation

↓

Cursor Locked
```

---

# 06.82 Animated Morph Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Every cursor identity change becomes a short GPU animation driven by geometry interpolation.**

---

## Runtime Architecture

```text
Cursor Identity Change
        │
Morph Planner
        │
├── Shape Generator
├── Geometry Interpolator
├── Velocity Sync
├── Opacity Runtime
└── Completion Runtime
```

---

## Animation Pipeline

```text
Arrow Shape

↓

Intermediate Geometry

↓

Hand Shape

↓

Rendered Cursor
```

---

## Animation Curves

| Curve         | Use             |
| ------------- | --------------- |
| Ease Out      | Buttons.        |
| Ease In-Out   | Text fields.    |
| Spring Morph  | Drag states.    |
| Elastic Morph | Creative tools. |

---

## Morph Timing Profiles

| Interaction       | Duration |
| ----------------- | -------- |
| Pointer → Hand    | 80 ms    |
| Hand → Pointer    | 90 ms    |
| Pointer → Text    | 60 ms    |
| Grab → Grabbing   | 70 ms    |
| Resize Transition | 75 ms    |

---

## Interruptible Morph Runtime

Supports rapid transitions.

```text
Arrow

↓

Hand

↓

Text Cursor

↓

Resize Cursor
```

Animation adapts without flicker.

---

## Morph Metadata

```ts
interface CursorMorphAnimation {
  morphId: string;
  progress: number;
  easingCurve: CursorMorphCurve;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Morph animation updates every rendered frame until completion.

# 06.87 Context-Aware Cursor AI

## Mission Statement

> **AI predicts cursor identity even when applications do not expose cursor metadata.**

This is TryLipi's biggest cursor intelligence advantage.

---

## AI Runtime Architecture

```text
Pixel Tracking
OCR
Semantic Scene
Workflow Runtime
        │
Context Cursor AI
        │
Cursor Identity Prediction
```

---

## AI Detection Examples

### VS Code

Detect:

* Text editor.
* Terminal.
* Explorer.
* Resize divider.

### Chrome

Detect:

* URL bar.
* Tabs.
* Extension icon.
* Download bar.

### Canva

Detect:

* Text box.
* Image resize handle.
* Rotation handle.

### Terminal

Detect text insertion cursor using OCR + layout.

---

## Prediction Confidence

| Confidence | Action                   |
| ---------- | ------------------------ |
| High       | Immediate morph.         |
| Medium     | Wait 1–2 frames.         |
| Low        | Preserve current cursor. |

---

## AI Recovery Runtime

If prediction fails:

* Preserve previous cursor.
* Retry with Pixel Tracking.
* Retry with OCR.
* Retry with semantic workflow.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ContextAwareCursorPrediction {
  predictedCursor: CursorIdentityType;
  predictionConfidence: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

AI cursor prediction augments—not replaces—DOM cursor information.

# 06.90 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 06.5.2)

1. Animated Cursor Morph Runtime interpolates cursor geometry instead of replacing cursor images.
2. Universal Cursor Shape Library provides platform-independent vector cursor identities.
3. Resize Cursor Runtime intelligently detects window and panel resize interactions using DOM and Pixel Tracking.
4. Loading Cursor Runtime replaces OS-specific loading cursors with timeline-based animated cursors.
5. Canvas Cursor Runtime supports creative applications through semantic tool detection.
6. Context-Aware Cursor AI predicts cursor identities when applications expose no pointer metadata.
7. Cursor morph animations preserve hotspot coordinates and cursor physics continuity.
8. AI cursor prediction falls back through DOM → Pixel → OCR → Semantic hierarchy.
9. All cursor morphs remain deterministic across realtime preview and exported video.
10. Chapter 06.5.2 establishes TryLipi's intelligent cursor behavior system across browsers, desktop applications and creative tools.

# 06.91 Cursor Theme Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Creators should be able to make the cursor part of their visual identity without changing interaction semantics.**

Cursor themes are one of TryLipi's premium creator-branding features. Instead of exporting the native Windows or macOS pointer, TryLipi exports a fully rendered **virtual cursor** whose appearance can be customized while preserving the underlying cursor identity.

The cursor becomes another branding surface—similar to fonts, captions, colors, and transitions.

---

## Why Cursor Themes Exist

### Standard Screen Recording

```text
Windows Cursor
↓
Export Video
↓
Same Cursor Everywhere
```

No branding or customization.

### TryLipi Theme Runtime

```text
Cursor Identity
↓
Theme Tokens
↓
Brand Runtime
↓
GPU Cursor Renderer
↓
Final Cursor Layer
```

The interaction remains identical while appearance becomes creator-specific.

---

## Theme Design Principles

1. Cursor identity never changes.
2. Themes are vector-based.
3. Works across browser and desktop recordings.
4. Compatible with cursor morphing.
5. Supports accessibility overrides.
6. GPU rendered in realtime.
7. Export is deterministic.

---

## Theme Categories

| Category                | Examples                 |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------ |
| **System Themes**       | Windows, macOS, Linux    |
| **Creator Themes**      | Minimal, Neon, Gradient  |
| **Professional Themes** | Screen Studio, Cursorful |
| **Gaming Themes**       | RGB, Cyberpunk           |
| **Educational Themes**  | High Visibility Cursor   |
| **AI Themes**           | TryLipi AI Cursor        |

---

## Cursor Theme Lifecycle

```text
Creator Selects Theme
        ↓
Theme Loaded
        ↓
Cursor Identity Preserved
        ↓
GPU Appearance Generated
        ↓
Realtime Preview + Export
```

---

## Theme Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime         | Responsibility               |
| --------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Theme Loader    | Loads cursor theme manifest. |
| Theme Builder   | Generates cursor appearance. |
| Theme Validator | Validates compatibility.     |
| Theme Cache     | Reuses theme assets.         |
| Theme Renderer  | Supplies GPU renderer.       |

---

# 06.95 Cursor Accessibility Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Cursor visibility and usability must remain excellent for every viewer regardless of theme or export format.**

Accessibility always has higher priority than creator styling.

---

## Accessibility Runtime Architecture

```text
Accessibility Settings
        ↓
Override Runtime
        ↓
Theme Runtime
        ↓
GPU Cursor Renderer
```

---

## Accessibility Features

| Feature        | Purpose                  |
| -------------- | ------------------------ |
| Large Cursor   | Low vision support       |
| High Contrast  | Better visibility        |
| Thick Outline  | Cursor separation        |
| Reduced Motion | Motion-sensitive viewers |
| No Glow        | Simpler rendering        |
| No Trail       | Cleaner cursor           |

---

## Cursor Scaling Runtime

Cursor size automatically adapts.

| Export Format | Cursor Scale |
| ------------- | ------------ |
| 16:9 Desktop  | 1.0x         |
| Shorts (9:16) | 1.25x        |
| Square        | 1.15x        |
| Presentation  | 1.40x        |

---

## Contrast Detection Runtime

Automatically increases border thickness when:

* Background is white.
* Background is colorful.
* HDR export.
* Bright screenshots.

---

## Reduced Motion Runtime

Disables:

* Elastic cursor.
* Bounce.
* Motion blur.
* Trails.
* Glow pulse.

Keeps:

* Click ripple.
* Hover highlight.

---

## Accessibility Metadata

```ts
interface CursorAccessibilityRuntime {
  reducedMotion: boolean;
  highContrast: boolean;
  cursorScale: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Accessibility overrides creator theme during rendering but not timeline metadata.

# 06.96 GPU Export Cursor Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Realtime preview and exported cursor rendering must be pixel-identical across all resolutions.**

The export engine never captures the operating system cursor.

---

## Export Architecture

```text
Cursor Timeline
        ↓
Theme Runtime
        ↓
Accessibility Runtime
        ↓
GPU Cursor Pipeline
        ↓
Video Encoder
```

---

## GPU Cursor Render Stack

```text
Cursor Render Layer
│
├── Shadow Layer
├── Trail Layer
├── Motion Blur Layer
├── Cursor Shape Layer
├── Glow Layer
├── Ripple Layer
└── Highlight Layer
```

---

## Export Timeline Metadata

Each cursor frame stores:

| Property        | Stored |
| --------------- | ------ |
| Cursor Identity | ✅      |
| Theme ID        | ✅      |
| Morph Progress  | ✅      |
| Glow Strength   | ✅      |
| Ripple Timeline | ✅      |
| Trail Geometry  | ✅      |
| Physics State   | ✅      |

---

## Multi-Resolution Rendering

| Resolution  | Rendering Strategy       |
| ----------- | ------------------------ |
| 1080p       | Native vector rendering  |
| 1440p       | High DPI rendering       |
| 4K          | Retina-quality rendering |
| 8K (Future) | Infinite vector scaling  |

---

## HDR Cursor Rendering

Supports:

* HDR glow.
* HDR shadow.
* HDR ripple.
* Wide color gamut exports.

---

## Export Optimization Runtime

* Cursor rendered on separate texture layer.
* Cached vector geometry.
* GPU instancing.
* Motion replay instead of bitmap recording.

---

## Export Runtime Metadata

```ts
interface CursorExportRuntime {
  renderScale: number;
  replayVersion: number;
  hdrEnabled: boolean;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Export runtime consumes immutable cursor timeline metadata and reproduces identical output across hardware.

# 06.99 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 06.5.3)

1. Cursor Theme Runtime separates cursor appearance from cursor identity.
2. Brand Cursor System enables creator and company-specific cursor branding without affecting interaction semantics.
3. Cursor Packs Marketplace distributes reusable, versioned cursor themes built from SVG + JSON manifests.
4. Accessibility Runtime always has higher rendering priority than creator themes.
5. GPU Export Cursor Runtime renders cursor layers independently from operating system cursors.
6. Exported cursor rendering is deterministic across preview, export resolution and hardware.
7. Cursor themes remain fully compatible with cursor morphing, trails, glow, ripple and motion blur.
8. Theme switching never changes cursor hotspot, click location or timeline metadata.
9. Cursor appearance remains infinitely scalable through vector rendering.
10. **Chapter 06.5 completes TryLipi's Cursor Morphing Engine — a production-grade intelligent cursor system combining semantic detection, animated morphing, creator branding, accessibility and deterministic GPU export rendering.**

# 10.41 Viewport Tracking Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **TryLipi reconstructs a virtual viewport that knows exactly what the viewer is seeing at every frame, independent of the physical screen.**

Viewport Tracking is **not screen recording**.

It is the runtime responsible for answering questions like:

* What part of the webpage is currently visible?
* What elements are inside the viewport?
* Which elements are partially visible?
* Which elements are sticky?
* Which nested containers are scrolling?
* Where is the safe camera framing area?

Everything Smart Zoom does depends on this runtime.

---

## Why Virtual Viewports Exist

### Physical Screen

```text
3840 × 2160 Desktop Monitor
```

### Browser Window

```text
Chrome Window
1920 × 1040
```

### Actual Visible Viewport

```text
Viewport

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ Visible Portion of Page    │
│                            │
│                            │
│                            │
└────────────────────────────┘
```

The webpage may be **20,000+ pixels tall**, but the viewer only sees a small viewport.

TryLipi tracks the **visible region**, not the entire document.

---

## Why This Engine Is Critical

Without a Viewport Engine:

* Camera zooms to hidden elements.
* Blur masks include off-screen objects.
* Sticky headers drift during scrolling.
* AI annotations appear outside the visible screen.
* Scroll replay becomes inaccurate.

With Viewport Tracking:

* Camera only focuses visible content.
* Scroll-aware zooms remain stable.
* Sticky UI stays anchored.
* Nested scroll containers behave correctly.

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime                  | Responsibility                              |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| Virtual Viewport Runtime | Defines visible viewing rectangle.          |
| Scroll Runtime           | Tracks viewport movement over the document. |
| Visibility Runtime       | Computes which objects are visible.         |
| Safe Zone Runtime        | Reserves protected camera regions.          |
| Reconstruction Runtime   | Rebuilds viewport during replay/export.     |

---

## Design Principles

1. Viewport is a **virtual camera**, not a browser property.
2. Independent of monitor resolution.
3. Independent of browser zoom.
4. Fully scroll-aware.
5. Supports nested scrolling.
6. Supports sticky/fixed UI.
7. Deterministic timeline replay.

---

## Viewport Lifecycle

```text
Browser Opens
      │
      ▼
Virtual Viewport Created
      │
      ▼
Scroll / Resize Updates
      │
      ▼
Viewport Timeline Updated
      │
      ▼
Camera & Zoom Consume Viewport
```

---

# 10.42 Virtual Viewport Runtime Architecture

## Mission Statement

> **Every recording owns a continuously evolving virtual viewport timeline that represents exactly what the viewer sees.**

---

## High-Level Architecture

```text
Screen Capture Runtime
DOM Tracking Runtime
Pixel Tracking Runtime
Window Tracking Runtime
          │
          ▼
Virtual Viewport Runtime
          │
 ┌────────┼──────────┐
 │        │          │
 ▼        ▼          ▼
Geometry Visibility Safe Zones
Runtime  Runtime    Runtime
          │
          ▼
Viewport Timeline Recorder
```

---

## Runtime Pipeline

```text
Captured Frame
      │
      ▼
Viewport Geometry
      │
      ▼
Visible Region Computation
      │
      ▼
Visible Objects
      │
      ▼
Timeline Metadata
```

---

## Runtime Layers

```text
Viewport Runtime
│
├── Geometry Runtime
├── Visibility Runtime
├── Scroll Runtime
├── Safe Zone Runtime
├── Reconstruction Runtime
└── Timeline Runtime
```

Each layer is independent and replayable.

---

## Coordinate Spaces

| Coordinate Space | Description                      |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------- |
| Screen Space     | Entire monitor pixels.           |
| Window Space     | Browser window rectangle.        |
| Viewport Space   | Currently visible document area. |
| Document Space   | Entire scrollable webpage.       |
| Camera Space     | Smart Zoom camera coordinates.   |

---

## Coordinate Transformation Pipeline

```text
Document Coordinates
        │
Scroll Offset Applied
        │
        ▼
Viewport Coordinates
        │
Camera Transform Applied
        │
        ▼
Rendered Camera Coordinates
```

Every tracked object exists in **Document Space** before being projected into the viewport.

---

## Viewport Metadata

```ts
interface VirtualViewport {
  viewportId: string;

  width: number;
  height: number;

  scrollX: number;
  scrollY: number;

  devicePixelRatio: number;
  browserZoomFactor: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

* Viewport Runtime is the **single source of truth** for visible geometry.
* Camera systems never consume raw screen coordinates directly.
* Every frame references one immutable viewport snapshot.

---

# 10.43 Browser Viewport Tracking Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Track browser viewport position, dimensions and movement independently from webpage content.**

---

## Browser Viewport Architecture

```text
Browser Window
      │
      ▼
Viewport Runtime
      │
      ▼
Visible Document Region
```

---

## Browser Signals Captured

| Signal              | Purpose                   |
| ------------------- | ------------------------- |
| `innerWidth`        | Visible browser width.    |
| `innerHeight`       | Visible browser height.   |
| `scrollX`           | Horizontal scroll offset. |
| `scrollY`           | Vertical scroll offset.   |
| `devicePixelRatio`  | Retina / HiDPI scaling.   |
| `browserZoomFactor` | Browser zoom percentage.  |

---

## Viewport Timeline Example

```text
Frame 120
Viewport Y = 0

↓

Frame 180
Viewport Y = 320

↓

Frame 240
Viewport Y = 840
```

The viewport moves while the document stays fixed.

---

## Partial Visibility Runtime

Objects may be:

| Visibility State | Description                    |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Fully Visible    | Entire object inside viewport. |
| Top Clipped      | Hidden above viewport.         |
| Bottom Clipped   | Hidden below viewport.         |
| Left Clipped     | Hidden horizontally.           |
| Right Clipped    | Hidden horizontally.           |

---

### Example

```text
Viewport

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ Header                     │
│ Pricing Card               │
│ Pricing Card               │
│ Half Visible Card          │
└────────────────────────────┘
```

The last card is only partially visible.

---

## Visibility Percentage Runtime

Every object receives:

```ts
interface ViewportVisibility {
  visiblePercent: number;
  clippedTop: boolean;
  clippedBottom: boolean;
}
```

Used by:

* Smart Zoom.
* Blur engine.
* AI saliency.
* Auto screenshot generation.

---

## Viewport Edge Runtime

Tracks four dynamic viewport edges:

| Edge   | Used By                  |
| ------ | ------------------------ |
| Top    | Sticky header detection. |
| Bottom | Scroll prediction.       |
| Left   | Horizontal scrolling.    |
| Right  | Camera framing.          |

---

## Engineering Rules

Viewport geometry is stored in **Document Space**, never Screen Space.

---

# 10.44 Nested Scroll Container Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Modern applications contain multiple independent viewports that scroll simultaneously.**

---

## Why Nested Viewports Matter

Applications like:

* Notion
* Slack
* Discord
* VS Code
* Figma
* GitHub

have multiple independently scrolling regions.

---

## Nested Viewport Architecture

```text
Browser Page
│
├── Sidebar Viewport
├── Chat Viewport
├── Main Content Viewport
├── Modal Viewport
└── Dropdown Viewport
```

Each receives its own timeline.

---

## Nested Viewport Pipeline

```text
Container Detected
      │
      ▼
Container Viewport Created
      │
      ▼
Independent Scroll Tracking
      │
      ▼
Visibility Timeline Updated
```

---

## Supported Container Types

| Container   | Example           |
| ----------- | ----------------- |
| Sidebar     | Notion sidebar.   |
| Chat        | Slack messages.   |
| Modal       | Settings dialog.  |
| Explorer    | VS Code explorer. |
| Spreadsheet | Large tables.     |
| Comments    | YouTube comments. |

---

## Independent Scroll Timelines

```text
Main Page Scroll
Y = 920

Sidebar Scroll
Y = 180

Chat Scroll
Y = 2450
```

All scroll independently.

---

## Nested Visibility Runtime

Objects reference their parent viewport.

```text
Sidebar
 ├── Workspace
 ├── Pages
 └── Templates

Main Viewport
 ├── Heading
 ├── Paragraph
 └── Code Block
```

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface NestedViewport {
  containerId: string;

  viewportWidth: number;
  viewportHeight: number;

  scrollOffsetX: number;
  scrollOffsetY: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Nested viewport timelines remain isolated and composable.

---

# 10.45 Sticky Element Tracking Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Sticky UI elements remain anchored while the viewport moves underneath them.**

---

## Sticky Runtime Architecture

```text
Viewport Scroll
      │
      ▼
Sticky Detector
      │
      ▼
Sticky Timeline
      │
      ▼
Camera Runtime
```

---

## Sticky Detection Sources

| Detection Source       | Example           |
| ---------------------- | ----------------- |
| CSS `position: sticky` | Navbar.           |
| CSS `position: fixed`  | Floating CTA.     |
| Pixel Tracking         | Floating toolbar. |
| Semantic Detection     | Cookie banner.    |

---

## Sticky Timeline Example

```text
Scroll Begins

Navbar Position = Y 0

↓

Content Scrolls Down

↓

Navbar Still Y 0
```

Navbar never moves relative to viewport.

---

## Sticky Categories

| Category               | Example               |
| ---------------------- | --------------------- |
| Navigation             | Top navbar.           |
| Toolbar                | Figma toolbar.        |
| Floating Action Button | Mobile FAB.           |
| Cookie Banner          | Consent popup.        |
| Chat Composer          | WhatsApp input field. |
| Music Controls         | Floating player.      |

---

## Sticky Anchor Runtime

Sticky objects store:

```ts
interface StickyAnchor {
  edge: "top" | "bottom" | "left" | "right";

  offset: number;
}
```

---

## Camera Integration

Smart Zoom treats sticky objects differently:

* Ignores page scroll.
* Anchors camera to viewport coordinates.
* Maintains blur alignment.

---

## Engineering Rules

Sticky elements always use **Viewport Space**, not Document Space.

---

# 10.46 Camera Safe Zone Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Every viewport reserves protected framing regions for captions, branding, facecam and overlays.**

---

## Safe Zone Architecture

```text
Viewport

┌────────────────────────────┐
│ Top Title Safe Zone        │
│                            │
│ Camera Focus Region         │
│                            │
│ Caption Safe Zone           │
└────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## Safe Zone Categories

| Safe Zone           | Purpose                  |
| ------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Top Title Zone      | Video titles.            |
| Bottom Caption Zone | Auto captions.           |
| Facecam Zone        | Creator webcam overlay.  |
| Watermark Zone      | Brand watermark.         |
| CTA Zone            | Subscribe/Follow button. |

---

## Dynamic Safe Zones

Different export formats generate different safe zones.

| Export Format  | Safe Zone Behavior           |
| -------------- | ---------------------------- |
| 16:9           | Bottom captions only.        |
| 9:16 Shorts    | Larger bottom + top margins. |
| Square         | Symmetric margins.           |
| Facecam Layout | Facecam exclusion region.    |

---

## Camera Constraint Runtime

Before zooming:

```text
Zoom Target
      │
      ▼
Safe Zone Validation
      │
      ▼
Adjusted Camera Frame
```

The camera automatically shifts away from captions.

---

## Safe Zone Metadata

```ts
interface CameraSafeZone {
  topInset: number;
  bottomInset: number;
  leftInset: number;
  rightInset: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Safe Zones are evaluated **before every camera path calculation**.

---

# 10.47 Viewport Reconstruction Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Rebuild the exact viewport for every frame during replay and export rendering.**

---

## Reconstruction Architecture

```text
Viewport Timeline
      │
      ▼
Frame Rebuilder
      │
      ▼
Virtual Viewport Snapshot
      │
      ▼
Camera Renderer
```

---

## Reconstruction Pipeline

```text
Frame Number

↓

Viewport Geometry

↓

Scroll Offsets

↓

Sticky Offsets

↓

Visible Objects

↓

Camera Output
```

---

## Stored Timeline Metadata

Every frame stores:

* Viewport width.
* Viewport height.
* Scroll X/Y.
* Nested viewport states.
* Sticky element anchors.
* Device Pixel Ratio.
* Browser Zoom Factor.

---

## Replay Example

```text
Frame 180

Viewport
Y = 540

↓

Sidebar
Y = 120

↓

Camera Rebuilds Scene
```

The replay engine reconstructs the viewport exactly.

---

## Viewport Replay Metadata

```ts
interface ViewportReplayFrame {
  frameNumber: number;

  viewportId: string;

  scrollStateId: string;
}
```

---

## Replay Guarantees

* Deterministic export.
* Deterministic AI screenshot generation.
* Deterministic Smart Zoom replay.
* Identical browser state reconstruction.

---

## Engineering Rules

Viewport reconstruction is independent from the live browser state.

---

# 10.49 Acceptance Principles

## Viewport Tracking Tests

* Browser resize updates viewport geometry.
* Vertical scroll updates viewport correctly.
* Horizontal scroll updates correctly.
* Partial visibility percentages remain accurate.

---

## Nested Scroll Tests

* Sidebar scroll tracked independently.
* Chat scroll tracked independently.
* Modal scroll tracked independently.
* Spreadsheet viewport tracked independently.

---

## Sticky Tests

* Sticky navbar anchored correctly.
* Floating toolbar remains fixed.
* Cookie banner detected correctly.
* Floating action button remains viewport-relative.

---

## Safe Zone Tests

* Shorts safe zones generated correctly.
* Landscape safe zones generated correctly.
* Facecam exclusion zones respected.
* Caption overlap prevented.

---

## Replay Tests

* Viewport reconstruction deterministic.
* Scroll replay deterministic.
* Sticky replay deterministic.
* Nested viewport replay deterministic.

---

# 10.50 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 10.4.1)

1. Viewport Tracking Engine reconstructs a **virtual viewport** independent of physical screen resolution.
2. Browser Viewport Runtime tracks visible document geometry using viewport coordinates.
3. Nested Scroll Runtime creates independent timelines for every scrollable container.
4. Sticky Element Runtime anchors fixed UI elements relative to the viewport instead of document coordinates.
5. Camera Safe Zone Runtime reserves protected framing areas for captions, overlays, branding and facecam.
6. Viewport Reconstruction Runtime rebuilds the exact viewport during replay and export rendering.
7. Viewport coordinates become the canonical coordinate space for Smart Zoom and Camera Panning.
8. Partial visibility percentages are computed continuously for every tracked object.
9. Nested viewports are first-class runtime objects with independent geometry and scroll history.
10. **Chapter 10.4.1 establishes the Virtual Viewport Runtime—the foundation for scroll-aware camera movement, sticky UI handling, AI tutorials and deterministic viewport replay.**

# 10.51 Responsive Viewport Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **The same recording should understand browser zoom, HiDPI scaling, responsive layouts, split screens and floating windows without breaking camera intelligence.**

Modern recordings aren't limited to a single browser window.

Creators frequently:

* Zoom Chrome to 125%.
* Record on Retina displays.
* Use side-by-side browser windows.
* Record VS Code + Browser together.
* Open floating Picture-in-Picture videos.
* Resize windows during recording.

The Viewport Runtime must adapt continuously.

---

## Why Responsive Viewports Matter

### Browser Zoom Changes Geometry

```text
100% Zoom

┌────────────────────┐
│ Button             │
└────────────────────┘

125% Zoom

┌────────────────────┐
│ Larger Button      │
└────────────────────┘
```

The button occupies different viewport coordinates.

---

### Split Screen Recording

```text
┌────────────┬────────────┐
│ VS Code    │ Chrome      │
│            │             │
└────────────┴────────────┘
```

Two simultaneous viewports exist.

---

### Floating PiP Window

```text
Browser Viewport

┌────────────────────────┐
│                        │
│   Video Player         │
│                ┌────┐  │
│                │PiP │  │
│                └────┘  │
└────────────────────────┘
```

Camera must understand overlapping viewports.

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime                | Responsibility              |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Browser Zoom Runtime   | Browser zoom scaling.       |
| DPR Runtime            | HiDPI normalization.        |
| Responsive Runtime     | Layout breakpoint tracking. |
| Multi-Viewport Runtime | Multiple visible viewports. |
| Split Screen Runtime   | Side-by-side layouts.       |
| PiP Runtime            | Floating viewport tracking. |

---

## Design Principles

1. Browser zoom never breaks object tracking.
2. DPR normalized before camera calculations.
3. Layout breakpoints stored in timeline.
4. Multiple viewports coexist.
5. Responsive transitions replay deterministically.
6. Floating windows become viewport objects.
7. Export independent from recording display.

---

# 10.52 Browser Zoom Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Track browser zoom independently from operating system display scaling.**

Browser zoom changes CSS pixels while the monitor resolution stays constant.

---

## Zoom Runtime Architecture

```text
Browser Window
        │
Browser Zoom Listener
        │
Viewport Geometry Runtime
        │
Normalized Viewport
```

---

## Browser Zoom Signals

| Signal | Description          |
| ------ | -------------------- |
| 50%    | Zoomed out.          |
| 67%    | Reduced scale.       |
| 80%    | Slight zoom out.     |
| 90%    | Custom zoom.         |
| 100%   | Native viewport.     |
| 110%   | Slight zoom in.      |
| 125%   | Common desktop zoom. |
| 150%   | Large zoom.          |
| 175%   | Accessibility zoom.  |
| 200%   | Presentation zoom.   |

---

## Zoom Timeline Example

```text
Frame 100

Zoom = 100%

↓

Frame 180

Zoom = 125%

↓

Frame 240

Zoom = 150%
```

---

## Viewport Scaling Formula

<math block value="Viewport_{normalized}=\\frac{Viewport_{css}}{BrowserZoomFactor}"/>

Camera calculations always use normalized coordinates.

---

## Object Scaling Runtime

Every tracked object stores:

```ts
interface BrowserZoomAdjustedObject {
  cssRect: DOMRect;
  normalizedRect: DOMRect;
}
```

---

## Smart Zoom Integration

Smart Zoom always targets normalized geometry rather than raw CSS pixels.

---

## Engineering Rules

Browser zoom changes viewport scale—not document coordinates.

# 10.53 Device Pixel Ratio (DPR) Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Normalize cursor, viewport and pixel coordinates across Retina, HiDPI and standard displays.**

---

## DPR Runtime Architecture

```text
Operating System Display
        │
Device Pixel Ratio Runtime
        │
Normalized Pixels
        │
Viewport Runtime
```

---

## Common DPR Values

| Device               | DPR  |
| -------------------- | ---- |
| Windows Standard     | 1.0  |
| Windows 125% Scaling | 1.25 |
| Windows 150% Scaling | 1.5  |
| MacBook Retina       | 2.0  |
| MacBook Pro Retina   | 2.0  |
| iPhone Retina        | 3.0  |
| Android HiDPI        | 2–4  |

---

## Coordinate Conversion

```text
Physical Pixels

↓

DPR Conversion

↓

CSS Pixels

↓

Viewport Coordinates
```

---

## Cursor Normalization Example

| Physical | DPR  | Normalized |
| -------- | ---- | ---------- |
| 3000 px  | 2.0  | 1500 px    |
| 2400 px  | 1.5  | 1600 px    |
| 1800 px  | 1.25 | 1440 px    |

---

## Pixel Grid Runtime

Maintains:

* Physical pixels.
* Logical pixels.
* CSS pixels.
* Camera pixels.

All camera engines operate on DPR-normalized viewport coordinates.

# 10.60 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 10.4.2)

1. Browser Zoom Runtime normalizes viewport geometry independently from operating system scaling.
2. Device Pixel Ratio Engine converts physical pixels into logical viewport coordinates before camera calculations.
3. Multi-Viewport Runtime manages multiple simultaneous viewport timelines inside a recording session.
4. Responsive Layout Runtime records breakpoint transitions as immutable timeline events.
5. Split Screen Runtime tracks independent application windows sharing a monitor.
6. Picture-in-Picture Runtime treats floating overlays as viewport objects with their own geometry timeline.
7. Smart Zoom consumes normalized viewport geometry regardless of browser zoom or DPR.
8. Camera planning always resolves active viewport before target prediction.
9. Responsive layout transitions remain deterministic during replay and export.
10. **Chapter 10.4.2 establishes TryLipi's cross-device responsive viewport engine supporting browser zoom, Retina displays, responsive websites, split-screen recordings and floating overlay windows.**

# 10.61 Deterministic Viewport Replay Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Every exported frame should reconstruct the exact viewport the creator saw — including scroll position, browser zoom, sticky elements, nested containers, split windows, and overlays.**

Viewport replay is one of TryLipi's foundational rendering systems.

Instead of replaying pixels...

TryLipi replays **viewport state**.

That means exports are:

* Resolution independent.
* Browser independent.
* Frame deterministic.
* AI reproducible.

---

## Why Viewport Replay Exists

### Traditional Screen Recorder

```text
Recorded Pixels

↓

Encoded Video

↓

Replay Pixels
```

Everything is flattened into video.

### TryLipi Viewport Replay

```text
Viewport Timeline

↓

Viewport Reconstruction

↓

Smart Camera

↓

GPU Renderer

↓

Encoded Video
```

Viewport becomes a structured timeline.

---

## What Gets Replayed

| Component                | Replay |
| ------------------------ | ------ |
| Browser Viewport         | ✅      |
| Scroll Position          | ✅      |
| Sticky Elements          | ✅      |
| Nested Scroll Containers | ✅      |
| Browser Zoom             | ✅      |
| Device Pixel Ratio       | ✅      |
| PiP Windows              | ✅      |
| Split Screen Layouts     | ✅      |
| Safe Zones               | ✅      |

---

## Design Principles

1. Replay is deterministic.
2. Resolution independent.
3. Timeline driven.
4. Camera driven.
5. GPU rendered.
6. Export identical to preview.
7. AI reusable.

---

## Replay Lifecycle

```text
Recording Timeline

↓

Viewport Timeline

↓

Viewport Reconstruction

↓

Camera Planner

↓

GPU Renderer
```

---

# 10.62 Viewport Timeline Serialization Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Every viewport mutation becomes immutable timeline metadata.**

Nothing during replay depends on the original browser.

---

## Serialization Architecture

```text
Viewport Runtime

↓

Viewport Snapshot

↓

Timeline Serializer

↓

Binary Timeline
```

---

## Snapshot Frequency

Viewport snapshots are stored only when something changes.

### Tracked Events

| Event                 | Snapshot |
| --------------------- | -------- |
| Scroll Update         | ✅        |
| Resize Window         | ✅        |
| Browser Zoom Changed  | ✅        |
| Sticky Layout Changed | ✅        |
| Nested Scroll Updated | ✅        |
| Breakpoint Changed    | ✅        |
| PiP Window Moved      | ✅        |
| Split Layout Changed  | ✅        |

---

## Snapshot Structure

```ts
interface ViewportSnapshot {
  timestampMs: number;

  viewportId: string;

  scrollStateId: string;

  geometryStateId: string;

  zoomStateId: string;

  nestedViewportStateIds: string[];
}
```

---

## Timeline Compression Runtime

Instead of storing every frame...

```text
Frame 120
Scroll = 320

Frames 121–160
No Changes

Frame 161
Scroll = 480
```

Only changed states are serialized.

---

## Delta Encoding Runtime

Stores only viewport differences.

```text
Previous Snapshot

↓

Changed Scroll Offset

↓

Changed Zoom Factor

↓

Changed Sticky Anchor
```

---

## Timeline Metadata

```ts
interface ViewportTimelineMetadata {
  totalSnapshots: number;

  compressionRatio: number;

  recordingDurationMs: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Viewport timeline serialization is append-only and immutable.

---

# 10.63 Viewport Replay Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Reconstruct viewport geometry frame-by-frame using serialized timeline metadata.**

---

## Replay Engine Architecture

```text
Viewport Timeline

↓

Snapshot Loader

↓

Frame Reconstructor

↓

Viewport State Cache

↓

Renderer
```

---

## Replay Pipeline

```text
Frame Number

↓

Nearest Snapshot

↓

Apply Delta Updates

↓

Reconstructed Viewport

↓

Camera Runtime
```

---

## Replay Components

| Component          | Responsibility       |
| ------------------ | -------------------- |
| Snapshot Loader    | Load viewport state. |
| Delta Runtime      | Apply changes.       |
| Geometry Builder   | Build viewport.      |
| Visibility Builder | Visible objects.     |
| Sticky Runtime     | Anchor fixed UI.     |

---

## Frame Reconstruction Example

```text
Frame 180

Viewport Height
1040

↓

Scroll Y
620

↓

Sidebar Scroll
140

↓

Browser Zoom
125%
```

Everything rebuilds deterministically.

---

## Random Access Replay

Supports seeking directly to any frame.

```text
Jump to Frame 1200

↓

Load Latest Snapshot

↓

Apply Deltas

↓

Viewport Ready
```

Used by timeline scrubbing.

---

## Replay Cache Runtime

Caches nearby snapshots.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ViewportReplayState {
  currentSnapshotId: string;

  reconstructedFrameNumber: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Replay runtime never depends on live DOM state.

# 10.65 GPU Viewport Rendering Pipeline

## Mission Statement

> **Viewport rendering is performed as a GPU compositing pipeline before encoding video.**

---

## GPU Rendering Architecture

```text
Viewport Replay

↓

Viewport Texture Builder

↓

Camera Crop Pass

↓

Overlay Pass

↓

GPU Composite

↓

Encoder
```

---

## Rendering Layers

```text
Viewport Render Stack
│
├── Background Frame
├── Visible Viewport
├── Sticky Layer
├── Overlay Layer
├── PiP Layer
├── Cursor Layer
├── Blur Layer
└── Caption Layer
```

---

## Render Passes

| Pass           | Purpose                  |
| -------------- | ------------------------ |
| Geometry Pass  | Viewport reconstruction. |
| Crop Pass      | Camera crop.             |
| Overlay Pass   | Sticky/PiP overlays.     |
| Cursor Pass    | Cursor rendering.        |
| Caption Pass   | Captions/subtitles.      |
| Composite Pass | Final frame.             |

---

## Viewport Texture Runtime

Each viewport becomes its own GPU texture.

Supports:

* Browser.
* VS Code.
* PiP.
* Modal.
* Split screen.

---

## GPU Optimization

Uses:

* Texture reuse.
* Tile rendering.
* Dirty region rendering.
* Viewport cache.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ViewportRenderTexture {
  textureId: string;

  viewportId: string;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Viewport rendering occurs before cursor compositing.

# 10.66 Performance Optimization Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Viewport tracking must scale to multi-hour recordings without excessive memory or CPU usage.**

---

## Performance Architecture

```text
Viewport Timeline

↓

Compression Runtime

↓

Snapshot Cache

↓

Viewport Streaming

↓

GPU Renderer
```

---

## Optimization Strategies

| Strategy             | Benefit                      |
| -------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Snapshot Compression | Smaller timeline.            |
| Delta Encoding       | Less storage.                |
| Lazy Reconstruction  | Faster seeking.              |
| Tile Rendering       | GPU efficiency.              |
| Dirty Viewports      | Render only changed regions. |

---

## Memory Runtime

Viewport cache automatically evicts unused snapshots.

---

## Large Recording Strategy

Example:

| Recording Length | Optimization            |
| ---------------- | ----------------------- |
| 5 min            | Full cache.             |
| 30 min           | Sliding cache.          |
| 2 hr             | Streaming snapshots.    |
| 6 hr             | Chunked reconstruction. |

---

## Timeline Chunking

```text
Recording

↓

Chunk 1

↓

Chunk 2

↓

Chunk 3

↓

Replay Stream
```

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ViewportPerformanceState {
  activeChunkId: string;

  cachedSnapshots: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Viewport reconstruction streams timeline chunks during export.

---

# 10.70 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 10.4.3)

1. Viewport Timeline Serialization stores immutable viewport snapshots rather than pixel frames.
2. Viewport Replay Engine reconstructs viewport geometry deterministically for any frame.
3. AI Camera Viewport Runtime consumes reconstructed viewport geometry instead of raw screen pixels.
4. GPU Viewport Rendering composites viewport layers before cursor and captions.
5. Performance Runtime uses snapshot compression, delta encoding and streaming replay for long recordings.
6. Export Integration Runtime reconstructs identical viewport geometry across preview and exported video.
7. Responsive layouts, split screens and PiP windows replay independently from browser state.
8. Viewport replay supports random frame seeking without replaying the entire timeline.
9. Camera planning always operates on normalized viewport coordinates after DPR and browser zoom normalization.
10. **Chapter 10.4 completes TryLipi's Viewport Tracking Engine — the canonical virtual viewport system enabling cinematic camera movement, AI tutorials, deterministic exports and multi-viewport intelligence.**
