# 12.61 Screen Change Detection Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **TryLipi understands *what changed on the screen*, *why it changed*, *where it changed*, and *whether the viewer should care*.**

Screen recording isn't just a sequence of frames.

Every frame contains **events**:

* A button appeared.
* A modal opened.
* Text changed.
* A spinner started.
* A notification disappeared.
* A sidebar expanded.
* A dropdown collapsed.
* A page navigated.

The Screen Change Detection Engine converts raw pixels into meaningful UI events.

---

## Why This Engine Exists

### Traditional Recorder

```text
Frame N

↓

Frame N+1

↓

Encode Pixels
```

Pixels change, but meaning is lost.

### TryLipi

```text
Frame N

↓

Detect Pixel Difference

↓

Classify UI Mutation

↓

Assign Confidence

↓

Trigger AI Camera
```

The recording becomes an **event timeline** instead of a bitmap sequence.

---

## Problems This Engine Solves

| Recording Problem        | Engine Solution                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------ |
| Dropdown opens unnoticed | Detect UI expansion.           |
| Spinner starts           | Detect loading state.          |
| Page changes             | Detect navigation event.       |
| Button color changes     | Ignore insignificant mutation. |
| Large modal appears      | Trigger Smart Zoom.            |
| Tooltip flashes          | Ignore transient change.       |

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime             | Responsibility               |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Frame Diff Engine   | Detect changed pixels.       |
| Pixel Runtime       | Measure change magnitude.    |
| UI Mutation Runtime | Classify interface changes.  |
| DOM Sync Runtime    | Map DOM mutations to pixels. |
| Confidence Runtime  | Score importance of changes. |
| Timeline Runtime    | Store UI events.             |

---

## Design Principles

1. Detect meaningful changes, not every pixel.
2. Separate visual noise from UI events.
3. DOM-first when available.
4. Pixel fallback everywhere.
5. Timeline deterministic.
6. Camera-trigger friendly.
7. AI reusable.

---

## Screen Change Lifecycle

```text
Captured Frame

↓

Frame Difference

↓

Region Extraction

↓

Mutation Classification

↓

Confidence Scoring

↓

Timeline Event
```

Every change becomes structured metadata.

---

# 12.62 Runtime Architecture

## Mission Statement

> **Screen Change Detection sits between screen capture and AI understanding.**

It transforms low-level rendering changes into semantic events.

---

## High-Level Architecture

```text
Screen Capture Runtime
Pixel Tracking Runtime
DOM Tracking Runtime
Object Tracking Runtime
Viewport Runtime
        │
        ▼
Screen Change Detection Runtime
        │
 ┌──────┼────────┬──────────┐
 ▼      ▼        ▼          ▼
Frame   Pixel    DOM      Confidence
Diff    Runtime  Runtime    Runtime
        │
        ▼
UI Event Timeline
        │
        ▼
Smart Zoom + AI Camera + Saliency Engine
```

---

## Processing Pipeline

```text
Captured Frame

↓

Compare Previous Frame

↓

Locate Changed Regions

↓

Merge DOM + Pixel Information

↓

Classify Mutation

↓

Timeline Serialization
```

---

## Runtime Layers

```text
Screen Change Runtime
│
├── Frame Difference Layer
├── Pixel Change Layer
├── Mutation Classification Layer
├── DOM Synchronization Layer
├── Confidence Layer
└── Timeline Layer
```

Each layer produces reusable metadata.

---

## Input Sources

| Source           | Information                 |
| ---------------- | --------------------------- |
| Screen Frames    | Raw RGB pixels.             |
| DOM Observer     | Element mutations.          |
| Pixel Tracker    | Persistent object movement. |
| Viewport Runtime | Visible geometry.           |
| Cursor Runtime   | Interaction context.        |

---

## Runtime Metadata

```ts
interface ScreenChangeRuntimeState {
  currentFrameNumber: number;
  previousFrameNumber: number;
  detectedRegions: number;
  uiEventsGenerated: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Screen Change Runtime executes before Saliency and Camera Planning.

---

# 12.63 Frame Difference Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Identify which pixels changed between consecutive frames using deterministic GPU-friendly algorithms.**

Frame Difference is the foundation of every UI mutation.

---

## Frame Difference Architecture

```text
Frame N

↓

Frame N+1

↓

Difference Engine

↓

Changed Regions
```

---

## Difference Pipeline

```text
Previous Frame

↓

Current Frame

↓

Pixel Comparison

↓

Difference Mask

↓

Bounding Regions
```

---

## Difference Mask

```text
Frame Difference Mask

□□□□□□□□□□□□

□□■■■■□□□□

□□■■■■□□□□

□□□□■■■□□□

□□□□□□□□□□□□
```

White pixels represent changed regions.

---

## Difference Categories

| Difference Type | Example           |
| --------------- | ----------------- |
| Appearance      | New button.       |
| Disappearance   | Closed modal.     |
| Movement        | Dragged card.     |
| Resize          | Expanded sidebar. |
| Color Change    | Hover state.      |
| Opacity Change  | Fade animation.   |

---

## Difference Threshold Runtime

Small changes are ignored.

| Difference Magnitude | Result              |
| -------------------- | ------------------- |
| 1–2 pixels           | Ignore noise.       |
| 3–20 pixels          | Candidate mutation. |
| 20+ pixels           | Significant region. |

---

## Bounding Box Generation

Every difference cluster becomes:

```ts
interface ChangedRegion {
  x: number;
  y: number;
  width: number;
  height: number;
}
```

---

## Region Merge Runtime

Nearby regions merge into one UI mutation.

---

## Engineering Rules

Frame Difference uses viewport-normalized coordinates before clustering.

---

# 12.64 Pixel Difference Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Measure how much each region visually changed instead of simply detecting that something changed.**

---

## Pixel Runtime Architecture

```text
Changed Region

↓

Pixel Analyzer

↓

Difference Metrics

↓

Importance Candidate
```

---

## Difference Metrics

| Metric             | Description          |
| ------------------ | -------------------- |
| Changed Pixels     | Pixel count.         |
| Area Changed       | Region size.         |
| Brightness Delta   | Luminance shift.     |
| Color Distance     | RGB distance.        |
| Edge Difference    | Shape change.        |
| Texture Difference | Structural mutation. |

---

## Pixel Difference Formula

<math block value="DifferenceScore=\\sum_{pixels}|RGB_{new}-RGB_{old}|"/>

---

## Difference Heatmap

```text
High Difference

███████

████

██

Low Difference
```

Heatmap becomes AI input.

---

## Color Change Runtime

Detects:

* Hover colors.
* Button active states.
* Dark/light theme switch.
* Progress bar changes.

---

## Structural Difference Runtime

Edge detection distinguishes:

* Color-only mutation.
* Layout mutation.
* Shape mutation.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface PixelDifferenceMetrics {
  changedPixels: number;
  averageColorDistance: number;
  structuralDifference: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Pixel Difference Runtime never classifies semantic meaning—it only measures visual change.

---

# 12.65 UI Mutation Detection Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Convert changed pixel regions into meaningful interface mutations.**

This is where TryLipi begins understanding UI.

---

## Mutation Detection Architecture

```text
Changed Regions

↓

Region Classification

↓

Mutation Type

↓

Timeline Event
```

---

## Mutation Categories

| Category            | Example              |
| ------------------- | -------------------- |
| Element Appeared    | Modal opens.         |
| Element Disappeared | Toast removed.       |
| Element Moved       | Card dragged.        |
| Element Resized     | Sidebar expands.     |
| Element Replaced    | Page navigation.     |
| Element Updated     | Button text changed. |

---

## UI Mutation Timeline

```text
Frame 140

Dropdown Closed

↓

Frame 142

Dropdown Open

↓

UI Mutation Event
```

---

## Mutation Sources

| Source              | Confidence |
| ------------------- | ---------- |
| DOM Mutation        | Very High  |
| Pixel Mutation      | High       |
| OCR Change          | Medium     |
| Semantic Prediction | Medium     |

---

## Compound Mutations

Example:

```text
Button Click

↓

Spinner Appears

↓

↓

```

Grouped into one logical interaction.

---

## Mutation Metadata

```ts

  mutationType: MutationType;
  affectedObjectId?: string;

}
```

---

---

# 12.66 DOM ↔ Pixel Synchronization Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Synchronize DOM mutations with pixel mutations to produce reliable UI events.**

This gives TryLipi browser-level intelligence.

---

## Synchronization Architecture

```text
DOM Mutation

↓

Pixel Mutation

↓

Synchronization Engine

↓

Unified Mutation Event
```

---

## Synchronization Pipeline

```text
DOM Observer

↓

Element Geometry

↓

Pixel Region Match

↓

Mutation Confidence Updated
```

---

## DOM Signals

| Signal             | Example           |
| ------------------ | ----------------- |
| Child Added        | Modal inserted.   |
| Attribute Changed  | Button disabled.  |
| Text Changed       | Counter updated.  |
| Style Changed      | Color transition. |
| Visibility Changed | Dropdown hidden.  |

---

## Pixel Matching Runtime

```text
DOM Bounding Box

↓

Pixel Difference Box

↓

IoU Match

↓

Unified Region
```

---

## Conflict Resolution

| Scenario          | Result                   |
| ----------------- | ------------------------ |
| DOM + Pixel Agree | High confidence.         |
| DOM Only          | Browser mutation event.  |
| Pixel Only        | Canvas/Desktop fallback. |
| Neither           | Ignore noise.            |

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface DOMPixelSyncState {
  domMutationId?: string;
  pixelRegionId: string;
  synchronizationScore: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

DOM synchronization always increases mutation confidence when geometry overlaps.

---

# 12.67 Change Confidence Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Score how important a detected screen change is for viewers and AI camera movement.**

Every mutation receives a confidence score.

---

## Confidence Architecture

```text
Mutation Event

↓

Feature Extractor

↓

Confidence Model

↓

Importance Score
```

---

## Confidence Inputs

| Signal                  | Weight |
| ----------------------- | ------ |
| Region Size             | High   |
| Cursor Proximity        | High   |
| DOM Mutation            | High   |
| Persistent Object Match | High   |
| Animation Detection     | Medium |
| Saliency Prediction     | Medium |

---

## Confidence Levels

| Score     | Meaning                   |
| --------- | ------------------------- |
| 0.00–0.25 | Ignore visual noise.      |
| 0.25–0.50 | Minor UI update.          |
| 0.50–0.75 | Meaningful mutation.      |
| 0.75–0.90 | Important interaction.    |
| 0.90–1.00 | Camera trigger candidate. |

---

## Confidence Example

```text
Button Hover

↓

0.22

(No Camera)

Dropdown Opens

↓

0.86

(Camera Candidate)

Modal Appears

↓

0.97

(Camera Trigger)
```

---

## Confidence Metadata

```ts
interface ScreenChangeConfidence {
  confidenceScore: number;
  shouldTriggerCamera: boolean;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Confidence Engine never triggers camera directly—it only emits recommendation metadata.

---

# 12.68 Runtime APIs

## Detection APIs

| API                             | Purpose                      |
| ------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `computeFrameDifference()`      | Generate pixel diff mask.    |
| `extractChangedRegions()`       | Cluster changed pixels.      |
| `measurePixelDifference()`      | Compute visual metrics.      |
| `detectUIMutations()`           | Classify interface mutation. |
| `synchronizeDOMAndPixels()`     | Merge DOM + pixel events.    |
| `scoreScreenChangeConfidence()` | Generate importance score.   |

---

## Runtime Interface

```ts
interface ScreenChangeDetectionAPI {
  supportsDOMSynchronization: boolean;
  supportsPixelFallback: boolean;
  supportsConfidenceScoring: boolean;
}
```

---

## Runtime Events

```text
screen.frame.changed
screen.region.detected
screen.mutation.detected
screen.dom.synchronized
screen.change.scored
screen.timeline.updated
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Screen Change APIs emit immutable mutation events into the timeline.

---

# 12.69 Acceptance Principles

## Frame Difference Tests

* Pixel differences detected correctly.
* Noise filtered.
* Bounding boxes generated.

### Mutation Tests

* Modal appearance detected.
* Dropdown expansion detected.
* Sidebar resize detected.
* Button text change detected.

### DOM Sync Tests

* DOM + Pixel merge succeeds.
* Canvas fallback works.
* Hidden element ignored.

### Confidence Tests

* Hover ignored.
* Loading spinner medium confidence.
* Modal high confidence.
* Navigation highest confidence.

---

# 12.70 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 12.6.1)

1. Screen Change Detection Engine transforms frame differences into semantic UI mutation events.
2. Frame Difference Engine detects changed pixel clusters using viewport-normalized coordinates.
3. Pixel Difference Runtime measures visual magnitude without assigning semantic meaning.
4. UI Mutation Detection Runtime classifies appearance, disappearance, movement, resize and update events.
5. DOM ↔ Pixel Synchronization Runtime merges browser mutation events with pixel regions using geometry matching.
6. Change Confidence Engine scores every mutation for downstream AI systems.
7. Mutation events become immutable timeline metadata independent of captured pixels.
8. Camera, Saliency and Intent Prediction consume confidence-scored mutation events rather than raw pixel differences.
9. Browser recordings prefer DOM synchronization while desktop recordings fall back to pixel-only mutation detection.
10. **Chapter 12.6.1 establishes the foundational Screen Change Detection Engine that converts raw visual changes into structured AI-readable events powering Smart Zoom, Saliency, Tutorials and Export Rendering.**

# 12.71 Dynamic Screen Intelligence Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Not every screen change is a new interface. Many changes are temporary, continuous, animated or state-driven. TryLipi distinguishes between static mutations and dynamic interface behavior.**

Part 12.6.1 detected **what changed**.

Part 12.6.2 detects **how the screen is changing over time**.

This allows AI to understand:

* Loading animations.
* Scrolling motion.
* Progress bars.
* Video playback.
* Skeleton loaders.
* Typing indicators.
* Carousel animations.
* Infinite scrolling.
* Animated transitions.

These are treated differently from ordinary UI mutations.

---

## Static vs Dynamic Screen Changes

| Static Mutation     | Dynamic Mutation      |
| ------------------- | --------------------- |
| Modal appears       | Spinner rotates       |
| Sidebar expands     | Progress bar fills    |
| Button text changes | Video keeps playing   |
| New notification    | Chat typing animation |
| Dialog closes       | Carousel auto-scrolls |

Dynamic mutations persist across multiple frames.

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime               | Responsibility                           |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Animation Runtime     | Detect animated UI regions.              |
| Scroll Runtime        | Detect viewport and container scrolling. |
| Loading Runtime       | Detect loading states and skeletons.     |
| Progress Runtime      | Detect progress indicators.              |
| Media Runtime         | Detect video/audio playback.             |
| Dynamic State Runtime | Build continuous UI state timeline.      |

---

## Design Principles

1. Understand continuous motion.
2. Ignore decorative animations when appropriate.
3. Detect interaction-driven animations.
4. Detect autonomous animations.
5. Timeline continuous states.
6. Camera reacts only to meaningful dynamics.
7. GPU-friendly implementation.

---

## Dynamic Change Lifecycle

```text
Frame Difference
      │
      ▼
Dynamic Region Candidate
      │
      ▼
Motion Analysis
      │
      ▼
Animation Classification
      │
      ▼
Continuous State Timeline
```

---

# 12.72 Animation Detection Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Detect interface animations independently from user interactions.**

Animations often indicate important UI transitions.

Examples include:

* Dropdown opening.
* Toast fading.
* Button hover.
* Modal scaling.
* Skeleton shimmer.
* Floating tooltip.

---

## Animation Detection Architecture

```text
Frame Timeline
      │
      ▼
Motion Vector Runtime
      │
      ▼
Animation Region Builder
      │
      ▼
Animation Classifier
```

---

## Animation Detection Pipeline

```text
Frame N

↓

Frame N+1

↓

Frame N+2

↓

Motion Continuity

↓

Animation Event
```

Instead of one frame difference, TryLipi analyzes multiple consecutive frames.

---

## Animation Categories

| Category           | Example                   |
| ------------------ | ------------------------- |
| Fade In            | Modal opening             |
| Fade Out           | Notification disappearing |
| Scale Animation    | Dialog grows              |
| Slide Animation    | Sidebar enters            |
| Rotation Animation | Spinner                   |
| Pulse Animation    | Button pulse              |
| Bounce Animation   | Success animation         |
| Morph Animation    | FAB expands               |

---

## Motion Vector Runtime

Every changed region receives a motion vector.

```text
Button

Frame 120
X = 300

Frame 121
X = 305

Frame 122
X = 311
```

Continuous movement indicates animation.

---

## Animation Curves Runtime

Recognizes:

| Curve       | Example           |
| ----------- | ----------------- |
| Linear      | Progress bar      |
| Ease In     | Modal open        |
| Ease Out    | Dropdown close    |
| Ease In-Out | Sidebar animation |
| Spring      | Button bounce     |
| Elastic     | Tooltip pop       |

---

## Persistent Animation Detection

Animations longer than threshold become continuous runtime states.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface AnimationDetectionState {
  animationType: AnimationType;
  durationMs: number;
  regionId: string;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Animation detection uses temporal consistency across multiple frames before classification.

---

# 12.73 Scroll Change Detection Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Detect every type of scrolling across webpages, nested containers and virtualized lists.**

Scrolling is not treated as generic motion.

```text
Viewport Runtime

↓

Scroll Analyzer

↓

↓
```

| Source            | Example          |
| ----------------- | ---------------- |
| Window Scroll     | Entire webpage   |
| Container Scroll  | Chat window      |
| Horizontal Scroll | Spreadsheet      |
| Carousel Scroll   | Product carousel |
| Infinite Scroll   | Social feeds     |
| Code Scroll       | VS Code editor   |

---

## Scroll Detection Pipeline

```text
Previous Viewport

↓

Current Viewport

↓

Scroll Offset Delta

↓

Scroll Event
```

---

## Scroll Event Types

| Event           | Description            |
| --------------- | ---------------------- |
| Scroll Start    | Motion begins.         |
| Scroll Continue | Continuous movement.   |
| Scroll Stop     | Velocity reaches zero. |
| Scroll Snap     | CSS snap scrolling.    |
| Momentum Scroll | Inertial scrolling.    |

---

## Scroll Velocity Runtime

Computes:

<math block value="Velocity=\\frac{ScrollOffset_{new}-ScrollOffset_{old}}{FrameDelta}"/>

Used for Smart Zoom smoothing.

---

## Infinite Scroll Runtime

Detects:

* Newly inserted content.
* Virtualized DOM lists.
* Lazy-loaded cards.
* Feed expansion.

---

## Scroll Confidence

| Pattern              | Confidence |
| -------------------- | ---------- |
| Continuous offset    | High       |
| DOM insertions       | High       |
| Pixel-only movement  | Medium     |
| Background animation | Low        |

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ScrollChangeState {
  scrollDirection: ScrollDirection;
  scrollVelocity: number;
  containerId?: string;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Scroll detection distinguishes viewport motion from object motion.

### Loading Tests

# 12.80 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 12.6.2)

1. Animation Detection Engine classifies continuous UI animations across multiple frames.
2. Scroll Change Detection Runtime distinguishes viewport scrolling from object movement.
3. Loading State Detection Runtime groups spinner, skeleton and placeholder animations into loading sessions.
4. Progress Indicator Detection Runtime continuously tracks visual completion indicators.
5. Media Playback Detection Runtime detects playing, paused, buffering and seeking states independently from generic animations.
6. Dynamic UI State Machine converts continuous UI behavior into persistent timeline states.
7. Continuous UI states remain active until explicit completion conditions occur.
8. Smart Zoom and Camera Planner consume dynamic states rather than raw frame differences.
9. Timeline serialization stores animation sessions instead of per-frame animation events whenever possible.
10. **Chapter 12.6.2 establishes TryLipi's Dynamic Screen Intelligence Runtime—the layer that understands scrolling, loading, animation and media playback as meaningful UI behavior rather than simple pixel movement.**

# 12.81 Scene Intelligence Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **TryLipi understands when the recording has entered a new visual scene, not merely when pixels changed.**

A "scene" is a meaningful visual context.

Examples:

* Home page → Pricing page.
* Modal closed → Dashboard visible.
* Sidebar collapsed → Editor expanded.
* Empty chat → Conversation started.
* VS Code → Browser window.

This chapter converts mutation timelines into **semantic scenes**.

---

## Mutation vs Scene

| Mutation                  | Scene |
| ------------------------- | ----- |
| Button hover              | No    |
| Spinner starts            | No    |
| Modal opens               | Maybe |
| New page loaded           | Yes   |
| Window switched           | Yes   |
| Full-screen editor opened | Yes   |

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime                | Responsibility                 |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Scene Classification   | Identify scene boundaries.     |
| Camera Trigger Runtime | Decide when AI camera reacts.  |
| AI Timeline Runtime    | Serialize interaction events.  |
| Replay Runtime         | Replay semantic events.        |
| Export Runtime         | Feed Smart Zoom/export engine. |

---

## Design Principles

1. Scene boundaries are semantic.
2. Ignore cosmetic changes.
3. Trigger camera only on meaningful transitions.
4. Timeline-first architecture.
5. Deterministic replay.
6. AI-friendly metadata.
7. Export identical to preview.

---

## Scene Lifecycle

```text
Screen Mutations

↓

Mutation Clustering

↓

Scene Classification

↓

AI Timeline Event

↓

Camera Planner
```

---

# 12.82 Scene Change Classification Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Group multiple UI mutations into meaningful visual scene transitions.**

---

## Scene Classification Architecture

```text
Mutation Timeline

↓

Scene Candidate Builder

↓

↓

Scene Timeline
```

---

## Classification Pipeline

```text

↓

↓

↓

```

---

## Scene Categories

| Scene Type            | Example                         |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| Navigation            | Page changes.                   |
| Modal Scene           | Dialog opens/closes.            |
| Context Switch        | Window changes.                 |
| Workspace Change      | Different editor/tab.           |
| Content Reveal        | Hidden section becomes visible. |
| Fullscreen Transition | Video enters fullscreen.        |

---

## Navigation Scene Detection

Signals combined:

* Large DOM replacement.
* Scroll reset.
* URL changed.
* New persistent objects.
* Old objects disappear.

---

## Modal Scene Detection

```text
Dashboard

↓

↓

Dashboard
```

Three scenes are recorded.

---

## Scene Boundary Confidence

| Score     | Meaning                 |
| --------- | ----------------------- |
| 0–0.30    | Ignore                  |
| 0.30–0.55 | Minor transition        |
| 0.55–0.80 | Important UI transition |
| 0.80–1.00 | New scene               |

# 12.89 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 12.6.3)

1. Scene Change Classification Engine groups multiple mutations into semantic visual scenes.
2. Camera Trigger Runtime recommends cinematic camera actions without directly moving the camera.
3. AI Event Timeline serializes every meaningful interaction into immutable metadata.
4. Replay Runtime reconstructs semantic screen state without rerunning detection algorithms.
5. Export Runtime consumes timeline metadata rather than raw frame differences.
6. Loading sessions, scroll sessions and animation sessions persist until explicit completion events.
7. Scene boundaries are confidence-scored before becoming camera candidates.
8. Screen intelligence remains deterministic across preview and export.
9. All downstream AI systems consume semantic events instead of raw pixels.
10. **Chapter 12.6 completes TryLipi's Screen Change Detection Engine — the event intelligence layer connecting pixel tracking, viewport tracking, Smart Zoom, saliency prediction, AI tutorials and deterministic exports.**

# 18.6A.11 Visual Attention Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **TryLipi predicts where a human viewer will naturally look before moving the camera.**

This is arguably the **most important AI system** inside TryLipi.

Instead of following the cursor blindly...

The camera follows **human attention**.

---

## Cursor ≠ Attention

A cursor is only one signal.

Example:

```text id="cnlkk8"
Cursor Here

↓

Viewer Looking Here
```

People often look ahead of the cursor.

Examples include:

* Reading text.
* Watching progress bars.
* Watching dropdown menus.
* Watching loading spinners.
* Watching highlighted code.
* Watching charts.

---

## Human Visual Attention Sources

| Attention Signal    | Example                 |
| ------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Cursor              | Mouse movement.         |
| Motion              | Animated UI.            |
| Color Contrast      | Red notification badge. |
| Size                | Large modal.            |
| Position            | Center content.         |
| Text Hierarchy      | Headings.               |
| Faces               | Webcam bubble.          |
| Semantic Importance | Primary CTA button.     |

---

## Why This Engine Exists

### Traditional Smart Zoom

```text id="ol2wnf"
Cursor

↓

Zoom Cursor
```

Works for tutorials, fails for reading.

### TryLipi Smart Zoom

```text id="tnu34g"
Cursor

Motion

Text

DOM

Objects

↓

Attention Engine

↓

Camera Target
```

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime            | Responsibility                      |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------- |
| Heatmap Runtime    | Visual attention probability map.   |
| Eye-Gaze Runtime   | Viewer gaze prediction.             |
| Importance Runtime | Object importance scoring.          |
| Hierarchy Runtime  | UI visual priority ranking.         |
| Fusion Runtime     | Combine multiple attention signals. |
| Timeline Runtime   | Store attention metadata.           |

---

## Design Principles

1. Predict human attention.
2. Multi-signal fusion.
3. Cursor is one feature.
4. Dynamic heatmaps.
5. Viewport-aware.
6. Camera-aware.
7. Replay deterministic.

---

## Attention Lifecycle

```text id="rw4kk9"
Viewport Objects

↓

Attention Signals

↓

Saliency Heatmap

↓

Attention Scores

↓

Camera Candidate Regions
```

## Eye-Gaze Prediction Sources

| Cursor Velocity     | High         |
| Cursor Direction    | High         |
| Reading Direction   | High         |
| Motion Regions      | High         |
| Object Contrast     | Medium       |
| Screen Center Bias  | Medium       |
| Semantic Importance | Medium       |

---

## Gaze Prediction Pipeline

```text id="v0sgvl"
Cursor Heading Right

↓

Predict Viewer Looks Ahead

↓

Heatmap Shifted Right
```

---

## Reading Direction Runtime

Supports:

| Language Direction | Prediction       |
| ------------------ | ---------------- |
| Left → Right       | English          |
| Right → Left       | Arabic           |
| Top → Bottom       | Vertical layouts |
| Bidirectional      | Mixed UI         |

---

## Anticipatory Gaze Runtime

Viewer gaze often precedes cursor.

```text id="kvx0vs"
Cursor Here

↓

Predicted Gaze 120 px Ahead
```

---

## Gaze Confidence

| Score     | Meaning                  |
| --------- | ------------------------ |
| 0–0.25    | Uncertain gaze.          |
| 0.25–0.50 | Weak attention.          |
| 0.50–0.75 | Likely focus.            |
| 0.75–1.00 | Strong focus prediction. |

---

## Metadata

```ts id="0x4scy"
interface EyeGazePrediction {
  gazeCenter: ViewportPoint;
  confidence: number;
  predictionWindowMs: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Eye-gaze prediction is probabilistic and continuously updated.

---

# 18.6A.14 Visual Saliency Heatmap Generator

## Mission Statement

> **Generate a probability heatmap showing viewer attention intensity across the viewport.**

---

## Heatmap Architecture

```text id="qscyp2"
Viewport

↓

Feature Maps

↓

Weighted Fusion

↓

Attention Heatmap
```

---

## Heatmap Generation Pipeline

```text id="22qqwu"
Objects

↓

Attention Features

↓

Weighted Pixels

↓

Blur + Normalize

↓

Heatmap
```

---

## Heatmap Representation

```text id="dcwulr"
Low Attention

░░░░░░░░░

▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒▒

▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓

█████████

High Attention
```

---

## Heatmap Layers

| Layer         | Example               |
| ------------- | --------------------- |
| Motion        | Moving cursor.        |
| Text          | Headings.             |
| Contrast      | CTA button.           |
| Faces         | Webcam bubble.        |
| Semantic      | Important UI.         |
| Screen Change | Newly appeared modal. |

---

## Multi-Layer Fusion

```text id="dm3ek4"
Motion Heatmap

+

Text Heatmap

+

Cursor Heatmap

+

Semantic Heatmap

↓

Final Heatmap
```

---

## Heatmap Normalization

<math block value="HeatmapProbability=\\frac{PixelWeight}{\\sum PixelWeights}"/>

Every viewport heatmap sums to **1.0**.

---

## Metadata

```ts id="h1y70l"
interface SaliencyHeatmap {
  heatmapId: string;
  resolution: ViewportSize;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Heatmaps exist in viewport coordinates, never screen coordinates.

# 18.6A.15 Object Importance Scoring Runtime

| Minor     | 0.20–0.45 |

# 18.6A.19 Acceptance Principles

## Heatmap Tests

* Modal dominates heatmap.
* CTA highlighted.
* Decorative icons ignored.

### Eye-Gaze Tests

* Cursor look-ahead prediction.
* Reading direction prediction.
* Center bias prediction.

### Importance Tests

* Modal highest importance.
* Spinner important.
* Footer ignored.

### Hierarchy Tests

* Heading ranked primary.
* CTA secondary.
* Decorative icons peripheral.

### Fusion Tests

* Motion + cursor fusion.
* Text + hierarchy fusion.
* Mutation increases attention score.

---

# 18.6A.20 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 18.6A.1)

1. Visual Focus Runtime predicts viewer attention before camera planning.
2. Saliency Heatmaps represent normalized attention probability across the viewport.
3. Eye-Gaze Prediction estimates future viewer gaze using cursor, motion and reading direction.
4. Object Importance Scoring ranks UI elements using semantic, visual and interaction signals.
5. Visual Hierarchy Runtime reconstructs the UI's perceptual importance tree.
6. Attention Fusion Runtime combines cursor, motion, semantic and hierarchy signals into unified attention regions.
7. Heatmaps exist entirely in viewport coordinates for deterministic replay.
8. Attention scores are timeline metadata consumed by downstream AI systems.
9. Camera Planner never consumes raw cursor position directly; it consumes fused attention regions.
10. **Chapter 18.6A.1 establishes TryLipi's Visual Attention Brain—the AI system that predicts where viewers naturally look before Smart Zoom decides where the camera should move.**

# 18.6A.21 Dynamic Attention Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Viewer attention is dynamic. The saliency engine continuously redistributes attention as the interface changes over time.**

Static heatmaps are insufficient.

The viewer's attention constantly shifts because of:

* Motion.
* Cursor movement.
* Text reading.
* Color changes.
* Animations.
* Notifications.
* Scene transitions.

This chapter models **dynamic visual attention**.

---

## Static vs Dynamic Attention

| Static Attention | Dynamic Attention        |
| ---------------- | ------------------------ |
| Hero heading     | Cursor moving toward CTA |
| Logo             | Spinner begins rotating  |
| Button           | Progress bar filling     |
| Modal            | Notification sliding in  |
| Image            | Carousel auto-scroll     |

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime                 | Responsibility                        |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| Motion Saliency         | Attention caused by movement.         |
| Cursor Saliency         | Cursor-driven attention prediction.   |
| Text Saliency           | Reading behavior prediction.          |
| Contrast Saliency       | Color-driven attention.               |
| Multi-Object Runtime    | Multiple competing attention targets. |
| Temporal Fusion Runtime | Attention changes across time.        |

---

## Dynamic Attention Lifecycle

```text
Viewport

↓

Attention Sources

↓

Temporal Fusion

↓

Attention Redistribution

↓

Updated Heatmap
```

---

# 18.6A.22 Motion Saliency Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Moving objects naturally attract visual attention before static objects.**

Motion is one of the strongest biological attention cues.

---

## Motion Saliency Architecture

```text
Pixel Tracking Runtime

↓

Motion Feature Extractor

↓

Motion Saliency Runtime

↓

Heatmap Layer
```

---

## Motion Sources

| Motion Type       | Example        |
| ----------------- | -------------- |
| Cursor Motion     | Mouse movement |
| Object Motion     | Dragging card  |
| Scroll Motion     | Page scrolling |
| Animation Motion  | Spinner        |
| Playback Motion   | Video playing  |
| Background Motion | GIF            |

---

## Motion Pipeline

```text
Frame Sequence

↓

Optical Motion

↓

Velocity Map

↓

Motion Heatmap
```

---

## Motion Velocity Categories

| Velocity        | Attention Weight |
| --------------- | ---------------- |
| Static          | Very Low         |
| Slow Motion     | Medium           |
| Moderate Motion | High             |
| Fast Motion     | Very High        |
| Flick Motion    | Burst Attention  |

---

## Motion Persistence Runtime

Attention decays gradually after movement stops.

<math block value="Attention_t=Attention_0e^{-\\lambda t}"/>

---

## Motion Heatmap Contribution

Moving objects temporarily increase local saliency probability.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface MotionSaliencyState {
  motionVectorId: string;
  velocity: number;
  persistenceMs: number;
}
```

# 18.6A.25 Color & Contrast Saliency Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Visual contrast naturally attracts attention even without movement.**

## Contrast Runtime Architecture

## Contrast Features

## Contrast Calculation

<math block value="Contrast=\\frac{|L_1-L_2|}{L_{max}}"/>

Where L = luminance.

# 18.6A.27 Temporal Attention Fusion Runtime

## Motion Tests

* Drag path tracked.
* Scroll motion detected.

### Cursor Tests

* Hover attention.
* Click prediction.
* Drag prediction.

### Text Tests

* Reading progression.
* Heading priority.
* Code reading flow.

### Contrast Tests

### Fusion Tests

* Competing objects ranked.

---

# 18.6A.30 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 18.6A.2)

1. Motion Saliency Engine increases viewer attention for moving objects using temporal motion analysis.
2. Cursor Saliency Runtime predicts future attention based on trajectory, hover duration and interaction probability.
3. Text Saliency Engine models human reading behavior independently from cursor movement.
4. Color & Contrast Saliency Runtime boosts attention for visually dominant interface elements.
5. Multi-Object Attention Runtime resolves competing attention candidates into ranked attention clusters.
6. Temporal Attention Fusion Runtime smooths attention across consecutive frames using historical memory and decay.
7. Burst attention events receive temporary high priority without permanently affecting attention history.
8. Attention clusters become the primary inputs for Smart Zoom target selection.
9. Temporal smoothing prevents camera jitter during rapid UI changes.
10. **Chapter 18.6A.2 establishes TryLipi's Dynamic Attention Runtime — the AI system that continuously redistributes viewer attention across motion, cursor behavior, text reading, contrast changes and competing interface objects.**

# 18.6A.31 Camera Attention Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **The Visual Focus Engine does not move the camera. It tells the Camera Planner where the camera should look next.**

This is the final layer connecting visual attention with cinematic camera movement.

The previous chapters generated attention scores.

This chapter converts those scores into:

* Camera targets.
* Camera timing.
* Camera transitions.
* Camera confidence.
* Export-ready attention timelines.

---

## Attention vs Camera

### Attention Runtime

```text
Viewport

↓

Heatmap

↓

Attention Regions
```

### Camera Runtime

```text
Attention Regions

↓

Camera Planner

↓

Zoom

↓

Pan

↓

Export Timeline
```

Attention proposes.

Camera decides.

---

## Why Separate These Engines?

| Visual Focus Engine        | Camera Planner                 |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Predicts viewer attention. | Chooses camera path.           |
| Scores UI regions.         | Computes zoom/pan.             |
| Builds heatmaps.           | Generates animation curves.    |
| Doesn't know safe zones.   | Uses safe zones & constraints. |

This separation makes Smart Zoom modular.

---

## Responsibilities

| Runtime             | Responsibility                |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Attention Planner   | Choose camera candidates.     |
| Timeline Runtime    | Store attention history.      |
| Confidence Runtime  | Decide camera certainty.      |
| GPU Heatmap Runtime | Visualize attention maps.     |
| Export Runtime      | Serialize attention timeline. |

---

# 18.6A.32 AI Camera Attention Planner

## Mission Statement

> **Choose the most important viewport region that deserves camera attention right now.**

---

## Planner Architecture

```text
Attention Heatmap

↓

Candidate Extractor

↓

Priority Solver

↓

Camera Candidate Regions
```

---

## Candidate Generation Pipeline

```text
Heatmap

↓

Top Regions

↓

Constraint Filter

↓

Ranked Candidates
```

---

## Candidate Types

| Candidate          | Example        |
| ------------------ | -------------- |
| Primary Object     | CTA Button     |
| Reading Region     | Heading        |
| Motion Region      | Spinner        |
| Modal              | Dialog         |
| Cursor Destination | Upcoming click |

---

## Candidate Ranking

| Signal            | Weight |
| ----------------- | ------ |
| Attention Score   | 30%    |
| Importance Score  | 20%    |
| Scene Importance  | 20%    |
| Cursor Prediction | 15%    |
| Motion Prediction | 15%    |

---

## Top-K Attention Runtime

The planner keeps multiple future candidates.

```text
Rank 1 → CTA Button

Rank 2 → Heading

Rank 3 → Illustration
```

Camera transitions smoothly between them.

---

## Camera Target Metadata

```ts
interface CameraAttentionCandidate {
  candidateId: string;

  regionId: string;

  attentionScore: number;

  recommendedZoomLevel: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Attention Planner never produces camera animations directly.

# 18.6A.34 Focus Confidence Engine

| Motion Persistence   | High   |

| Text Reading         | Medium |

## Confidence Levels

| Score     | Meaning               |

| 0–0.25    | Ignore                |
| 0.25–0.50 | Peripheral            |
| 0.50–0.70 | Candidate             |
| 0.70–0.90 | Strong Camera Target  |
| 0.90–1.00 | Critical Focus Region |

Important objects remain camera candidates longer.

## Engineering Rules

Confidence influences camera timing, not object importance.

# 18.6A.39 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 18.6A.3)

1. AI Camera Attention Planner converts attention regions into ranked camera candidates.
2. Saliency Timeline Runtime serializes attention shifts into immutable timeline metadata.
3. Focus Confidence Engine measures certainty for camera target selection.
4. GPU Heatmap Renderer visualizes attention for debugging and editing.
5. Export Runtime consumes serialized saliency metadata instead of recomputing heatmaps.
6. Camera Planner receives ranked attention regions rather than raw heatmaps.
7. Attention sessions persist across reading, scrolling and interaction workflows.
8. Heatmaps remain deterministic across replay and export resolutions.
9. Saliency metadata becomes a first-class timeline alongside viewport, cursor and camera timelines.
10. **Chapter 18.6A completes TryLipi's Visual Focus / Saliency Engine — the AI system that predicts human attention and supplies cinematic camera targets for Smart Zoom, tutorials, thumbnails and AI-generated video editing.**

# 03.41 Window Tracking Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **TryLipi understands desktop applications as independent, living viewports instead of one giant screen.**

Unlike browser-only recorders, TryLipi records **desktop intelligence**.

The recording understands:

* Chrome window.
* VS Code.
* Cursor AI.
* Figma.
* Terminal.
* Notion.
* Slack.
* Discord.
* Electron applications.
* Native Windows applications.

Each application becomes its own tracked runtime object.

---

## Why Window Tracking Exists

### Traditional Recorder

```text id="fmnqut"
Entire Screen

↓

Video
```

Everything is flattened into pixels.

### TryLipi

```text id="x5wfwk"
Desktop

↓

Window Registry

↓

Tracked Windows

↓

Independent Viewports

↓

AI Camera
```

The desktop becomes a structured scene graph.

---

## Problems Solved

| Desktop Problem             | Window Engine Solution   |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Browser + VS Code recording | Independent windows.     |
| Switching applications      | Focus timeline.          |
| Floating windows            | Overlay windows tracked. |
| Resizing browser            | Geometry timeline.       |
| Window overlaps             | Z-order runtime.         |
| Electron apps               | Native window tracking.  |

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime            | Responsibility              |
| ------------------ | --------------------------- |
| Window Registry    | Track every visible window. |
| Geometry Runtime   | Window size and position.   |
| Focus Runtime      | Active window detection.    |
| Z-Order Runtime    | Window stacking order.      |
| Coordinate Runtime | Desktop coordinate system.  |
| Timeline Runtime   | Window history.             |

---

## Design Principles

1. Windows are first-class runtime objects.
2. Independent geometry timelines.
3. Resolution independent.
4. Multi-window aware.
5. Focus-aware.
6. Replay deterministic.
7. Multi-monitor compatible.

---

## Window Lifecycle

```text id="zpv0ks"
Window Created

↓

Registered

↓

Focused

↓

Moved / Resized

↓

Hidden / Closed

↓

Timeline Serialized
```

Every state transition becomes timeline metadata.

---

# 03.4B Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 03.4.1)

1. Window Registry Runtime assigns stable identities to every desktop application during recording.
2. Window Geometry Engine tracks desktop position, size, visibility and window state continuously.
3. Active Window Detection Runtime determines which application owns interaction at any moment.
4. Focus Timeline Runtime serializes desktop focus sessions into immutable timeline metadata.
5. Z-Order Runtime reconstructs visual stacking order independently from pixel capture.
6. Desktop Coordinate Space Runtime normalizes coordinates before viewport projection.
7. Window geometry is resolution-independent and replay deterministic.
8. Cursor, viewport and camera runtimes always reference active window metadata.
9. Hidden or minimized windows remain in history but stop contributing to camera planning.
10. **Chapter 03.4.1 establishes TryLipi's Desktop Window Intelligence Runtime—the foundation for recording Chrome, VS Code, Cursor IDE, Figma, Notion and every desktop application as structured, replayable windows instead of raw pixels.**

# 03.4.21 Dynamic Window Geometry Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Desktop windows are constantly changing shape, size, position, and hierarchy. TryLipi tracks every transformation as structured timeline events.**

Unlike browser recording, desktop recording must understand:

* Window resizing.
* Dragging windows.
* Snap Assist.
* Floating tool palettes.
* Electron overlays.
* Dialog windows.
* Picture-in-picture windows.
* System popups.

Every geometry change becomes deterministic metadata.

---

## Why Dynamic Window Tracking Matters

### Traditional Screen Recorder

```text
Resize Browser

↓

Pixels Stretch

↓

Video Recorded
```

### TryLipi Runtime

```text
Resize Browser

↓

Geometry Timeline

↓

Viewport Recomputed

↓

Camera Reframed
```

The camera understands **layout changes**, not just stretched pixels.

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime          | Responsibility                      |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Resize Runtime   | Detect geometry changes.            |
| Move Runtime     | Track desktop translation.          |
| Floating Runtime | Detect detached tool windows.       |
| Modal Runtime    | Understand temporary dialogs.       |
| Electron Runtime | Track Electron application windows. |
| Snap Runtime     | Detect Windows Snap Assist layouts. |
| Overlay Runtime  | Detect always-on-top overlays.      |

---

## Dynamic Window Lifecycle

```text
Window Visible

↓

Move

↓

Resize

↓

Snap

↓

Floating Overlay

↓

Modal Opens
```

Every transition updates the Window Timeline.

---

# 03.4.22 Window Resize Detection Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Detect every window dimension change without relying on pixel stretching.**

---

## Resize Detection Architecture

```text
Window Geometry

↓

Resize Observer

↓

Dimension Delta Runtime

↓

Geometry Timeline
```

---

## Resize Detection Pipeline

```text
Width Changed

↓

Height Changed

↓

Aspect Ratio Updated

↓

Viewport Projection Updated
```

---

## Resize Event Types

| Resize Type   | Example             |
| ------------- | ------------------- |
| Manual Resize | Dragging edge.      |
| Maximize      | Full desktop.       |
| Restore Down  | Exit maximize.      |
| Snap Resize   | Half-screen layout. |
| DPI Resize    | Monitor scaling.    |

---

## Resize Timeline Example

```text
Frame 120

1600×900

↓

Frame 160

1700×950

↓

Frame 240

1920×1080
```

---

## Resize Delta Metadata

```ts
interface WindowResizeEvent {
  previousSize: DesktopSize;
  newSize: DesktopSize;
  resizeReason: ResizeReason;
}
```

---

## Aspect Ratio Runtime

Detects transitions:

| Previous    | New         |
| ----------- | ----------- |
| 16:9        | 4:3         |
| 16:9        | Portrait    |
| Portrait    | Landscape   |
| Half Screen | Full Screen |

---

## Smart Zoom Reaction

| Resize          | Camera Behavior          |
| --------------- | ------------------------ |
| Small Resize    | Smooth reframing.        |
| Maximize        | Reset viewport camera.   |
| Snap Resize     | Horizontal reframe.      |
| Portrait Resize | Vertical camera padding. |

---

## Engineering Rules

Resize detection emits geometry updates before viewport reconstruction.

---

# 03.4.23 Window Move Detection Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Track desktop window translation independently from viewport scrolling.**

---

## Move Runtime Architecture

```text
Window Geometry

↓

Position Delta Runtime

↓

Desktop Timeline

↓

Camera Runtime
```

---

## Move Detection Pipeline

```text
Frame 210

X=200

↓

Frame 220

X=310

↓

Move Event Generated
```

---

| Move Type         | Example                 |
| ----------------- | ----------------------- |

| Snap Move         | Snap Assist reposition. |
| Restore Move      | Window restored.        |
| Monitor Move      | Between displays.       |
| Programmatic Move | OS animation.           |

---

## Move Velocity Runtime

Calculates desktop translation velocity.

<math block value="Velocity=\\frac{Position_{new}-Position_{old}}{FrameDelta}"/>

---

## Cursor-to-Window Sync

When dragging:

* Cursor owns window.
* Window trajectory follows cursor.
* Camera predicts destination.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface WindowMoveEvent {
  startPosition: DesktopPoint;
  endPosition: DesktopPoint;
  moveVelocity: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Window translation is independent from viewport movement inside the window.

# 03.4.31 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 03.4.2)

1. Window Resize Detection Runtime tracks geometry changes independently from pixel stretching.
2. Window Move Detection Runtime serializes desktop translation without confusing it with viewport scrolling.
3. Floating Window Runtime recognizes detached utility windows and parent-child relationships.
4. Modal Window Runtime creates temporary interaction scenes with focus trapping.
5. Electron Application Runtime combines desktop geometry with Chromium viewport intelligence.
6. Windows Snap Layout Runtime detects reusable workspace layouts and informs Smart Zoom framing.
7. Overlay Window Intelligence tracks transient windows separately from primary application focus.
8. Snap layouts become reusable workspace metadata for replay and export.
9. Dynamic window geometry updates always occur before viewport reconstruction.
10. **Chapter 03.4.2 establishes TryLipi's Dynamic Desktop Window Runtime — enabling intelligent recording of floating tools, dialogs, Electron applications, Snap Assist layouts and transient overlays across Windows desktop workflows.**

# 03.4.31 Desktop Replay Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **A desktop recording is not a flat video — it is a replayable operating system timeline.**

TryLipi stores enough metadata to recreate:

* Window creation.
* Focus switching.
* Window movement.
* Resize history.
* Overlay appearance.
* Modal sessions.
* Snap layouts.
* Camera context.

This enables **non-destructive editing**.

---

## Traditional Replay vs TryLipi Replay

### Traditional Recorder

```text
Recorded Video

↓

Seek Frame 1200

↓

Decode Pixels
```

### TryLipi

```text
Window Timeline

↓

Replay Runtime

↓

Reconstruct Desktop State

↓

Camera + Cursor + Viewport
```

The desktop is rebuilt from structured metadata.

---

## Replay Responsibilities

| Runtime               | Responsibility                          |
| --------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Window Replay Runtime | Rebuild desktop window state.           |
| Camera Switch Runtime | Decide cross-window camera transitions. |
| GPU Window Runtime    | Render desktop composition.             |
| Timeline Serializer   | Store immutable window history.         |
| Export Runtime        | Produce identical output.               |

---

## Replay Lifecycle

```text
Window Timeline

↓

Seek Timestamp

↓

Restore Windows

↓

Restore Camera

↓

Render Frame
```

Every exported frame is deterministic.

---

# 03.4.32 Window Replay Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Reconstruct the complete desktop workspace at any frame without replaying the recording from the beginning.**

---

## Replay Architecture

```text
Window Timeline

↓

Replay State Builder

↓

Desktop Workspace

↓

Viewport Runtime
```

---

## Replay Pipeline

```text
Seek Frame 5400

↓

Load Active Windows

↓

Load Geometry

↓

Load Focus

↓

Load Z-Order

↓

Render Workspace
```

---

## Replay Reconstruction

Recreates:

| State            | Restored |
| ---------------- | -------- |
| Active windows   | ✅        |
| Hidden windows   | ✅        |
| Floating windows | ✅        |
| Modals           | ✅        |
| Snap layouts     | ✅        |
| Cursor ownership | ✅        |

---

## Instant Seeking Runtime

Jump directly to any timestamp.

No frame-by-frame replay required.

---

## Replay Metadata

```ts
interface WindowReplayState {
  replayFrame: number;

  activeWindowIds: string[];

  focusedWindowId: string;
}
```

---

## Historical Reconstruction

Example timeline:

```text
00:00 Chrome

↓

00:18 VS Code

↓

00:42 Cursor IDE

↓

01:10 Chrome
```

Seeking to **00:42** restores Cursor IDE instantly.

---

## Engineering Rules

Replay Runtime never reruns detection algorithms.

It only consumes serialized metadata.

---

# 03.4.33 Smart Camera Window Switching Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Camera transitions between desktop applications should feel like a human editor switching focus, not a hard cut.**

---

## Camera Switching Architecture

```text
Window Timeline

↓

Attention Planner

↓

Window Transition Solver

↓

Camera Timeline
```

---

## Window Switch Categories

| Transition           | Camera Behavior   |
| -------------------- | ----------------- |
| Chrome → VS Code     | Smooth pan.       |
| VS Code → Terminal   | Small pan + zoom. |
| Chrome → Modal       | Zoom in.          |
| Chrome → DevTools    | Horizontal shift. |
| Figma → Color Picker | Context zoom.     |

---

## Transition Pipeline

```text
Focused Window Changed

↓

Attention Region Computed

↓

Camera Target Generated

↓

Transition Animation
```

---

## Transition Curves

| Curve       | Use Case                 |
| ----------- | ------------------------ |
| Ease In-Out | Most switches.           |
| Spring      | Small floating windows.  |
| Fast Linear | Alt+Tab rapid switching. |
| Hold + Zoom | Modal dialogs.           |

---

## Context Preservation Runtime

Previous window remains visible briefly.

```text
Chrome

↓

Pan

↓

VS Code
```

Avoids disorienting cuts.

---

## Transition Metadata

```ts
interface WindowCameraTransition {
  fromWindowId: string;

  toWindowId: string;

  transitionType: CameraTransitionType;
}
```

---

## Camera Hold Rules

Camera pauses if:

* Loading state active.
* Drag operation active.
* Progress bar active.
* Video playback active.

---

## Engineering Rules

Camera switching consumes Attention Timeline and Window Timeline simultaneously.

---

# 03.4.34 GPU Window Rendering Pipeline

## Mission Statement

> **Render every desktop window as an independent GPU layer before compositing the final frame.**

---

## GPU Rendering Architecture

```text
Window Timeline

↓

Window Layer Builder

↓

GPU Texture Cache

↓

Compositor

↓

Final Frame
```

---

## Layer Stack

```text
Overlay Layer

Floating Layer

Primary Window Layer

Background Window Layer

Desktop Wallpaper Layer
```

Every window has its own GPU texture.

---

## Rendering Pipeline

```text
Window Geometry

↓

Viewport Crop

↓

Texture Upload

↓

Transform

↓

Composite
```

---

## Dirty Region Rendering

Only changed windows redraw.

| Window         | Re-render? |
| -------------- | ---------- |
| Chrome changed | Yes        |
| VS Code idle   | No         |
| Wallpaper      | Cached     |

---

## GPU Optimizations

* Texture atlas cache.
* Tile invalidation.
* Dirty rectangle updates.
* Multi-layer compositing.
* Hardware scaling.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface WindowRenderTexture {
  windowId: string;

  textureId: string;

  isDirty: boolean;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

GPU renderer never re-renders unchanged windows.

---

```text
↓

↓
```

| Focus Changed       | ✅          |
| Geometry Changed    | ✅          |
| Z-Order Changed     | ✅          |
| Overlay Appeared    | ✅          |
| Modal Opened        | ✅          |
| Snap Layout Changed | ✅          |

```text
Frame 240

Chrome Maximized

Frame 560

Frame 740

Frame 900

Chrome Restored
```

---

## Compression Runtime

Repeated geometry updates compress into sessions.

---

## Timeline Metadata

```ts
interface SerializedWindowTimeline {
  timelineVersion: number;

  events: WindowTimelineEvent[];
}
```

---

## Deterministic Replay Guarantee

Timeline always reconstructs identical desktop state.

---

## Engineering Rules

Timeline metadata is append-only.

---

# 03.4.39 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 03.4.3)

1. Window Replay Engine reconstructs desktop state entirely from serialized metadata.
2. Smart Camera Window Switching Runtime generates cinematic transitions between desktop applications.
3. GPU Window Rendering Pipeline renders each application as an independent compositing layer.
4. Window Timeline Serialization Runtime stores immutable desktop events for deterministic replay.
5. Export Runtime consumes replay metadata instead of recomputing desktop state.
6. Active window focus determines primary attention ownership.
7. Floating windows and overlays remain independent GPU layers.
8. Snap layouts become reusable workspace compositions.
9. Replay seeking restores desktop state instantly without frame iteration.
10. **Chapter 03.4 completes TryLipi's Desktop Window Tracking Engine — enabling browser-first and Windows desktop recordings with semantic application awareness, replayable workspaces, AI camera transitions, and deterministic exports.**

# 08C.11 Visual Anchor Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **A Visual Anchor is a UI landmark that the camera remembers, even if the screen scrolls, changes layout, or temporarily disappears.**

This is one of TryLipi's biggest differentiators.

Unlike Cursorful or Screen Studio, TryLipi doesn't only follow the cursor.

It remembers **what the cursor interacted with**.

---

## What is a Visual Anchor?

A Visual Anchor is a persistent identity attached to an interface element.

Examples include:

* "Generate Script" button.
* Search input.
* Pricing card.
* Hero title.
* Sidebar icon.
* Chat composer.
* Upload button.
* Progress indicator.
* Code block.
* AI response bubble.

Even if that element moves...

The camera still knows it's the same object.

---

## Cursor Tracking vs Visual Anchors

### Cursor Tracking

```text id="rdr7p3"
Cursor

↓

Moves Away

↓

Lost
```

### Visual Anchors

```text id="s4ofw8"
Button Clicked

↓

Anchor Created

↓

Page Scrolls

↓

Anchor Reidentified
```

The camera follows the button, not the cursor.

---

## Why This Engine Exists

Without anchors:

| Problem           | Result                |
| ----------------- | --------------------- |
| Scroll page       | Camera loses object.  |
| Responsive layout | Zoom jumps.           |
| Modal closes      | Camera resets.        |
| Infinite feed     | Wrong object tracked. |

With anchors:

* Stable camera.
* Persistent focus.
* Intelligent replay.
* Better AI tutorials.

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime            | Responsibility                    |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------- |
| Landmark Detector  | Discover anchor candidates.       |
| Anchor Registry    | Persistent anchor identities.     |
| Landmark Graph     | Relationships between anchors.    |
| Confidence Runtime | Confidence over time.             |
| Scroll Runtime     | Maintain anchors while scrolling. |
| Timeline Runtime   | Anchor lifecycle history.         |

---

## Design Principles

1. Anchors survive scrolling.
2. Anchors survive DOM changes.
3. Anchors survive resizing.
4. Anchors survive viewport movement.
5. Anchors have stable identities.
6. Anchors are semantic.
7. Replay deterministic.

---

## Anchor Lifecycle

```text id="ukztvk"
UI Element Visible

↓

Anchor Created

↓

Tracked Across Frames

↓

Scrolled

↓

Reidentified

↓

Anchor Retained
```

---

# 08C.18 Acceptance Principles

## Landmark Tests

* CTA becomes anchor.
* Hero heading becomes anchor.
* Decorative icon ignored.

### Registry Tests

* Stable IDs.
* Visibility updates.
* Parent changes tracked.

### Graph Tests

* Parent-child edges.
* Spatial edges.
* Sequential edges.

### Confidence Tests

* DOM recovery.
* Pixel recovery.
* Scroll recovery.

### Scroll Tests

* Scroll away.
* Scroll back.
* Anchor recovered with high confidence.

---

# 08C.19 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 08C.1)

1. Persistent Landmark Detection Engine identifies semantically important UI elements as long-lived anchors.
2. Anchor Registry Runtime assigns immutable anchor identities for the duration of a recording session.
3. UI Landmark Graph Runtime stores semantic and spatial relationships between anchors.
4. Anchor Confidence Engine continuously evaluates whether a detected object matches an existing anchor.
5. Scroll-Resistant Anchoring Runtime preserves anchor identity even when objects leave the viewport.
6. Anchors are viewport-independent semantic objects, not pixel coordinates.
7. Anchor recovery combines DOM identity, pixel similarity and graph relationships.
8. Landmark graphs provide contextual information for Smart Zoom and Tutorial Generation.
9. Anchors survive viewport scrolling until confidence drops below recovery threshold.
10. **Chapter 08C.1 establishes TryLipi's Persistent Visual Anchor Runtime — enabling Smart Zoom to remember important UI landmarks across scrolling, navigation and interface changes instead of following only the cursor.**

# 08C.21 Anchor Persistence Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **An anchor should survive almost every UI transformation that a creator performs during recording.**

A creator may:

* Scroll hundreds of pixels.
* Collapse a sidebar.
* Resize the browser.
* Switch between desktop and mobile layouts.
* Open a modal.
* Refresh content.
* Change themes.

The **Visual Anchor Engine remembers the same logical object** across all of these transformations.

---

## Why Persistence Matters

### Without Persistence

```text
Click "Generate Script"

↓

Scroll Down

↓

Anchor Lost

↓

Camera Starts Following Cursor
```

### With Persistence

```text
Click "Generate Script"

↓

Anchor Created

↓

Scroll Down

↓

Anchor Stored In Memory

↓

Scroll Back

↓

Anchor Instantly Recovered
```

The recording remains cinematic.

---

## Persistence Goals

| Scenario          | Expected Behavior        |
| ----------------- | ------------------------ |
| Vertical scroll   | Anchor recovered.        |
| Horizontal scroll | Anchor recovered.        |
| DOM rerender      | Same anchor identity.    |
| Lazy loading      | Anchor relocated.        |
| Responsive layout | Anchor projected.        |
| Browser resize    | Anchor geometry updated. |

---

## Persistence Layers

```text
Anchor Identity

↓

Anchor Memory

↓

Anchor Projection

↓

Anchor Recovery

↓

Anchor Confidence
```

---

## Runtime Responsibilities

| Runtime            | Responsibility             |
| ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| State Machine      | Anchor lifecycle.          |
| Memory Runtime     | Hidden anchor persistence. |
| Recovery Runtime   | Re-identification.         |
| Projection Runtime | Predict future position.   |
| Timeline Runtime   | Persistence history.       |

---

# 08C.22 Persistent Anchor State Machine

## Mission Statement

> **Every anchor follows a deterministic lifecycle regardless of viewport visibility.**

---

## State Machine Architecture

```text
Anchor Candidate

↓

Active

↓

Hidden

↓

Projected

↓

Recovered

↓

Archived
```

---

## Anchor States

| State     | Description                 |
| --------- | --------------------------- |
| Candidate | Newly detected landmark.    |
| Active    | Visible and tracked.        |
| Hidden    | Outside viewport.           |
| Projected | Future position predicted.  |
| Recovered | Successfully matched again. |
| Archived  | Permanently removed.        |

---

## Lifecycle Example

```text
Button Visible

↓

Scroll Down

↓

Hidden

↓

Projection Active

↓

Scroll Up

↓

Recovered
```

---

## Hidden State Runtime

Hidden anchors continue updating:

* Expected position.
* Parent relationship.
* Neighbor anchors.
* Scroll delta.

---

## Projection Timeout

| Timeout | Behavior           |
| ------- | ------------------ |
| Short   | Keep active.       |
| Medium  | Lower confidence.  |
| Long    | Archive candidate. |

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface AnchorLifecycleState {
  anchorId: string;
  lifecycleState: AnchorLifecycle;
  hiddenDurationFrames: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Hidden anchors remain part of camera planning until archived.

---

# 08C.23 Scroll Recovery Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Recover anchors instantly after scrolling without scanning the entire viewport.**

---

## Scroll Recovery Architecture

```text
Viewport Scroll

↓

Scroll Delta Runtime

↓

Predicted Anchor Position

↓

Anchor Matcher

↓

Recovered Anchor
```

---

## Recovery Pipeline

```text
Anchor Hidden

↓

Store Scroll Offset

↓

User Scrolls

↓

Predict Position

↓

Search Nearby Region

↓

Recovered
```

---

## Prediction Window

Instead of scanning the full screen:

```text
Predicted Area

████████

████████

████████
```

Only nearby regions are searched.

---

## Recovery Signals

| Signal            | Weight |
| ----------------- | ------ |
| Scroll Offset     | High   |
| DOM Path          | High   |
| Pixel Fingerprint | High   |
| Landmark Graph    | Medium |
| Saliency History  | Medium |

---

## Scroll Memory Buffer

Stores historical viewport offsets.

```ts
interface ScrollAnchorBuffer {
  anchorId: string;
  viewportOffsetHistory: number[];
}
```

---

## Infinite Scroll Recovery

Supports feeds like:

* Instagram.
* Twitter/X.
* Reddit.
* LinkedIn.
* ChatGPT conversations.

Anchors survive virtualized scrolling.

---

## Engineering Rules

Recovery search begins near predicted coordinates before expanding outward.

---

# 08C.24 DOM Mutation Recovery Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Recover anchors after React, Vue, Next.js or Electron rerender the DOM.**

---

## DOM Recovery Architecture

```text
DOM Mutation

↓

Affected Elements

↓

↓

```

---

## DOM Mutation Types

| Mutation           | Recovery                   |
| ------------------ | -------------------------- |
| Node recreated     | Preserve anchor ID.        |
| Attributes changed | Update metadata.           |
| Parent changed     | Rebuild graph edge.        |
| Text changed       | Update fingerprint.        |
| Style changed      | Ignore if identity stable. |

---

## React Example

```text
Button Destroyed

↓

Button Recreated

↓

Same Semantic Button

↓

Anchor Preserved
```

---

## Fingerprint Components

| Fingerprint  | Example               |
| ------------ | --------------------- |
| DOM Path     | Stable hierarchy.     |
| Text         | "Generate Script".    |
| Role         | Button.               |
| Icon         | Wand icon.            |
| Bounding Box | Approximate geometry. |

---

## DOM Similarity Runtime

<math block value="Similarity=0.4DOM+0.3Text+0.2Role+0.1Geometry"/>

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface DOMRecoveryState {
  previousDOMFingerprint: string;
  newDOMFingerprint: string;
  similarityScore: number;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Anchor identity survives DOM recreation if semantic similarity exceeds threshold.

| Mobile → Desktop | Navigation expands.     |

```text
↓

↓

↓

```



---

# 08C.26 Window Resize Recovery Runtime

## Mission Statement

> **Recover anchors after browser or application window resizing.**

---

## Resize Recovery Architecture

```text
Window Resize

↓

Viewport Transform

↓

Anchor Projection

↓

Recovered Geometry
```

---

## Resize Categories

| Resize          | Recovery                     |
| --------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Width increase  | Horizontal projection.       |
| Width decrease  | Compression projection.      |
| Height increase | Vertical projection.         |
| Maximize        | Full viewport recalculation. |
| Snap Layout     | Half-screen projection.      |

---

## Geometry Transformation

<math block value="ProjectedX=OldX\\times\\frac{NewWidth}{OldWidth}"/>

---

## Smart Padding Runtime

Camera keeps anchor inside safe margins after resize.

---

## Metadata

```ts
interface ResizeAnchorState {
  previousViewport: ViewportSize;
  newViewport: ViewportSize;
}
```

---

## Engineering Rules

Resize recovery executes before camera path recomputation.

# 08C.29 Acceptance Principles

## Scroll Tests

* Scroll away.
* Scroll back.
* Infinite scroll recovery.

### DOM Tests

* React rerender.
* Vue rerender.
* Parent changed.
* Attribute changed.

### Responsive Tests

* Desktop → Mobile.
* Mobile → Desktop.
* Tablet breakpoint.

### Resize Tests

* Snap Assist resize.
* Browser maximize.
* Half-screen layout.

### Viewport Tests

* Nested scroll container.
* iframe recovery.
* Canvas viewport projection.

---

# 08C.30 Canonical Engineering Rules (Part 08C.2)

1. Persistent Anchor State Machine preserves anchor identity across visibility changes.
2. Scroll Recovery Runtime predicts anchor locations using viewport offset history before searching pixels.
3. DOM Mutation Recovery Runtime survives component rerenders by matching semantic fingerprints.
4. Responsive Layout Runtime projects anchors across desktop, tablet and mobile breakpoints.
5. Window Resize Recovery Runtime transforms anchor geometry before camera recalculation.
6. Cross-Viewport Projection Runtime maps anchors between nested viewport coordinate systems.
7. Hidden anchors retain timeline history until archived by lifecycle rules.
8. Anchor recovery combines DOM similarity, pixel similarity and landmark graph relationships.
9. Responsive projection is semantic-first rather than pixel-first.
10. **Chapter 08C.2 establishes TryLipi's Anchor Persistence Runtime — enabling Smart Zoom to keep following the same logical UI element through scrolling, rerenders, responsive layouts, window resizing and nested viewports.**

# 08C.31 Anchor Timeline Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Every important UI landmark becomes part of a replayable timeline that the AI camera can revisit, prioritize and transition between.**

A Visual Anchor is no longer just an object.

It becomes a **storytelling waypoint**.

Examples:

* "Start Recording" button.
* Search bar.
* "Generate Script" CTA.
* AI output.
* Export button.

The camera knows **when each anchor became important**, **how long it stayed important**, and **when to transition away**.

---

## Anchor Timeline vs Cursor Timeline

| Cursor Timeline            | Anchor Timeline              |
| -------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| Physical pointer movement. | Semantic UI landmarks.       |
| Exists every frame.        | Exists only when meaningful. |
| Short-lived.               | Persistent across scenes.    |
| Can leave viewport.        | Can be recovered later.      |

---

## Timeline Responsibilities

| Runtime             | Responsibility              |
| ------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Anchor Timeline     | History of anchor states.   |
| Importance Timeline | Priority over time.         |
| Camera Planner      | Uses anchor history.        |
| Replay Runtime      | Restores anchor sessions.   |
| Export Runtime      | Serializes anchor metadata. |

---

## Timeline Lifecycle

```text id="c1i7g3"
Anchor Created

↓

Anchor Focused

↓

Anchor Hidden

↓

Anchor Recovered

↓

Anchor Archived
```

Each phase is serialized.

---

# 08C.32 Anchor Timeline Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Serialize anchor lifecycle into immutable replayable timeline events.**

---

## Timeline Architecture

```text id="ckfhmq"
Anchor Registry

↓

Timeline Builder

↓

Anchor Timeline

↓

Replay Runtime
```

---

## Timeline Event Types

| Event            | Description              |
| ---------------- | ------------------------ |
| Anchor Created   | First appearance.        |
| Anchor Focused   | Viewer attention begins. |
| Anchor Updated   | Geometry changed.        |
| Anchor Hidden    | Leaves viewport.         |
| Anchor Recovered | Returns.                 |
| Anchor Destroyed | Permanently removed.     |

---

## Timeline Example

```text id="kylqrz"
00:01 Hero Heading

↓

00:05 CTA Button

↓

00:12 AI Response

↓

00:18 Export Button

↓

00:26 CTA Hidden

↓

00:40 CTA Recovered
```

---

## Timeline Session Runtime

Nearby focus events merge into one attention session.

---

## Timeline Metadata

```ts id="ywwphk"
interface AnchorTimelineEvent {
  anchorId: string;

  eventType: AnchorTimelineEventType;

  timestampMs: number;
}
```

---

## Timeline Compression

Continuous anchor visibility becomes one timeline segment.

---

## Engineering Rules

Anchor Timeline is append-only and replay deterministic.

---

9. Tutorial generation and thumbnail selection reuse persistent anchor metadata.
10. **Chapter 08C completes TryLipi's Visual Anchor Engine — the persistent semantic landmark system that makes Smart Zoom remember interface objects through scrolling, layout changes, window resizing and replay.**

# 09.4.11 Camera Constraint Philosophy

## Mission Statement

> **Smart Zoom is only allowed to move the camera if the resulting frame is visually valid.**

The Camera Constraint Solver is the **last decision layer** before camera motion.

Its job is to prevent ugly framing.

Examples:

* Cropping a button.
* Cutting off text.
* Zooming into a facecam.
* Hiding subtitles.
* Leaving excessive empty space.
* Cropping code editor line numbers.
* Cropping browser tabs unintentionally.

---

## Why This Engine Exists

### AI Without Constraints

```text id="kl4a0e"
Target Found

↓

Zoom

↓

Button Cut Off
```

### AI With Constraints

```text id="f1lpwz"
Target Found

↓

Constraint Solver

↓

Camera Reframed

↓

Entire CTA Visible
```

---

## Constraint Responsibilities

| Runtime            | Responsibility                    |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------- |
| Safe Framing       | Maintain padding around targets.  |
| Boundary Solver    | Keep camera inside viewport.      |
| Overlay Solver     | Avoid facecam and captions.       |
| Composition Solver | Frame multiple objects correctly. |
| Timeline Solver    | Apply constraints over time.      |

---

## Camera Decision Pipeline

```text id="z6zwuw"
Attention Region

↓

Anchor Planner

↓

Constraint Solver

↓

Camera Path

↓

Renderer
```

The constraint solver can modify camera targets.

---

## Constraint Principles

1. Never crop important UI.
2. Preserve readability.
3. Preserve cinematic margins.
4. Avoid overlays.
5. Maintain context.
6. Respect export aspect ratio.
7. Smooth transitions.

---

# 09.4.12 Safe Framing Engine

## Mission Statement

> **Every camera frame must include enough visual breathing room around important content.**

---

## Safe Framing Architecture

```text id="g0l6np"

↓

Padding Runtime

↓

Safe Frame

↓

Camera Crop
```

---

## Safe Frame Concept

### Raw Target

```text id="qccs8m"
██████
Target
██████
```

### Safe Frame

```text id="wbyyfv"
□□□□□□□□□□

██ Target ██

□□□□□□□□□□
```

Padding protects readability.

---

## Safe Padding Types

| Padding | Use                     |
| ------- | ----------------------- |
| Global  | Entire camera frame.    |
| Anchor  | Around selected object. |
| Text    | Reading padding.        |
| Face    | Webcam padding.         |
| Caption | Subtitle padding.       |

---

## Default Safe Margins

| Export | Margin |
| ------ | ------ |
| 16:9   | 6–8%   |
| 9:16   | 8–12%  |
| 1:1    | 7%     |
| 4:5    | 8–10%  |

---

## Adaptive Padding Runtime

Padding grows for:

* Dense code.
* Paragraphs.
* Tables.
* Dashboards.
* Forms.

Padding shrinks for isolated buttons.
